en: The Source of the Vinaya School (with the General Table of Contents for the Ten Gates and Brief Explanations for Each Gate), Volume One (Ending with the Original Teachings).
Compiled reverently by the monk Shouyi, Dharma-heir of Mount Ri in Taizhou.
Gate One: The Original Teachings of Various Texts.
I said: "The teachings that respond to capacities differ across the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka), yet the fundamental intent they convey is solely devoted to the Way.
The present text, in its original teaching, relies exclusively upon the Vinaya Piṭaka. However, since the Vinaya arises from specific events, these events vary and their underlying meanings differ.

Some provisions concern prohibitions and natures; some involve permissions, restrictions, or allowances; some rely on the four modes of deportment, while others depend on the four requisites; some distinguish themselves from non-Buddhist paths, while others address [specific circumstances]."

There are four gates; though they differ in breadth and brevity, their reception of the *svacchanda* (formal permission) is distinct. Although the specific circumstances upon which they rely vary, there is nothing that does not serve the Way.
If one considers their provisional intent, it is as the Vinaya states: "To subdue the three poisons and to seek the four fruits, the training in increased precepts (*adhiśīla*) is established."
It is so. If one investigates the Tathāgata’s original intent for appearing in the world, it is surely to cause all sentient beings to ascend together to the precious abode.

This is especially true since the *Lotus Sūtra* opened the assembly and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* supported the discourse, pointing out that the partial is the perfect (pointing out that the coarse is the subtle and resolving the Dharma of the Śrāvakas).
These are the kings among sūtras. Thus we know that the Vinaya Piṭaka is itself the One Buddha Vehicle; its ultimate destination is nothing other than the Single Reality. Therefore...

The lofty aspiration of our patriarch for the propagation of the Vinaya is the ultimate destination and core purpose of this school’s original teachings. The *Yuanwen* (Complete Text) provides the following citation, wherein the wondrous meaning is clearly revealed.
Second, the various texts on the gate of contemplating the dharmas.
I said: That those who study the Vinaya must practice contemplation is indeed based on a fundamental principle.

According to the Vinaya texts, the Buddha ordained that bhikṣus maintain their dignified deportment—whether regarding robes, medicine, food, drink, speech, silence, movement, or stillness—and always remain single-mindedly mindful, contemplating the removal of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
To violate this constitutes an offense. The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: "For a bhikṣu of sharp faculties, at every mouthful of food..."
When putting on a robe, one should form the thought as one puts it on; when entering a room, one should form the thought as one enters.

For those of dull faculties, they should form a single thought upon first obtaining food or clothing. Furthermore, all the precepts that enjoin the practice of contemplation as an antidote are none other than means for dispelling attachment.
Furthermore, throughout the extensive Vinaya texts, the phenomena, principles, and contemplative practices elucidated therein all belong to the provisional and the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Therefore, our ancestor Nanshan was able to exhaustively investigate the Buddha’s intention and profoundly accorded with the spirit of the Great Assembly (Mahāyāna). He established the wondrous contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) as a divine method for harmonious guidance.

As shown in the commentaries (*śāstra*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*), he demonstrated that for those first entering the Path, *vijñapti-mātra* is the very foundation of the monastic life, and he caused them to...

From the very first thought, one knows the destination to which one returns. To cause the recipient to give rise to the highest grade of resolve, the texts concerning the realization that objects are mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), as well as the sections on receiving the essence [of the precepts], following the practice, and repenting of transgressions, all take wondrous contemplation as their essential pivot.

The intention is such that every single reception and every single compliance is nothing other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); every single cessation and every single action is entirely True Suchness (*tathatā*); every single opening and every single prohibition is likewise so.

This is precisely the Supreme Vehicle. Whether light or heavy, all things return to the eternally abiding. Thus we know that our Patriarch’s propagation of the Vinaya was entirely centered upon wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, he composed the *Gujingyi* (Ritual of Reverent Homage), wherein every chapter and every matter clarifies the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*).
Moreover, for his disciple Cirin, he wrote the thirty chapters of the *Jingxin guan* (Contemplation of the Pure Mind), which exclusively discusses Chan contemplation; its words are most [profound].
Indeed! Were it not for the accumulation of study within our school, how could one know its profundity?
Regarding the third section, the "Gate of Mind and Objects" in the *Sanwenzhijinjing*:
this is the passage concerning the object of the aspiration for awakening (*cittotpāda*) within the ritual for receiving the precepts. According to the Vinaya and the Śāstras, the mind...

There are only the six consciousnesses, and their objects are limited to the six realms of ordinary beings. Even if one speaks of "predominance," it still belongs to the provisional vehicles (*upāyayāna*).
My Patriarch’s commentaries rely upon the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*niṣpanna-svabhāva*): they inspire the superior grade of mind to take the Dharma-realm as its object.

This is achieved by employing the wondrous contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), whereby one realizes that mind and objects are of one suchness (*tathatā*), and that the substance of the mind and the measure of the object are identical. The details are cited in the following section. If one does not grasp this essential meaning, one remains like a mere enumerator.
Regarding the treasures of others, one should clarify the mind; there is nothing that surpasses the three vows:

severing evil, cultivating good, and delivering sentient beings. One must know that good and evil sentient beings ultimately share a single mark: there is nothing to sever in severing, nothing to cultivate in cultivation, and nothing to deliver in delivering.

This is called the wondrous arousal [of the bodhicitta]. Our school bears a heavy responsibility, which rests solely upon the conferral of the precepts. If one does not understand this, it is for naught.
The Master feared it would be difficult [to maintain], and those who receive it would gain nothing.
Regarding the "Private Commentary on the Dharma-Gate of the Various Scriptural Precepts," it says:
As for what is called the "Dharma of the Precepts," it was established by all Buddhas and transmitted by the various sages; this is that which we have received.
It is so. This is because the ten realms of existence, both the environment and its inhabitants, are entirely identical to the substance of the mind.

Because sentient beings do not realize this, they create karma and transmigrate in the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, the Tathāgata, in accordance with their mental states and environments, established boundless precepts.

Whether for good or evil, he established rules and regulations, which are called the Dharma. By relying on these regulations to receive and uphold them, one follows the proper path to achieve liberation; this is the merit of the Dharma. However—
This Dharma of the precepts encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate through its teachings. According to the teachings, it belongs to the provisional and is thus the *śrāvaka* dharma;
yet, if one thoroughly investigates the Buddha’s intention and reaches the point of the "opening and merging" (*kaikai*), it is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) dharma.

As for the essential nature and measure of this dharma of the precepts, they are explained extensively and with great detail in the section on the "Precept-essence" (*jìtǐ*) within the *Xīnjìng*. Here, however, we shall provisionally rely on the *Shìchāo* (Commentary on the Essentials) to establish the fundamental principles and explain the characteristics.
These two chapters both clarify the efficacy of the precepts and reveal the meaning of the established ritual procedures. They are recorded hereafter;
I request that you investigate the various preceding and following texts to discern whether they pertain to essence or application, and may you understand them well.
5. The Section on the Essential Nature of the Precepts in Various Texts.

[Private Commentary]: This section clarifies only the essential nature received through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of four announcements) within the ordination platform. Since the Tathāgata established his teachings according to the capacities of beings, these four gates differ;

here in this land, they are widely propagated, generally returning to either the Emptiness or Existence schools. Within the Emptiness school, there are not two [positions], while in the Existence school, some calculate them as provisional.

"Form (*rūpa*) was established by my ancestors as something far surpassing ordinary categories. Initially, they relied on the two schools [of Yogācāra] to provide a detailed analysis of its essence and characteristics;

subsequently, they used the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) to harmonize all conceptual reckonings. Thus, provisional form is neither dualistic nor non-dual; it is nothing other than the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*).

Consciousness itself possesses the constant nature and virtues, and these seeds have been inherently present from time immemorial. Now, relying on the fundamental tenets of the Nanshan school, we provide perfect guidance and perfect revelation. And so, that..."
Regarding the recipient: they suddenly give rise to perfect understanding and thoroughly penetrate all phenomena as pure, perfectly interfused, and ultimately of one mark.
They form a firm vow and solemn commitment; through the convergence of causes and conditions, seeds arise from conditions to constitute the essence of the precepts (*śīla*).

Thus, the mind is great and the essence is great; the mind is wondrous and the essence is wondrous. This is what Jingxi meant when he said: "The precepts have no magnitude; it depends on the recipient’s mental aspiration."
It is so. Furthermore, there are the substance of the saṃgha, the substance of the *karmavācanā*, the substance of the great precepts (*mahāśīla*), and the substances of the seven non-transgressions;
all of these are appended to this section. Six: The Section on Various Texts Concerning Preceptual Practice.

I said: "Since you have already received the essence [of the precepts], you must certainly practice them, so that your reception may correspond to its characteristics and your vows may accord with your conduct.
Regarding the single phrase 'preceptual conduct,' it consists entirely of cessation and performance. Cessation is based on the *Śīla-sūtra*; by upholding it, one commits no transgressions.

Reception of the essence and performance are centered on the *Karmavācanā*. Furthermore, performance follows one's original vow-mind. Moreover, according to the *Sìshìchāo*, conduct is divided into three stages."

That is, the community itself is together with the community. According to the *saṃgha-dharma* and the *karmavācanā*, they must necessarily abide by the same rules. They personally bind themselves to maintain the precepts, guarding their own conduct with constant urgency.

They personally examine their communal interactions; regarding the four requisites, everyone collectively provides for them. Although the subsequent text is extensive, [the essential points are as follows].

There is nothing that surpasses this. Should one deviate from it even slightly, the Vinaya rules shall all result in transgressions. For those of dull faculties and small capacity, the teaching still allows for exceptions;
however, for those of superior character and perfect potential, the slightest indulgence constitutes a violation.

Having already awakened to the perfect understanding and received the perfect essence, one should cultivate perfect practice, taking the disciplinary forms of the Vinaya as the vessel and the subtle contemplation of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) as the sails and oars.
Wandering through the ocean of the Perfect Teaching on the South Mountain, one reaches the shore of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa.

Regarding the seventh section, the "Gate of the Characteristics of the Precepts in Various Texts," my private commentary states: The characteristics of the phrases in various texts generally fall into two categories: first, the characteristics of practice (*caryā-lakṣaṇa*); second, the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Thus it is said.

Regarding the "aspects of practice" (*ākāra*): based on upholding them within the inner mind, virtuous characteristics manifest externally; whether in deportment, speech, or silence, one does not need to apply deliberate effort, as one naturally accords with the Dharma.
This corresponds to what the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya-śikṣā-samuccaya* says: "Virtuous qualities shining forth constitute the aspect. Regarding the "characteristics of the Dharma" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*):

from the perspective of the objective realm, every single thing is it; from the perspective of the text, it refers to that which is listed in the *Prātimokṣa* and so forth. As for the "one great... [the text continues].
In the Vinaya Piṭaka, that which is prohibited and that which is permitted—the dharmas of good and evil matters—can be distinguished by surveying them; they are all mutually inclusive.

As for the practices and the characteristics of those practices, they may overlap, as is clear from the text itself. Question: What is the difference between the two categories of "conduct" (*caryā*) and "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) of the precepts? Answer:

Conduct refers to the mind that engages in practice, while characteristics refer to the outward manifestations of body and speech. These may be set forth in writing and can be observed with the eyes; their forms are thus evident.
This is what can be divided. Regarding the eighth section, the "Gate of Observance and Violation" (*dhāraṇa-aticāra-mukha*), my personal commentary states:

The meaning of this single gate of observance and violation is vast. If one relies upon the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, it encompasses everything from the preliminary applications (*prayoga*) to the final fruition (*phala*).

This entire compendium, categorized by object and based on the realms of rebirth, addresses the permissions and prohibitions, the light and heavy offenses, and the myriad variations of observance and transgression common to the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Whether concerning virtuous or non-virtuous matters and dharmas—whether they are prescribed or permitted, ceased or enacted, general or specific—if one does not study, one remains ignorant;
being fundamentally deluded by doubt and conceptualization, the mind and its objects become discordant, leading to errors, omissions, and forgetfulness, both gradual and sudden.

Regarding the distinctions between the unobstructed and the obstructed, the noble and the ordinary, and their respective degrees of excellence—as well as such characteristics as opposition or compliance, and the observance or violation of precepts—the Tathāgata has exhaustively analyzed the dispositions of sentient beings through his wondrously luminous and singular discernment.
From Mañjuśrī downward, none dared to offer a word; how could those of us with the coarse minds of ordinary beings possibly comprehend this?
Our Grand Master, who propagated the Vinaya over three lifetimes, was commanded by the Teacher to expound it, yet he declined, saying, "It is not within my capacity."
When the monk Huisheng was about to pass away, he looked at his disciples and said: "When I listened to the sutras and śāstras, I attained spiritual insight after hearing them only once.

Yet now, as I listen to the Vinaya-piṭaka, I find myself becoming increasingly darkened in my understanding. One could say that in the Vinaya school, there is nothing more fundamental than upholding and violating the precepts. The characteristics of upholding and violating are truly profound;

unless one has accumulated learning to penetrate the subtle, exhaust the obscure, and fully realize the underlying principles, this meaning will be difficult to perceive. I request [you all to study it]."
Examine these supreme instructions thoroughly; you should apply your mind well to them.
Ninth, regarding the section on the Repentance of Offenses through Various Texts, I privately remark:

When a bhikṣu commits an offense, both the Vinaya (rules of discipline) and the Sūtras (doctrinal teachings) prescribe the necessary measures. Why is this? For instance, if the substance of the offense constitutes one of the ten unwholesome paths of action, it is logically not...

One ought to perform [the rites]. This is because the Buddha established the Dharma and further added the Vinaya regulations. To violate the principle (li) constitutes an offense against the transformative karma (huà-yè);

to violate the Vinaya constitutes a transgression of the prescribed rules (zhì-zuì). To extinguish the transformative [offense], one relies on the integration of the principle; to repent for the prescribed [offense], one follows the Vinaya methods.

Therefore, our Patriarchs’ commentaries and sub-commentaries cite the Vinaya to set forth the methods for repenting the six classes of offenses (liù-zǒu), and their ritual procedures (jié-mó xíng-xiàng) are detailed and complete in every respect, following the Sūtras.
This clarifies the three types of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). The principles and ritual protocols provide a systematic framework that can be relied upon.

If one practices only through prohibitions while not forgetting the transformative function of karma, the Way will not be realized. If one relies solely on principle while the prohibitive function of karma still persists, the precepts will not be pure.

Therefore, the practitioner must ensure that principle and practice are mutually requisite so that both transformation and prohibition are fulfilled; when the vessel of the precepts is polished and immaculate, the Buddha-way manifests before one.
[Section Ten: The Private Commentary on the Gate of the Three Refuges] Question:
This gate seems to be non-essential for the Vinaya; why, then, does the *Lülu* (Record of the Vinaya) require its recitation? Answer:

The meaning of the Three Refuges is deeply connected to the study of the Vinaya. I shall briefly explain it. As stated in the Vinaya texts: when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he was beneath a tree...
The deity and the Brahmin woman received the two refuges of the Buddha-dharma; next, for Yaśodharā’s parents, he administered the three refuges;
subsequently, for the bhikṣu, he conferred full ordination through the three utterances. Furthermore, as with the five precepts and the ten precepts, these are all preceded by the three refuges.
This work brings forth the essence of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). If one is not refined and brilliant, what purpose would there be in receiving instruction from a teacher?

Furthermore, both the *Vinaya-anukrama* and the *Śīla-anukrama* must first pay homage to the Triple Gem and seek its protection; these two commentaries on the precepts and their practice explain this at length.

The single volume of the *Gongyang-i* (Ritual of Reverence) sets forth the sequence and enumerates the forms; its text is extremely precise and essential, intending that the fivefold assembly of renunciants shall have no other orientation in mind.

One’s resolve must inevitably seek refuge [in the Triple Gem]. However, regarding the Triple Gem, there are distinctions between cause and effect, delusion and awakening, the past and the present, as well as differences in name and essence.
One must thoroughly master these so that one’s refuge has a proper locus. (End of the Explanation of the Title;
from the Section on the Original Teachings of Various Texts)
The *Yuanfohuayi tongxu jiaozong jieshu* (卷一上) states:
"This was when the Great Sage descended, first establishing the foundation of his transformative teachings, intending to rescue and deliver all beings within the realms of existence."

Together we shall ascend to the other shore. The precepts were established for the sake of the Way; they are fundamentally not for worldly merit. Nevertheless, as afflictions and delusions are difficult to purify, one must rely on skillful means.

Thus, the Three Learnings (triśikṣā) were instituted as the primary remedy. Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Precept is like catching the thief, concentration is binding him, and wisdom is killing him.
These three practices are mutually dependent and must provide support at every moment. Consequently, if the activities of body and speech deviate from principle, [if one does not...]

First, one must prevent the mind from following after delusions, sensory objects, and desires; otherwise, the pathways of the mind will be turbulent and disturbed, and for what cause could there be stillness and concentration?

If concentration is not cultivated, one will lack the mental discernment to examine the various inversions, and clear wisdom will naturally remain hidden, leaving no means by which to realize the truth.

Therefore, a beginner must first apply themselves to training in the precepts, restraining and subduing all transgressions so that the three karmas are pure; thus, right concentration and right wisdom will be established spontaneously. For this reason:
The Sūtra says: "Depending on and because of this precept, one attains birth in the latter two [realms]. If this precept were absent, no wholesome dharmas would arise. Question:

Reasoning from the perspective of principle, the precept serves to still the three miserable realms (trāyastriṃśa) and certainly eliminates existence in the desire realm; wisdom is not bound to any realm. How then can it be said, as stated above, that [the precept] is for the sake of the Path and not for the sake of merit?

Answer: One must understand the underlying intent. From the beginning, when the Buddha descended into the world, was it ever for the purpose of increasing [rebirth]? Whether as celestial lords or human kings, [his aim was liberation].
All that arises is taught as existent; if the Buddha were to say it exists [in the same way], he would be no different from ordinary people. Measured by this standard, there is a vast disparity.

Since karma is accumulated through the observance of precepts, yet the matter is merely gathered in disorder and its substance sinks into the lower realms, it is judged not to be "existence with form" (rūpa-bhava). Thus, the *Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra* says:

The precepts are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and tainted (*sāsrava*); they are mundane dharmas. Nevertheless, if one intends to fundamentally regulate the mind as a skillful means for the Path, practitioners of the Three Vehicles must necessarily follow this track.
Thus, the Vinaya states: "In order to subdue the three poisons and bring them to an end, the training in higher morality (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) was established."
Furthermore, many treatises state: "The precepts were established in order to open the gate to Nirvana. As the text below says:
"With pure precepts and wisdom, one attains the foremost path. This is excellent evidence.

The *Xingzong* (Vol. 1, Part 1) states: "To speak of 'those who practice for the Way' in general terms refers to the Three Vehicles. Yet, if one infers the Buddha’s original intent, even those who turn away from heterodoxy ultimately serve as a preliminary lead toward the One Reality.

Moreover, since the sutras open and harmonize all paths so that diverse routes return to the same destination, and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* repeatedly supports this, there is nothing therein that does not reveal the [Buddha-]nature.
Now, when clarifying 'practicing for the Way,' it specifically refers to the Buddha Vehicle alone, which brings to rest the provisional city of transformation. Finally...

This was not his original intention. Thus we know that even the fundamental basis of transformation is beyond the reach of the Two Vehicles; how much less could these precepts have been established for the sake of worldly merit.
Master Xingzong further stated: "All sentient beings fundamentally possess the true reality and wondrous nature.

The essence of this nature is solely quiescence and solely illumination. Once one is deluded regarding this nature, it becomes obscured and dispersed, and is consequently termed 'ignorance' (avidyā), accumulating to form afflictions."
Deluded, they conceive of a self and a person; following after sensory objects, they give rise to poison, stirring their body, speech, and mind to create the karma of birth and death.

They transmigrate through the various realms for billions of kalpas without end. Out of great compassionate pity, the Great Awakened One intends to lead them away from suffering; he diagnoses the illness and prescribes medicine, establishing three categories in response.

To counter the inner mind’s darkness and agitation, he establishes meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). To counter physical and verbal transgressions, he establishes pure precepts (*śīla*). Although the holy teachings...
Much as there may be, it does not exceed the Three Trainings. That which is established by the Three Trainings relies solely upon form and mind.
Regarding their arising, they proceed from the root to develop the branches; regarding their application for cultivation, one begins with the coarse and proceeds to the subtle.

That the precepts were established first lies in this very principle. It is like turbid water where wind stirs up surging waves: as long as the wind and waves have not subsided, one cannot expect to obtain clarity. This is impossible.
The sequence of the three trainings is logically and necessarily so; to deviate from this constant model is to be entirely remote from the Way.

The *Yèshū* (Volume 2, Part B) quotes the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, saying: "From the Three Refuges and Five Precepts up to the Prātimokṣa, these dharmas were established because the Buddha appeared in the world.
However, while Wheel-turning Kings and Brahmā Kings teach worldly dharmas to benefit sentient beings, [the Buddha teaches] the ten wholesome paths and the four..."

Vast indeed. Since the beginning of the kalpa, [beings] have existed, yet they were unable to ascend purely or transcend the worldly realm. When the Dharma King appeared in the world, he did not merely teach worldly virtues;

rather, he sought to sever afflictions and bring about a distant departure from the bonds of the realms. Therefore, he clarified the goodness of the precepts, commanding that one rely upon them for complete cultivation.
This is the underlying intent behind the practices of concentration, wisdom, and so forth, which together constitute the root of birth and existence.

The *Zizhi* (Vol. 4, Part 2) states: "All Buddha-dharma does not transcend the Three Studies. Because sentient beings delude their minds, they produce afflictions; by stirring their thoughts, they create karma;
and through karma, they experience retribution, such that birth and death are without end. Desiring to escape the fruit of suffering, one must eliminate the cause of suffering.

Therefore, one first uses the precepts (*śīla*) to govern karma, and subsequently uses concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to clarify those afflictions. Since karma is divided into good and evil, there are [the categories of] abstention and performance."

The two [categories] are contrasted with one another. Since delusion consists solely of dullness and distraction, the two dharmas of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are applied as their antidotes.

Because the medicine must correspond to the illness, the *Śāstra* states that the Tripiṭaka is spoken of in this regard; yet because the Vinaya Piṭaka is preeminent and esoteric, it was taught by the Buddha alone.

Its regulations must be established within the Saṃgha, and its recitation is not permitted for other assemblies, as they are not those who train in it. The rest is as stated in the Preface to the *Shuō* (Commentary). (The *Jì* [Record] says:)

The internal assembly comprises five groups; this [rule] is restricted to the great monks (*bhikṣu*). The three other assemblies have not yet completed their full ordination and are not included among those who hear together. As for the nuns, they maintain their own distinct status and possess their own separate teachings; they do not usurp the position of the superior elders, and the rules regarding the time of their preaching are likewise distinct. Question: Regarding the fact that the original text is presented alone within the commentary, were there written records during the Buddha’s lifetime?

Answer: If one refers to the Buddha’s lifetime, originally there were no written characters; it was merely the various noble beings who heard and retained [the teachings]. Alternatively, it may be that there were indeed records during the Buddha’s lifetime, which later compilers edited into chapters; in terms of meaning, this is also without hindrance.

Question: Regarding the establishment of the teaching herein, does it refer to the formulation of the precepts (*śīla*) or to the recitation of the precepts (*prātimokṣa*)? Answer: If one discusses the formulation of the precepts, it belongs to the general meaning mentioned previously. Now, clarifying the period after twelve years, the essence of the precepts was separately compiled and ordered for disciples to recite;
this uniquely reveals the intent behind the origin of the present text, and is therefore called "separate" (*viśeṣa*).
The *Zichi* (upper volume, upper section) states: "The *Śāstra* refers to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*. It says: 'The *Sūtra* is taught as the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the ten powers:

(1) the power of what is possible and impossible; (2) the power of karma; (3) the power of meditative concentration; (4) the power of the faculties; (5) the power of aspiration; (6) the power of disposition; (7) the power of the path leading to all destinations; (8) the power of recollecting past lives; (9) the power of the divine eye; and (10) the power of the exhaustion of outflows.

'Outflow' means that which is untainted (*anāsrava*), and 'flow' means that which is non-discriminative. The *Vinaya* is taught as the outflow of great compassion. The *Abhidharma* is taught as the outflow of fearlessness.'"

Regarding the "Outflow" (niṣyanda) teachings—namely, the four fearlessnesses: the fearlessness of possessing all-knowledge, the fearlessness of having exhausted the outflows, the fearlessness of declaring what constitutes obstacles to the path, and the fearlessness of declaring the path that leads to the end of suffering—when considering the Buddha’s administration of the teachings, there are generally three mental states involved.

However, when categorized according to the specific dharmas and their respective capacities among sentient beings, each possesses its own particular predominance. Therefore, in opening understanding through the preaching of the Dharma, the emphasis lies primarily on the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*);
in refuting heterodox arguments, one specifically requires fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*); and in establishing precepts to restrain transgressions, it is solely through great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*).
It is because such was the case that the Tathāgata arose with compassion, appearing in the world desiring to proclaim the wondrous Dharma so as to bring universal awakening.

Since sentient beings were stubborn and dull-witted, he subsequently taught the Three Vehicles. Those who encountered the sound of the Dharma immediately ascended to the fruits of the Path; thus, he employed concise teachings to restrain their transgressions and faults.

As the faculties of human beings grew increasingly inferior, they violated the concise teachings and gave rise to further faults; therefore, he again opened up extensive teachings, pointing out their errors and establishing regulations. It was even so...

They were unable to follow [the precepts], leading to the transgression of the three thousand eight hundred thousand immeasurable rules of discipline (*vinaya*). Even during the time of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), there were still many who violated them;
how much more so in the Semblance and Final Ages—how can it be described? Following this sequence, he accommodated even the lowliest of ordinary beings, leaving not even the smallest being behind.
Were it not for his Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), how could he have reached such an extent?
The *Jiexingzong* (下) states:
"Within the great trichiliocosm, the Buddha is the Dharma King; the Vinaya is the Buddha’s decree, established solely by the Sage."

As for those in the remaining lower ranks, they may only rely upon and follow him. This is because the Tathāgata’s practice and fruition are utterly perfected, having exhausted the nature of the light and heavy karmas of all sentient beings;
even those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment downward are not yet capable of such realization, let alone other minor sages who would dare to venture into conjecture or deliberation.
It is like a state: rewards, punishments, and proclamations must issue from the sovereign; if subordinates usurp authority or commoners violate their word, ruin will come before long.

Affliction (*kleśa*). The activity of afflictions results in the retributions of suffering throughout the three realms and six paths;

all these are repayments for past karma. Karma produces retribution, and the substance of retribution is itself karma. Thus we know that the accumulation of karma forms delusion, and the transformation of karma becomes retribution.

The revolving cycle of the three paths is nothing other than karma. This explains karma by way of the three paths. Furthermore, karma arises from the mind, and the mind is produced in accordance with objects.
Since objects are immeasurable, karma is likewise not singular; though the objects of perception are manifold, that which creates them is threefold.

Body and speech are the instruments, while the mind is the master of karma. The mind is precisely volitional karma (*karmas-cetanā*), and volition is the active mind. This constitutes the characteristic of all wholesome and unwholesome karmic phenomena.

All are created by the mind; this explains karma in terms of the relationship between the mind and its objects. Furthermore, the ten unwholesome actions arising from the three poisons constitute the karma for the three miserable realms.

Thus, one knows that activity pervades all ten realms. Some say it consists of the three evil and three good realms; some say the four evil destinies and humans and devas constitute the good; others say there are six.

It is said: "The precepts are the foundation for correctly conforming to liberation; therefore, they are called *mokṣa* (liberation). It is clearly known that this is the fruit.
Furthermore, it is called *vinaya*, also named *vinaya*, *piṇāya*, *pi-nai-ye*, and so forth; these are all corruptions and substitutions in the transmission from Sanskrit.
The ancient translations rendered it as "extinction" (*mie*), because the seven types of *vinaya* are used to terminate the four kinds of disputes. By what meaning is it now translated [as such]?
*Vinaya*. "Vinaya" means "dharma. It is named after its teachings. Among the nine schools (*jiuliu*) of secular tradition, dharma is one of them; thus, worldly laws are all based on penal statutes.

The Way (*Dao*) differs from the secular, and their terminology regarding punishments is therefore distinct. Nevertheless, when it comes to adjudication, one must invariably rely on the constant law. Furthermore, the *Chao* (Vol. 1) states:
"Because the appearance and attire of the five groups of monastics differ from those of the world, it is manifested that the internal Dharma is also different. And:

Non-Buddhists and worldly commoners would have indiscriminately conflated themselves with the traces of the sages, making it impossible to distinguish them. It was through the subtle application of the Dharma that they were eliminated;

thus, the name *vinaya* (律, *lǜ*) was first propagated to manifest the knowledge of the Dharma. The *Zizhi* (資持) states: "In Sanskrit it is called *vinaya*; in Chinese it is termed *lǜ*. *Lǜ* means 'Dharma' (*dharma*).

It is named after its teaching, which adjudicates the gravity of offenses, determines what is permitted or prohibited, and defines upholding or violating the precepts. That which is not the Dharma is indeterminate. As the following text says:
Furthermore, just as worldly laws rely on penal codes and regulations, so too does the Way rely on the faculties [of practitioners] and its teachings;

each has its respective gradations and must not be transgressed. Hence it is called "Dharma" (fa). Second, "Vinaya" (lü) means "division. This refers to the necessity of deliberation and measurement, for there is a specific standard to be followed.

It is like the divisions of the pitch-pipes (lüyǔ): among the twelve months of the year, those with odd-numbered months belong to Yang and are called "lǜ," while those with even-numbered months belong to Yīn and are called "lǚ. Each lǜ and each lǚ corresponds to a specific division of the vital breath (*qi*).

When the [twelve] winds are divided, there are twenty-four winds). It is further stated: "The principles explained by the teachings are fully encompassed by these four terms: namely, transgression and non-transgression, light and heavy.
If one understands these four terms and attains unimpeded mastery without doubt, this is the pinnacle of the superior grade of upholding the Vinaya.

What is called 'transgression'? It is when the objective conditions are complete. What is called 'non-transgression'? It is when the antidote is applied. What is called 'light'? It concerns cause and effect..."

It is subtle. Why is it called "heavy"? It is the opposite of the preceding phrase. Furthermore, these four characteristics are not distinguished by the Vinaya, nor are they confused in terms of observance and violation;

they share a common seasonal climate. The third [commentary] states: "The character for *lǜ* (律, Vinaya) is composed of *ān* (安) and *yù* (聿). *Yù* means a writing brush (*bǐ*). As the *Zìshū zhù* (Notes on the Dictionary) states: 'In Chu it was called *yù*; in Qin it was called *bǐ*').

One must necessarily examine the teachings and verify the circumstances before committing them to the brush for a definitive judgment. It is further said: "To adjudicate, interrogate, decide, and rectify—this is not done without the brush."

Regarding "indefinite" and so forth: Question: By what means are the three meanings mentioned above distinguished? Answer: All three are worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*). To adopt a name from the north is the meaning of "teaching" (*jiao*);
to establish a definitive standard through instruction is the meaning of "dharma" (*fa*). To analyze and differentiate degrees of gravity is the meaning of "discrimination" (*bian*).
To issue a decisive judgment when facing a specific matter is the meaning of "penalty" (*bi*). Because it fully encompasses these three, it is called *vinaya* (the Vinaya).

The *Bieshi sijian mingyi zichi* (Upper Volume, Part One) states: "The 'Four Divisions' (*sifen*) is a specific name for the five schools and a general designation for this single tradition. It is named according to the number of its textual sections.
When translated here in this land [of China], it comprises sixty volumes in total. Those who have newly begun their studies find much flavor [in it]; I shall now cite from it in detail."
It was presented [to him]. The first division consists of twenty fascicles, which is the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra*. The second division consists of fifteen fascicles:
the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra* in eight fascicles, the *Upasampadā-khandhaka* in five fascicles, and the *Poṣadha-khandhaka* in two fascicles.

The third division consists of fourteen fascicles, comprising sixteen *khandhakas* in total. The fourth division consists of eleven fascicles, containing the two *khandhakas* on dwellings (*Vihāra*) and miscellaneous matters (*Kṣudraka*).
Regarding the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: five hundred and seven hundred [monks] gathered for the council. They compiled the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, the *Vinayottaragrantha*, and so forth.
The Venerable Upāli, from within the *Mūla-vastu*, selected and compiled the texts according to his own preference (beginning one hundred and sixteen years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa).

As each section was recited and concluded, it was established as a distinct part (*bhāga*). After four such rounds, the entire collection was completed; therefore, it is called the *Caturvarga* (Four-Part Vinaya). It is not the same as [the other schools].

The commentaries (*zhangshu*) analyze the text according to its underlying meaning. Thus, the *Yeshu* states: "In the *Sifen [vinaya]*, this refers to the section on 'stopping' (*duan*; the character is pronounced with an upper tone, meaning to cease)."

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The four *dharmas* transmit the text, exhausting all the characteristics of what is explained; this is based on the extent of the teaching, not a judgment of its meaning.

As for the twenty *khandakas*, they are divided into three parts—is this an opening up according to their meaning? When the teachings flowed into this land, four Vinayas had already been translated (the *Dharmaguptaka*, *Mahīśāsaka*, *Sarvāstivāda*, and *Mahāsāṃghika*).

For what reason did the Patriarchs single out the *Dharmaguptaka* as their primary school? Answer: Regarding the conditions for receiving [the teachings] in this land, it began with the *Dharmaguptaka*.
Although other schools have translated [the Vinaya], it has not been heard that they rely upon its practical application. The *Yejieshu* states: "The land of China is unified;

regarding the transmission [of the Vinaya], all recite the text of the Four-Part Vinaya (*Dharmaguptaka*). What we now judge and explain concerns the clarification of the 'following' (anuvartana) according to the transmission; therefore, we establish one school as our fundamental tenet."

The text below states: "Now, in judging the maintenance or violation [of precepts], we must still rely upon the substance of the ordination itself; this intention is clear" (Master Yijing’s reversal to the Sarvāstivāda school failed to grasp this point). Question:

There are passages citing the *Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan* that state the Dharmaguptaka school is superior to the others, yet you claim the four schools are equal. What is the meaning of this? Answer: It is not that such a principle does not exist.
However, if one necessarily relies on the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* for receiving the precepts, one may regard the school as inferior while adhering to the Dharmaguptaka tradition.

Yes. The introduction clarifies the distinctions between superior and inferior [teachings] in order to manifest the varying depths of the various schools' doctrines; it is only upon reaching the third gate that the discussion begins regarding the classification of teachings (*jiao*) and their respective positions.

Question: According to the currently translated version, there are sixty fascicles in total, yet the Sanskrit original is still more extensive. How, then, could one complete the recitation of the entire *Tripitaka* in four sessions?
Answer: It does not mean that a single sitting constitutes one "session" (*du*). Rather, "one session" refers to the entirety of a period, with no fixed time limit.

As they gathered at each location, the assembly would disperse before it was concluded; this constituted one session. In this manner, up to four sessions were held before a single division was finished.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* are largely similar to this. Only the *Aṣṭottaraśata-bhāṇavāra-vinaya* differs, as its chapters were titled according to the specific seating arrangements and established according to the occasion; thus, they cannot be treated as uniform.
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), Volume One, Part One, states:

"What is called the 'Brief Teaching' (*lüjiao*)? When the Buddha first attained enlightenment and was about to open the way for transformation through the Dharma, beings had newly begun to look up to him in aspiration, yet they had no ground upon which to fix their minds.
Therefore, he first showed them the methods of practice so that they might rely upon and follow them, before there was even the occasion for violating the precepts."
Because of these offenses, one must not harbor doubts or give rise to slander. Since the teachings have been presented in brief, it is called the "Brief Teaching" (*piṇḍīkṣepa-śāsana*).

As for the "Extensive Teaching" (*vistara-śāsana*), because the names in the brief version were all-encompassing, those who did not yet understand the preceding characteristics might commit various transgressions without realizing they had committed an offense.

Therefore, it was necessary to extensively set forth the detailed rules and categories to gather and contain the mass of offenses. When those of dull faculties hear this, they immediately attain understanding; because it is taught extensively, it is so named.
The Extensive Teaching.

Regarding the extensive and abbreviated [teachings], it is further said: Question: Since both the extensive and abbreviated teachings universally accord with the capacities of sentient beings, why did the Buddha not preach them all at once immediately upon his initial attainment of enlightenment? Answer:

The teaching of the Sage is not for no purpose; that the medicine and the ailment correspond is its fundamental intent. Therefore, it was not said from the outset that [the teaching] was merely for those without the capacity [to receive it].
Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If one were to preemptively impose restraints before the outflows have even arisen, people would give rise to slander.
We who have left the household life have abandoned wealth and sensual pleasure, and harbor no longing for worldly fame or profit. How [could we be slandered]?"
The Tathāgata, on the contrary, has bound us with the *vinaya*. How could this be called a skillful understanding of the mental capacities of worldly people?
Furthermore, they will fail to give rise to reverence for the Buddha’s teaching, causing the Dharma to perish quickly; therefore, he did not establish the precepts beforehand.
By waiting until an offense occurs before establishing them, one comes to recognize the Sage’s kindness—just as a physician lances an abscess only after it has ripened.

Regarding the mutual completion of the two teachings, it was further asked: "The purpose of the abbreviated teaching lies in benefiting those of sharp faculties; for those of dull faculties here, the matter is the same as not having taught it, and thus it was necessary to establish the extensive [teaching].

If the extensive [teaching] is established, it would lead to the disparagement of the abbreviated [teaching]; so what is the use of the abbreviated [teaching]? Answer: Originally, although the abbreviated teaching was established for the sake of those of sharp faculties...

The "concise" (jī) refers to brevity of words while encompassing the full meaning; it does not fail to include those of dull faculties. Because those of dull faculties do not understand, they violate the concise [teaching] and give rise to error; thus, both the teaching and the practice are deficient.

Thereupon, the "extensive" (guǎng) was subsequently established to supplement the previous conciseness. How is this known? It is simply that the concise possesses the principle of comprehensive inclusion, whereas the extensive lacks any capacity beyond that of the concise.

For a person of dull faculties who is suited to the occasion, following the concise [version] first constitutes no offense. Although the names differ, [the extensive] is no different from the concise.

This is equivalent to the merit of the abbreviated teaching; it is called the simultaneous fulfillment of both teaching and practice. Thus, the two teachings complement one another, and there is no contradiction or exclusion between them.
Depending on the conditions of the sharp or dull faculties of beings, and according to reality, they encompass both.

Regarding the second point, the timing of the teachings, it is further stated: "If one relies on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Ekottarika-āgama* of this school, the brief teaching was intended for the twelve years prior [to the full exposition];

subsequently, it was entrusted to the disciples, thereby encompassing both types of teaching. How is this known to be so? Because the brief teaching universally includes all, subsuming both those of sharp and dull faculties, before [the detailed] expansion."

Regarding gravity and lightness: furthermore, while the general *jī-kuan* (causal conditions) are extensive, the *pǐn-jìào* (detailed teachings) are not so; conversely, they do not speak of them. Thus, the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* states:

"All Buddhas only teach the *vinaya* of instruction (*jiàoshòu mùchā*), and do not teach the *vinaya* of majestic power (*wēidé mùchā*). [The detailed teaching merely points to the three karmas and directly indicates them; therefore, it is called 'instruction']."

(“Venerable Power” [威德] refers to the fact that expounding the teachings extensively to address past events involves fear; hence the term. Is this not a direct exposition of the three karmas (*trikarma*) that universally reaches all sentient beings?

If it were fully detailed with specific articles (*pāṭha*), it would be identical to the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa*. Thus, the Vinaya text states: "This is the Tathāgata’s final recitation of the precepts. This is excellent evidence.

Since the Buddha himself spoke these words, there is no room for misinterpretation or confusion. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* state: "If one were to preach this for those who have committed offenses, their heads would split into seven pieces."
The disciple is not like that; what is seen by the fleshly eye is the raising of charges by means of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), for it violates the Buddha’s regulations. The Record states:

In the *Prātimokṣa-vibhaṅga* (the section on the recitation of the precepts), it is said that when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Campā, during the fortnightly recitation of the precepts on the fifteenth day, he remained silent among the assembly and did not recite them.
When the first watch of the night had passed, Ānanda requested him to speak. The Buddha said: "I wish to cause the Tathāgata [to remain] in impurity..."

It is not reasonable for the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) to be performed within the assembly [while an offender remains]. The same applies to requests for answers during the middle watch and the last watch of the night.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana used his divine eye to observe those who had violated the precepts; seeing one not far from the Buddha, he pulled him out by the hand and permitted him to undergo the *svavacana-vinaya* (disciplinary action through self-accusation).
"From this day forward, you yourselves shall perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts. This is the final instruction of the Tathāgata."
Regarding the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*): based on this, it is clearly evident that the Buddha did not preach them in full detail.
Furthermore, it is said that the detailed rules were established to supplement the brief ones so that they might be easily understood;

this was truly because the five groups of monastics failed to restrain their sensory faculties and lacked any thought of self-restraint regarding fame and profit, thereby giving rise to extensive [transgressions].

With outflows (*āsrava*), defilements arise following sensory objects; externally, there are entanglements and false pride, while internally, delusion and confusion increase. Therefore, the Tathāgata, according to the specific transgressions committed, first provided brief teachings.

Once these were violated, he established extensive precepts to supplement them, ensuring that both the observance and the violation are clearly understood so that the ignorant and the wise may alike be enlightened.
The timing for the establishment of the precepts and prohibitions was of profound and vast benefit; these very teachings are known as the "Extensive Canon" (Vaipulya).

Initially, when the extensive teachings were first formulated, offenses were adjudicated immediately upon their commission, such that the distinctions between light and heavy, or earlier and later, became so intermingled and disordered as to be difficult to discern. It was not until after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa that they were consolidated into a single summer retreat.
The weighty [teachings] are the source of the Way; the light [teachings] merely stop worldly slander. The eight sections follow one another in sequence, gradually descending to a lack of uniformity.
The Buddha’s prophecy states that after his parinirvāṇa, five masters will hold differing views.
Furthermore, it cites the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, which says: "In a dream, a single piece of wool was seen; later, it was divided into five. The Buddha told the elder: "After my extinction..."

Later, there were certain disciples who misunderstood the meaning and taught the Dharma erroneously, thereby obscuring the treasury of the Dharma. They were called Dharmagupta, which means "Dharma-Rectitude.
Their Vinaya is known as the *Caturvarga* (Four Parts). Regarding the method of explaining and practicing the Dharma, they placed the result first and the cause last;

this was done according to their pedagogical approach so that the characteristics [of the teaching] would be clearly manifest. Thus, they inverted the order—for instance, in the Dharma of the Four Truths, they placed Suffering at the beginning and the Path at the end—thereby obscuring it.

"Constantly following the conventional" (*chángtú*) refers to the meaning of "preceding. Furthermore, the Preface to the Commentary states: "This person extensively examined the three capacities (*trividha-yāna*), took the two canons as a profound mirror, encompassed both the provisional and the real, and unified all names and principles.

He compiled this [work], which serves both the *Āgama* and the *Vaipulya*, to benefit those of the present age. Regarding the "Aids to Conditions" (*jìyuán*), it says: "Because he clarifies that all phenomena arise through conditions, they are empty;
thus it is called the 'Emptiness School' (*śūnyatā-vāda*). Because there are only names and designations, it is called the 'Provisionality School' (*prajñapti-vāda*). Furthermore...

They profoundly grasp the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) within the Mahāyāna; therefore, they are called the Sautrāntika masters. As stated in the *Xingzong* (卷一上): "The mind is the master of karma.

When consciousness encounters various objects, the mind turns back [to its source]. Their practice of giving and their attainment of Buddhahood are entirely distinct from the Sarvāstivāda school. They have a deep mastery of the true path;
however, because their teaching is restricted to the Hīnayāna and does not yet permit the direct revelation [of ultimate truth], [they remain at this stage]."
It is further stated: "He was able to discourse skillfully on the three periods of time and the internal and external [realms], thereby refuting the non-Buddhists.
He taught that all natures may receive the precepts; whatever questions were posed to him, he was adept at answering them. He was named Sarvāstivāda, which means 'Existence' (Savada).

The Dharma is called the *Daśabhāṇavāra* (Ten Recitations). The record states: 'To receive [the precepts] is to hold to the view that the five sense-objects and the four great elements all internally exist.'"
Externally, there are two types of worlds: the sentient and the insentient. They maintain that while the names of all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty, their essential substance is entirely real.
Furthermore, they state: "It is taught that there is no self (*ātman*) nor any experiencer; the transformation of the various afflictions is like a corpse.

This is called the Kāśyapīya school (translated here as the "School of Heavy Emptiness"). Their teachings on the nature of phenomena as liberation possess a *Prātimokṣa* (code of precepts) that is similar to the *Pañcavargika*.

The Record states: "The 'self' is the very root of the inversion of what is conceptualized; 'reception' (vedanā) is the deluded sentiment of grasping. Ordinary people claim it truly exists and thus give rise to attachment.
Since the self is fundamentally non-existent, to what could attachment possibly adhere? The subsequent reversal into 'heavy emptiness' (gurutara-śūnyatā) has its meaning in this."
It further states: "Not forming the marks of earth, water, fire, or wind, nor the marks of space or consciousness, is called Mīśāsaka;

this is translated as 'the contemplation that does not cling to existence or non-existence. The name of the dharma is Pañcavargika. The record states: 'The sutra cites the six great elements (ṣaḍdhātu) to encompass all phenomena of the world, such as form and mind.
By not forming the six marks, one does not cling to existence; by preserving these six, one does not cling to non-existence.'"

It is further stated: "They all claim there is a self and do not speak of the characteristic of emptiness; they are like children, called *bālaputraka*, which here means 'those attached to conditioned existence.

Their dharma is not transmitted. Furthermore, it is said that because they have extensively and universally studied the five divisions of the scriptures, they are called the Mahāsāṃghika, which here means 'The Great Assembly. They possess their own Vinaya."
Although the teachings they uphold differ, the Way they realize is no different.
The *Commentary* states: "As taught in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, because of these differing views, factions support one another and engage in mutual disputes;
yet all of them awaken to the Way. Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states: "Though the five schools are each distinct, this does not hinder the Buddha-dharmadhātu-nirvāṇa."
