However, this applies only to laypeople and does not extend to both monastic communities. How, then, should one judge such cases? Answer: Those matters included in the *Hua-jiao* (Transformation Teachings) that are clarified within the Vinaya are the sutras that follow the Vinaya;

citations and proofs for these are provided elsewhere. Such a detailed analysis serves as a brief means to recognize the practice of transformation teachings, yet further precise discernment is required.
Fearing excessive prolixity, I shall stop here. Even contemporary scholars do not know the names of these texts, let alone understand their practical applications. If one does not comprehend this...

In this regard, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna masters of the Tripiṭaka are all deluded. Furthermore, some claim that upon hearing of Vimalakīrti’s awakening of the mind, one is already fully endowed [with the precepts], thereby falsely judging whether the precepts exist or not.
Others, confused regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and transgressing established prohibitions, assert that such karma is equivalent to a single grade of offense.

Some say there is no fault in performing meritorious deeds even if they violate the precepts; others maintain that by simply holding to mental contemplation, one may destroy the code of discipline (*vinaya*); and still others claim that firm adherence [to the precepts] is unnecessary.
Lao Hui’s contemplation—whether based on the two repentances of the Vaipulya (fangděng) sutras, where he claims that all *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offenses) are entirely extinguished;

or based on the six methods of treatment for the *bhikṣu-prātimokṣa* categories, where he asserts that even *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherent offenses) are all eliminated—leads to such confusion and error as to suggest that one may repent a *pārājika* offense according to the Mahāyāna teachings and yet still fulfill the monastic requirements of the Hīnayāna.
Such delusions have persisted from antiquity to the present day. These matters will be discussed in further detail in the subsequent section on repentance.

The *Jiexing erjie jiaoyi jieshu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Two Precepts of Prohibitive Nature), fascicle two, part one, states: "Regarding what is called 'inherently evil' (*xing'e*): for example, the substance of the ten unwholesome actions is contrary to principle.

Regardless of whether a Great Sage has established a prohibition against them or not, if one performs such contrary conduct, one will experience bitter fruits [of suffering]. Therefore, they are said to be inherently evil. For this reason, the Tathāgata..."
The precepts are established to provide restraint and protection. If they were not established, one would be bound by karma to the three miserable realms and would not remain within the human path;

how then could one cultivate goodness? Therefore, the rules are established based on transgressions, and names are designated from their fundamental evils. Because they prohibit innate evil, they are called "inherent precepts" (*prakṛti-śīla*).

As for "prohibitory evils," these include such acts as cutting down plants and trees, tilling the soil, or digging the earth—actions that are coarse and unseemly in their deportment, which do not bring glory to the faith of the laity. Thus says the Sage...
Before it was prohibited, engaging in such actions incurred no fault; as they were not improper occupations, they did not obstruct merit or goodness.

After the prohibition was established, however, such defilements became even deeper, obstructing and distracting the cultivation of the Path and inviting worldly censure and slander; therefore, it is called a "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*).
Furthermore, it clarifies that the meaning of "prohibition" (śikṣāpada) applies to both natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) and prohibitive precepts.
It further states: "That which is called 'prohibitive' is so termed because it can obstruct the right path; thus, it is called the 'prohibition of evil.

As for the aforementioned 'natural evil,' because it can obstruct merit, this [other] evil may also be called 'prohibitive' because it arises as a prohibition established by the teaching. Some interpret this as follows: "If..."

Regarding *dharmatā-śīla* (inherent morality), one abandons transgressions to seek merit; regarding *pratikṣepaṇa-śīla* (prohibitory morality), one abandons merit to seek the Path. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The ten wholesome and ten unwholesome paths are called 'original precepts' (*paurāṇa-śīla*); the five categories and seven groups [of offenses] are called 'guest precepts' (*ātithya-śīla*).

The former ten wholesome and unwholesome paths exist independently of formal regulation, whereas the categories and groups necessarily depend upon the regulations established by the Sage. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that the Bodhisattva upholds...
The precepts that are inherently grave (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are no different from those intended to avoid worldly censure; the details are as extensive as those texts.

It is clearly understood that the regulations concerning the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are established to restrain worldly censure. When examined through their underlying meaning, those in the first category—such as sexual misconduct and killing—are termed "inherently grave.
Those regulated in the lower categories are termed "inherently light. That the prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) are likewise grave or light is self-evident.
It further states: "The gravity of the offenses of *pratikṣepa* (prohibited) and *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherently evil) differs.
Furthermore, it asks: Both prohibited and inherently evil acts possess two capacities—first, the capacity to violate prohibitions, and second, the capacity to obstruct the Path.
Why then are only those [acts] involving grasses and trees designated as 'prohibited' (*pratikṣepa*) based on the teachings? As for inherently evil acts..."

Because they are prohibited by instruction. The answer is: there are three faults regarding natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*): first, they are unrighteous misconduct; second, they contravene the Buddha’s extensive prohibitions;

and third, they are able to obstruct the work of the Path. Prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) possess only two [of these faults]. Since their essence does not involve unrighteousness, they are called "prohibited. This is as in the case of the three thousand rules of decorum (*tri-sahasra-īryāpatha*).

This is analyzed through four propositions: first, there are offenses against the Buddha-dharma that are not offenses against the world, such as possessing wealth or being separated from one’s robes after the precepts have been established;
second, there are offenses against the world that are not offenses against the Buddha-dharma, namely acts such as killing or stealing committed before the precepts were established.

"Both are threefold" refers to cases such as committing sexual misconduct or deception after the detailed precepts have been established. "Neither are fourfold" refers to cases such as killing plants and trees before the detailed precepts have been established.
Generally, the gravity [of an offense] is distinguished by whether it pertains to the monastic or the lay community based on the nature of what was prohibited.
Furthermore, it is said: "Inferring from this principle, prior to the establishment of the extensive precepts, there was no distinction between the monastic and the lay;

since there was no formal teaching to violate, whatever one did constituted a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). One merely incurred karmic action (*karma-patha*); thus the Sūtra says: 'This is killing; this is the retribution for killing,' and so forth. How could this be only..."

Laypeople do not observe the Path, yet when they commit a grave offense, their transgression is light; whereas for those who have left the household life, it is heavy. This is because laypeople may violate the non-manifest precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*), whereas monastics cannot.

Furthermore, it violates the summary teaching (*saṃkṣipta-śikṣā*). Therefore, the very first offense described in the Vinaya texts clarifies this violation of the summary teaching. As Śraddhākaravarman states:
"If two people commit the same offense, the one who has not received the precepts is light, while the one who has received them is heavy, because he has violated the Buddha’s word."

The *Zichih* (Commentary on the *Sifenlü Xingshichao*) clarifies the meaning of prohibitions (*pratikṣepa-śīla*) and nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). It states: "Among the precepts established in the Vinaya, there are none that do not fall within the categories of prohibition or nature. By employing these two gates, one seeks the One Vinaya Piṭaka.
The ten unwholesome paths of action are, by their very essence, evil deeds that contravene principle; thus, they are uniformly forbidden across the Tripiṭaka. Nevertheless, the Vinaya..."

Within this [category], only the seven branches [of the precepts] are established; by further increasing the *pāyattika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* sections, it thus encompasses both teachings. Acts such as destroying life or digging the earth are not inherently unwholesome (*akuśala*);

it is only when they provoke worldly censure or suspicion that their commission constitutes a transgression. Therefore, these are subject to the "prohibitive" (*pratikṣepaṇīya*) teachings. However, as for the "natural" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) precepts, they exist inherently;

regardless of whether a Great Sage establishes them or not, their violation invariably results in karma that leads to rebirth in the three miserable realms (*durgati*). This is not the case with the prohibitive precepts. Thus says the Buddha.

This establishes the system of classification. Therefore, within the sutras and śāstras, these may be termed "host and guest," or designated as "new and old," or divided according to whether they contradict principle or fact;
the rest is as explained in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts).
The Comprehensive Source of the Vinaya School (Lüzong Huìyuán), Volume One: The Original Teachings of All Texts;
Volume Two (concluding with the section on the essence of the precepts).

For those who have left the household life, the cultivation of contemplation based on principle (*li-guan*) is fundamental (as stated in the *Shami-pian* of the *Sifenlü shanbu suiji jiemo*, the "Receiving Precepts" chapter of the *Yejiao chao*, and the section on "Categorizing Teachings and Gathering Capacities" which lists three levels of contemplation; the intent is that for practitioners newly entering the Path, none of the various practices they cultivate shall fail to take contemplation based on principle as their foundation).

The *Shishi Yaolan* (Volume 4, Part 2) states: "To emerge upon the Noble Path has never occurred since beginningless time; this is entirely due to attachment to the mundane world and the difficulty of abandoning long-standing habits.
Now that one has transcended the secular, one must surely practice the holy deeds. Although these are numerous in the sutras, they may be summarized into three stages:

first, the practice of those of the Hīnayāna, who contemplate the arising and ceasing of phenomena and realize the non-existence of self or person, as well as the nature of good and evil; second, the practice of the Lesser Bodhisattvas."

Contemplating the arising and ceasing of phenomena—[the *Yejie shu* states: "contemplating that phenomena are empty"]—and being devoid of the characteristics of self, person, good, evil, and so forth. Third is the practice of the Great Bodhisattvas:

contemplating that phenomena are mind, which is the conceptualization of mental discourse (*manojalpa*). Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* says: "From the stage of aspiration (*adhimukti*) up to the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā*), it is called 'contemplation within.
It takes the conceptualization of mental discourse as its object; apart from this, there are no other distinct dharmas. (The text of the *Yejie shu* is identical.)

[Not recorded]. *Ming shang san guan* (The Three Contemplations of the Upper Section), regarding the objects and contemplations of the three contemplations as well as the principles of the *Zizhi* (Lower Four), states:

"Regarding the statement that all three contemplations 'contemplate phenomena' (*shi*), 'phenomena' (*shi*) refers to the object (*jing*). The mind arises in dependence upon the object. Following [this principle]...

Establishing contemplation upon objects refers to the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) of form and mind; sentient and insentient beings; and the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate (the aforementioned objects of observation).

As for intellectual understanding, it requires the thorough comprehension of all phenomena. Regarding the temporal aspect, the contemplation of the mind is essential; one should follow whatever arises within the mind.

Arising is itself the phenomenon—whether good or evil. When the three principles illuminate it, one then realizes that it is inverted; there is only false conceptualization, which fundamentally has no existence.
All movements and functions of the mind are entirely empty. Alternatively, by investigating phenomena to perceive the nature, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

By realizing that phenomena are known through their characteristics, it is called "emptiness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). By penetrating that phenomena are the mind, it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). It is just like a dream.

Regarding the phenomena: one may investigate from where dreams arise and cease; or one may realize that the characteristics of sleep and dreams are unreal; or one may realize that they are merely transformations of the mind and that there are no separate dream-objects.

These correspond to the three aforementioned contemplations, through which one briefly understands their relative depth and shallowness (the above clarifies the contemplating subject). There are two ways of seeing the principle (*tattva*):
although the nature and characteristics differ in the first two cases, both take emptiness as the principle; in the latter case, the mind itself is taken as the principle. The former...
The second is provisional (*upāya*), while the latter one is real (*tattva*). However, those who have left the household life transcend the world and study all three vehicles (*triyāna*).

Now, following the *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) and in accordance with the intent of the *Huayan jing kaihui pin* (Chapter on the Opening of the Assembly), this refers specifically to the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*) as the fundamental basis for those who have left the household life. (The above provides a general demonstration of the three principles. It further states:

Because the self, others, good, and evil are inherently non-existent by nature, they arise through the convergence of conditions and perish when conditions disperse. The place where arising and perishing cease is called... [the ultimate reality].
The principle of emptiness is precisely the ultimate limit reached by the two vehicles. Furthermore, it is said that all phenomena are fundamentally but a single consciousness;

outside of this single consciousness, there are no other dharmas. Since beginningless time, through deluded movement, one has erroneously conceptualized the mind and its objects as having "that" and "this," with distinctions between internal and external.
To exhaustively investigate these distinctions, they are all merely mental constructions, arising from false grasping and attachment. Due to this grasping...

Because of these attachments, one falsely constructs names and expressions. Therefore, when a wise person wishes to contemplate *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), they must take mental discourse (*manojalpa*) as the object of contemplation;
since all are but a single consciousness, this means that while not departing from conceptual thought, one realizes that which is beyond conceptual thought, even within the midst of differentiation.

"Attaining Non-differentiation" (the above separately clarifies the two principles of the emptiness of nature and consciousness-only). *Ji yuan* (Vol. 2, Part 2) states: "First, one perceives that appearances are as they truly are; one contemplates that their nature is fundamentally empty.

Second, one perceives that appearances are like illusions—like flowers in the sky or the moon reflected in water; they are empty in their very appearance, without waiting for the contemplation of their nature.

Finally, one contemplates that all phenomena are merely transformations of the mind, and that there are no phenomena outside the mind. First, one contemplates arising and ceasing; [then] cessation..."

Having already seen emptiness, one next contemplates illusory transformations. Seeing emptiness within the place of birth, one subsequently contemplates mind-only. The illusory transformations of arising and ceasing are none other than the manifestations of the mind;
as the mind arises, phenomena arise, and as the mind ceases, phenomena cease. Although these arisings and ceasings possess marks, those marks are like illusory transformations.
The Lesser Vehicle practitioners and small sages perceive this as emptiness, yet they do not know that arising and ceasing, coming and going, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

Therefore, the Great Bodhisattvas only realize that all is mind-only and perfectly cultivate the three contemplations without being biased toward either nature or characteristics; thus, it is called the Middle Way.
The Principle and Practice of the Wisdom of Emptiness within the Three Trainings of the Hīnayāna.

(Question: Why are the three trainings cited as principle and practice? Answer: This is based on the fact that for those such as the inner-worldly ordinary beings (*prthagjana*) and those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), all practices they cultivate constitute principle-practice. As with the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*) below, it causes one to eliminate attachment and transgressions regarding the two obstacles.)

The meaning is evident. This passage is a commentary that resolves points of agreement and difference: that which is cultivated by those of the three vehicles is none other than the three trainings; however, because their aspirations vary in breadth and narrowness, and their contemplations vary in partiality and completeness, they are distinguished as Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
The Commentary further states: "Now, the comprehensive resolution and rectification does not go beyond the Three Studies. No sage has ever failed to practice these. If we consider the Two Vehicles:

regarding the Precepts, they take body and speech as their object (this refers to the general regulations); yet when a transgression occurs, one must examine the mind (according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*). If one clings to them [as mere rules], they become obstacles;

though these are worldly wholesome dharmas, violating them obstructs the Path and one cannot escape the three miserable realms. Regarding Concentration, it is defined by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), taking the cultivation of arising and ceasing as its object."

As for the principle (*li*), those of the Two Vehicles observe it identically, and there is likewise no distinction between [the truths of] suffering and its causes. Thus, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states:

"The persons of the Two Vehicles take the characteristics of impermanence (i.e., the aforementioned arising and ceasing) and so forth—based on the false (i.e., the aforementioned name-and-form)—as *tathatā* (i.e., the principle of emptiness).

While their wisdom (*prajñā*) takes up contemplative observation, this differs from the meaning of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) though they share the same substance. (Meditative concentration is stillness and tranquility; wisdom takes up illuminating function; hence it is said that 'the meanings differ. Since their substance is emptiness and there is no difference, it is said that 'the substance is the same. — *Jingde chuandeng lu Yeyi shu*.

(2b) It is said: Therefore, verbal karma and livelihood constitute the precepts of the Path. Mindfulness, concentration, and skillful means (*upāya*)—wherein "skillful means" refers to right effort—are explained in terms of meditative stillness (*dhyāna-śamatha*).

Since mindfulness and skillful means are not themselves formal meditative absorption, it is said they are "explained in terms of [the meaning of] meditation. Right thought and right view constitute the insight of wisdom (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*). Regarding the four modes of deportment, the application of discernment (*vicaya*) consists solely in the understanding of wisdom.
As soon as the mind of wisdom moves, one follows with mindfulness and pursues with awakening; first there is thought, and subsequently there is seeing. This seeing is the Path.

This refers to the patience of dharma (*dharmakṣānti*); therefore, it is not an ordinary stage (the former referring to the first fruit, the latter to the inner ordinary beings). Nevertheless, because there is a partial realization of contact, it is also termed "vision" (*darśana*).
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "One who attains worldly right view and does not fall into the evil realms possesses a semblance of outflow-free [wisdom]."

This severs the three miserable realms; generally speaking, this constitutes attainment. (The preceding section judged the three trainings and identified at what stage a person practices them; the following section, based on the underlying meaning, further clarifies precept and concentration. Regarding these precepts and concentrations:

To speak in terms of their essential meaning: since the mind has already taken principle as its object, it encompasses [the sword]; body and speech naturally become free from evil, and thoughts settle into clarity, flowing spontaneously without distraction. Based on these two meanings, they are called "precept" (śīla) and "concentration" (samādhi).
When one correctly withdraws body and mind and focuses solely on the principle of wisdom, the mind no longer dwells on transgressions, and body and speech do not arise [in unwholesome ways].

Thus, the three paths—speech, action, and livelihood—are so named. From this point onward, one contemplates and crosses over by taking principle as the object; with thoughts concentrated on the outflow-free (anāsrava), the mind does not scatter. This is what is meant by the term [wisdom] (prajñā).

Dhyāna. Thus, the three [aspects of] the Path—concentration and mindfulness (the application of mindfulness)—arise from this. (The above clarifies the definitions of precepts and concentration. Below, it clarifies how one cultivates precepts and concentration through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), giving rise to untainted merit;

this is termed "the practice of the Path"). Fundamentally, there is only the contemplation of wisdom. Defilements (*āsrava*) are the obstacles. By discerning the root of these obstacles, one ultimately reaches a state of non-reliance.
From this practice arises the production of non-action (non-action being the untainted merit). This karma is precisely what is called the existence of the Path.

(The previously cited passage from the *Chao* [Commentary] distinguishes the three trainings according to their teaching and their characteristics; the subsequently cited passage from the *Ye-sou* [Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā] determines their inclusion and归宿 [final destination] according to their meaning and stages. Question: Regarding the three trainings for the practice of the Path explained above, at what stage does a person cultivate them? Answer: As shown in the text.

The first refers to the fruit of the first stage (srotāpanna); the second refers to the inner ordinary person (antarapudgala). Now, I shall further offer my private reflections. In cultivation there are those who are sharp and those who are dull; in insight there are those who are sudden and those who are gradual. For one who is dull in cultivation but sudden in insight, they must reach the first fruit before they can integrate their practice with principle through reasoning.

For one who is sharp in cultivation and gradual in clarity, although they remain at the stage of expedient means, they are able to dissolve [delusions] through wisdom. Thus, it is known that this text also addresses beginners. The preceding clarification regarding sharpness and dullness is based entirely upon the Hīnayāna.
The commentary further clarifies the principles of the objects [of meditation] and the teachings, as previously explained in the *Zizhi* (Vol.

4, Part 2). "Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*) that constitute the object of contemplation. One aggregate is form (*rūpa*), while four aggregates belong to the mind (*citta*).

Because the path of the mind is subtle and obscure, it can only be designated by the general term "name. Therefore, they are collectively referred to as "name. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Among all dharmas, there are only name and..."

Regarding form (*rūpa*): if one wishes to contemplate it as it truly is, one should simply contemplate name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). (The above clarifies the object. Through cultivation based on conditions, one is able to contemplate the mind;
arising and ceasing are the principle that is perceived. Because the two dharmas of form and mind arise and cease from moment to moment, they are impermanent due to their arising and ceasing.

Because they are impermanent, they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty and quiescent (*śūnya-śānta*). This emptiness and quiescence is the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), Nirvana, and True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The Nirvāṇa Verses state: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. (The above clarifies the principle.
Although the vehicles relied upon by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas differ, their realization of the principle is the same.

The Four Noble Truths of the Śrāvakas and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination of the Pratyekabuddhas are merely differences in the expansion and contraction of the pedagogical gateways. Since the teaching is harmonized with the principle, there is no distinction between them.

One should know that suffering (*duḥkha*) and its accumulation (*samudaya*), along with the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), are both worldly causes and effects.
The Path (*mārga*) and Cessation (*nirodha*), together with the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination, are all supramundane causes and effects (the above clarifies the Teaching).

In the *Buddhatva-śāstra*, regarding the distinctions between True Suchness (*tathatā*) in the two vehicles, Great and Small, the text appears in the fourth [chapter]. That text continues: "This false contemplation exists only within the stage of the cause (*hetu*)."

It exists [in the causal stage], but it is absent at the stage of fruition. Therefore, this *tathatā* (the *tathatā* of the Hīnayāna) is established in the causal stage but destroyed in the stage of fruition (because it abides in emptiness).
As for the *tathatā* of the Bodhisattva, it is free from falsehood; because one contemplates the real by means of the true nature (*dharmatā*), it is *tathatā*.
This *tathatā* is no different in either cause or fruit; therefore, it is established as being indestructible. Thus, the *tathatā* of the two vehicles—

Following its cessation and extinction, it departs and does not return. For the Bodhisattva who is "Suchness" (tathatā), cause and effect are eternally present; departure and arrival are no different.

Because he abandons the cause to reach the fruit, he is called "One Who Has Thus Gone" (Tathāgata). Because he emerges from the fruit to manifest activity, he is called "One Who Has Thus Come" (Tathāgata). (The above is from the *Śāstra*).

The Practice of the Path of Consciousness-Only in the Three Trainings of the Mahāyāna: First, the Exposition of the Training in Ethics (*śīla-śikṣā*). (This text also resolves points of agreement and difference. First, regarding the teaching:

the Great Precepts of the threefold aggregate of discipline (*tri-saṃvara*) are the same as those of the Hīnayāna; the other two [trainings] differ from the Hīnayāna. Furthermore, within the discipline itself, there are also points of agreement and difference, which may be seen below. Second, regarding the capacity of the practitioner (*yogin*):

if one’s wisdom is perfected and practice is sublime, then even through the Hīnayāna precepts one accomplishes the Great Vehicle practice. Such a person is not different from a Śrāvaka, yet they are a Bodhisattva. This is no different from the stages and positions of the Hīnayāna; it is simply that their position and aspiration are perfected through the Great Vehicle perspective. Regarding the contrast...
For those living at home, their aspirations and observations are the same, though their practice and stages differ.
The *Shisao* (Volume 4, Part 2) states: "If one relies on the Mahāyāna, precepts are divided into three grades; the first grade, the *vinaya-saṃvara*, is no different from that of the Śrāvakas."

It is not that there is no difference between the two or three [categories]; rather, the precept of guarding the mind exceeds the standard forms. The *Yeshu* (Vol. 2, Part B) states: "If one relies on the Mahāyāna, the precepts are divided into three grades.

When categorized by their meaning and encompassed by their conditions, they do not differ from the various Vinayas. How is this clarified? Take, for example, the single precept against killing, which fully incorporates all three positions:

to cease all conditions for killing is to embrace the restraint of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*); to constantly practice the life of wisdom is to embrace the cultivation of goodness (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*)."

This is the Dharma. Because it protects previous lives, it thereby encompasses sentient beings. Since this one case is thus, the others follow by analogy. The *Ji yuan* (Expedient Means), fascicle 2, states:

"The designation of the three grades refers to the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*). This is from the *Yingluo jing* (Necklace Sūtra): first, the precept of restraining conduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), which restrains evil and is the cessation of evil;

second, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), which is the cultivation of goodness; third, the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla*)."

The precept of restraint is also called the precept of benefiting sentient beings; it is precisely the saving of living beings. In the Hīnayāna, rules are established separately according to circumstances, whereas in the Mahāyāna, they are summarized based on the mind.
Therefore, by means of these three precepts, all are universally encompassed; thus, they are called a "collection. Consequently, in severing evil, there is no evil that is not severed;
in cultivating good, there is no good that is not cultivated; and in gathering in sentient beings, there is no being who is not gathered.

[This applies to] all [precepts]. To take the precept against killing as an example, the others are treated analogously. Regarding sexual misconduct: one ceases all conditions for defilement (this is the restraint of conduct);

one constantly cultivates pure conduct (this is the gathering of wholesome dharmas); and one does not defile those born before oneself (this is the gathering of sentient beings). Regarding stealing: one distances oneself from conditions of encroachment and damage;

one constantly practices giving; and one does not distress those born before oneself. Regarding false speech: one distances oneself from conditions of falsehood; one constantly practices truthful speech; and one does not deceive those born before oneself.
Down to the *śaikṣa* rules, every category and type of teaching is nothing other than the three clusters (*tri-skandha*).

If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the śrāvaka precepts consist only of the single cluster of "severing evil," as they do not deliver sentient beings and do not practice skillful means; thus, they lack the remaining two clusters.

Now, taking the general principle to resolve the specific school, if we clarify their commonality based on the underlying meaning, there is nothing that does not equally possess all three. Thus the verse says: "It is foul and putrid; it does not grow from among flowers, nor from the *campaka*, nor does it emerge from a mountain of jewels."
Third, one should contemplate the body as impure, consisting of the thirty-six constituent substances.

These form the body through twelve internal and twelve external factors, each category comprising twelve items. The twelve that constitute the body are: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, thin skin, thick skin, tendons, bones, flesh, marrow, blood, and the mind. The twelve internal [substances] are:

spleen, kidneys, gallbladder, liver, lungs, small intestine, large intestine, stomach, bladder (*piao*), fat (*fang*), lymph (*che*), and brain matter. The twelve external [substances] are: feces, urine, filth, sweat, tears, nasal mucus, saliva, pus, yellow phlegm, white phlegm, and rheumatism. Therefore, a verse says: "Earth, water, fire..."
Wind-nature. It can transform other impurities, yet even if one were to empty the ocean to wash this body, it could not be made fragrant or clean.

Regarding the four external impurities: the nine orifices constantly discharge [filth], and none of them are fit for use. Thus, the verse says: "Various kinds of impure things fill the interior of the body;
they flow out incessantly, like a leaking bag containing goods. Fifth, ultimate impurity: at the end...
Upon returning [to death], the body becomes bloated and unbearable to behold. Thus, a verse says: "Examine this body with discernment; it will ultimately return to the place of certain death.
It is difficult to restrain and does not turn back; it is as ungrateful as a small child."
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), Part Two, states:
"For those deluded regarding the mind, the *skandhas* (aggregates) are taught. Taking the characteristics of form as one, the mind is divided into four.

This causes one to know that consciousness, perception, and feeling have not yet become karma; if one reaches the stage of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), then the three poisons and the three virtues are manifested accordingly."
If one acts thus, it becomes incurable; therefore, one must always maintain single-mindedness and remain mindful of removing the various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

This constitutes the medicine. At the time the illness manifests, [the medicine] has already vanished; to remember it only when the illness is fully formed is beyond description. For those deluded regarding form (*rūpa*), entry [into the path] is taught.

The six sense objects (*viṣaya*) and the five faculties (*indriya*) are all form; the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is not deluded because it does not differentiate. This applies to delusion regarding both form and mind.
For their sake, the realms are explained: matter is divided into eleven categories, and mind is divided into seven. As for medicinal treatment, it may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
These persons and dharmas pertain to both ordinary beings and sages; however, the observation that consciousness is illusory is a realization unique to the sages.
To think "I am the one who observes" is an inverted notion of ordinary beings and is not to be trusted.
The Commentary clarifies that a bhikṣu should practice contemplation during the four modes of conduct (as explained in the Vinaya and Śāstras).

Regarding the expressions "single-mindedness" and "a single thought-moment," these encompass both principle and phenomena; they include both the provisional and the ultimate, and should be adopted or discarded according to the capacity of the practitioner, rather than being rigidly adhered to as mere literal text.
The Vinaya states: The Buddha ordained that one must maintain dignified deportment.

Whether entering or exiting, bending or stretching, looking down or looking up, holding the robes and bowl, drinking, eating, or taking medicine, whether defecating or urinating, sleeping, dozing, or waking, coming or going, sitting or lying down, speaking or remaining silent—one must always remain thus with a single-minded focus. Should one violate this regulation, [the offense is complete].

Regarding the binding of transgressions, the *Ji* (Record) states: "Thus we know that true renunciants never forget mindfulness. This regulation is subtle and applies even to those of superior faculties;
however, for the dull-witted of the末法 (mofa) age, it is beyond their capacity. According to the *Mātṛkā-vinaya-śāstra*, one should practice contemplation regarding food and clothing:

those of sharp faculties contemplate every morsel and every mouthful, while those of dull faculties contemplate them as a single thought-moment. Nevertheless, one must exert effort, aspiring to increase [one's practice] toward the higher [levels].
When practicing, one must not allow oneself to be disheartened by being content with inferior faculties, nor should one immediately succumb to indolence; therefore, one must exert diligent effort.
If one practices according to this guidance, then leaving the household life will not have been in vain.
Using contemplation to rectify transgressions, when transgressions arise, the body and mind turn toward reverence.
The ritual manual states: "Contemplating this through words, one recognizes the two paths of form and mind, and the dual tracks of phenomena and principle.

As for form, it is bound by worldly habits and the aggregate of suffering constantly entangles it; therefore, one must break and crush it to take refuge in its analysis. One analyzes and contemplates."

Regarding this delusion of pride: the mind is then sealed within confusion and inversion; inversion persists as the habitual state of birth. Therefore, one must use the mirror of arising and ceasing to chasten it through recollection.
Through recollection, one knows its false attachments. One deeply contemplates that the four mountains constantly press in, yet one does not realize it moment by moment;
it is urgent for the person. The eight inversions entwine and cling, yet one does not understand them anew at every instant; they are constricted within the mind.
Thus, the analytical discernment that brings tranquility to the delusions of pride is not what those who delight in craving seek;

the retrospective contemplation that breeds weariness with false attachments is what ordinary worldlings turn their backs upon. One must surely embrace the sincere teachings and examine them through the Dharma;
only then will one’s physical life not be cast away in vain among the lower dusts, and one’s lack of wisdom not remain idle in the higher realms.
At the initial stage of cultivating *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), one clearly discerns the ultimate and conventional truths (*tathatā-saṃvṛti*).

It is further stated: "One should also form this thought: although what is seen is form (*rūpa*), it arises from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*); that which realizes form as mind arises from dependent origination (*paratantra*).

Since there is no object outside of mind, one eliminates external objects by overturning the nature of pervasive conceptualization; this is called 'true contemplation' (*bhūtadarśana*). As for the statement that [objects] arise from mind, this refers to mental discourse (*manojalpa*); in reality, they are only..."
When consciousness exists [by appearing as if it were external objects, while in fact being "mere consciousness"], this is called conventional observation (*sāmvrta-darśana*).

As this gradually increases in clarity, continuing uninterruptedly from moment to moment, the power of practice accumulates and the perfuming (*vāsanā*) grows ever stronger. When the path of observation is cultivated until it is bright and clear, one no longer becomes deluded regarding the dependent nature of conditions;

this is called "aspiration and delight" (*adhimukti*). Such a person is a practitioner of the Way. Since the Way is cultivated by people, and people are able to cultivate the Way, they are called "practitioners" (*yogācāra*) or "people of the Way" (*mārga-jana*). (Jingjian says: One must...)

Based on the sharpness or dullness of the faculties and the shallowness or depth of the hindrances, one discusses the duration [of practice]. This treatise divides the fifty-two stages into four positions. It further states: "In the text, 'aspiration and joy' refers to the first position; 'cultivation of the path' refers to the third position; and 'contemplating the provisional' refers to the object of observation.

Regarding the passage on "penetrating the true," it asks: "At what stage can a person cultivate this contemplation? It answers: "Speaking in terms of practice, even an ordinary person at the initial stage of the mind can cultivate this contemplation. Such a person is then called a Great Bodhisattva, and this very practice is declared to be the fruit of Buddhahood."

Regarding the "Realization Practice" (*sākṣātkriyā-caryā*): speaking in terms of stages and according to the text based on the treatises, it is the practitioner who possesses aspiration and joy (*adhimukti-caryā*) who is able to realize this principle. Question: Various schools include all four stages within this; why do you now specifically differ from them? Please explain the reason for this. Answer:

Because they do not recognize the characteristics of this contemplation, there is an indiscriminate conflation. This contemplation only eliminates external objects (*bāhyārtha*), yet mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) still persists. How can one falsely claim that this stage extends to the higher positions? Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "If one has reached the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), then even that which resembles 'consciousness-only' (*vijñaptimātra*)—namely, mental verbal conceptualization—can no longer arise.

Since mental verbalization is present in this contemplation, how could it extend to the higher positions? The text clearly judges it as belonging to the stage of "aspiration and joy," the person practicing the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
"Penetrating principles and mastering affairs depend on the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties.

It is further said: "Now, based on two conditions, we establish the outward manifestations of practice. Although there are many gateways for entering the Way, they do not exceed principle (*li*) and affairs (*shi*).

'Principle' refers to the fundamental way, which penetrates the far-reaching intentions of the sages; 'affairs' refers to specific matters, which are measured according to the extended deliberations of ordinary sentiments. The Sage is not..."
From the sages onward, one ultimately relies on guidance to gradually attain clarity; even ordinary people are not fixed as ordinary, for they too reach understanding through the opening of the Way.

Thus we know that the distinctions between the ignorant and the wise, the shallow and the deep, and the various ranks of the worthy and the holy, arise from the distance or proximity of their understanding and practice, resulting in the divergence of sharpness and dullness.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Non-conceptual wisdom is itself the bodhisattva; the bodhisattva is himself non-conceptual wisdom.
Regarding the stages of the bodhisattva, more than fifty levels are enumerated in detail. Thus, one knows that non-conceptual wisdom fluctuates between sharpness and dullness from moment to moment;
this statement possesses profound significance.
It is further stated: "The two truths of the ultimate and the conventional have been elucidated to manifest perfect practice.
Moreover, these two truths of the ultimate and the conventional have existed since time immemorial; they manifest spontaneously without relying on deliberate effort. Thus, the treatise says:
'The Buddhas always rely upon the two truths when teaching the Dharma. Our current practice of paying respect likewise accords with this sacred word, and is therefore neither false nor erroneous."
Furthermore, Sudatta understood the basis for the two truths; thus the treatise states: "To know that objects have no existence is to penetrate the ultimate (paramārtha-satya);
to know that there is only consciousness is to penetrate the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya). If one does not penetrate the conventional, there is no means to penetrate the ultimate;

if one does not penetrate the ultimate, there is no means to eliminate the conventional, because the conventional has no separate essence. This treatise establishes contemplation so as to enable people to receive and practice it, precisely because...

The ultimate and the conventional are restored; emptiness and existence meet at their source. If one follows deluded thoughts and views, the path of birth increases daily; if one awakens the body and mind, the lofty track emerges in hidden majesty.
Is it not because the physical form is bound by shackles and the fruits of retribution cannot be extinguished all at once—that we speak of "conforming to the conventional"?

And is it not because the mind can be discussed through names yet its true nature remains unknown when subjected to analytical scrutiny—that we speak of "penetrating the ultimate"? While it is easy to purify [the mind] within words, the ultimate...
The principle may be sought by applying the mind, yet it is difficult to clarify based on practice because of beginningless habitual conditioning (*vāsanā*).

The *Tongzhengi* (Middle Volume), in discussing the ultimate and the conventional, states: "The single contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*) perfectly encompasses both the ultimate and the conventional. Now, following the names, we shall seek their essential nature.

Furthermore, based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), one may distinguish between the ultimate and the conventional truths. That is to say, the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)—which exists falsely and is precisely the conventional truth—is so called because the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*) cling to it as having a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*).

The dependent nature (this nature is conventionally existent and is also the conventional truth; it takes as its essence the manifestation of objects based upon those eight consciousnesses). The perfected nature (this nature is truly existent and is the ultimate truth;

its essence is suchness, for it is the common characteristic of both the real and the conventional). If considered in terms of perfect cultivation, then the three natures and the three truths are fully encompassed within a single thought-moment;

perfect realization is likewise so. Now, considering the progressive abandonment, these three natures are inverted to become the three non-natures; thus, there are the depths and shallows of the real and the conventional.

Regarding the differences in stages, this is the gate of sequential cultivation (*vipaśyanā*). Do not doubt that these are separate; rather, taking the stage prior to the [ten] grounds as an example, by relying on the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), one eliminates the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
Thus, the imagined nature is transformed into the *niṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). Because the imagined nature is empty, it is called the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).

Because it is manifested in dependence [upon others], it is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). As for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), its essence permeates both the real and the conventional; it is termed "according to existence or non-existence.

If one regards the conceptualized [nature] in light of the signless, then the conventional is shallow and the real is deep. If one regards the signless in light of the dependent [nature], then the conventional is deep and the real is shallow.

If one refers to the stage of entering the [first] ground (*bhūmi*), one correctly relies upon the perfected nature to eliminate the dependent nature and seek the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

Examining that dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as being of the nature of non-arising, it is said that one portion of this nature is non-arising and is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while another portion is conventionally existent and is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
By realizing non-arising, because consciousness is understood to be empty, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is thereby revealed.

Established according to principle, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the ultimate emptiness beyond all dependence. Since it is not an object of grasping, it fundamentally does not require translation.

Nevertheless, because one follows delusion, this name is established to manifest the real by means of the provisional. Now, when the wisdom of non-arising emptiness manifests, it reveals the perfected nature accordingly.

Regarding one aspect of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): since the false (*mṛṣā*) is already non-arising, how could the true (*satya*) be established? Thus, both existence and emptiness are simultaneously discarded, returning to the original absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Therefore, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is termed the "nature of the absence of nature" (*niḥsvabhāva-svabhāva*). If one compares the non-arising [perfected nature] with the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), then the true is profound and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) is shallow.
If one considers the perfected nature in relation to the preceding two natures, then both the true and the conventional are shallow, while the perfected nature alone is profound. This is because...

It is a single principle because it serves as the foundational substance for both the ultimate and the conventional truths; because from the stage of ordinary beings to that of the sages, it is universally observed from beginning to end;
because the cultivation of cause and fruit is perfected without distinction; and because it is the fruit realized by the Sublime Enlightenment.
It is said that contemplating the body as being merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) and its wondrous integration is the true form of respectful conduct.
Furthermore, it says: "This physical demeanor fundamentally exists only as consciousness; yet, deluded by fundamental habituation, one falsely perceives a self and others."

Therefore, one must investigate and examine this: cause others to practice respectful care and behold my body. Whether looking up or down, moving forward or backward, bending or stretching—these are merely the arising and ceasing of dust;
such coming and going follows worldly convention. Re-examine this body again: it is but dust and not the self, yet we delusively claim it as "mine."

To be able to practice respect based on this single principle is called "penetrating the true. The True is fundamentally not the mind; that it now arises in accordance with the mind is called "following the conventional.
To know that the True is not the mind is called "penetrating the true. Thus, in every thought-moment, the subsequent supersedes the former.
Gradually it increases in clarity, and after a long time it becomes sharp and penetrating.
When setting out to practice reverence, one must contemplate both the ultimate (paramārtha) and conventional (saṃvṛti) truths.

Furthermore, it is said: "Thus, the path of the sages and ordinary beings has been transmitted from antiquity. Ordinary beings are not fixed as ordinary; therefore, there are those who flow against the current."
Regarding the traces of returning to the source: the Sage is not inherently a sage; it is ultimately through the merit of gradual awakening and penetrating contemplation that one becomes so.

Thus, that which allows an ordinary person to become a sage takes the Buddha-nature as its fundamental principle, while that which prevents a sage from becoming ordinary takes awakened understanding as its refuge.

One should know that while the affairs of principle and phenomena are temporarily separated by form and mind, when it comes to dynamic application, the ultimate and the conventional are observed together. Therefore, in accordance with their manifestation...

This is sufficient. To conclude, one must understand that the manifest is non-existent and that true reality is revealed through this knowledge; that which is conventional arises from conditions, and only then can there be stages of progress.

If body and mind are divided into two parts, and the ultimate and the conventional into two separate paths, then the three inversions will persist constantly—on what day could one transform from the state of an ordinary person?
(The three inversions are as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: inversion of perception, inversion of thought, and inversion of view.)
To further demonstrate the complete cultivation [of the path] and to resolve doubts by establishing challenges, it is said:

There are those whose mental paths are terrified and distraught, finding no standard to which they can turn their hearts. Upon hearing this teaching of mine, they suddenly break out in protest, saying:
Clapping his hands, he laughed loudly and said, "How easy it is to speak! How utterly vain and extravagant! Alas, you have not studied; you speak recklessly without foundation.

I have heard that one contemplates both the ultimate and the conventional truths only upon reaching the stages of realization (*bhūmi*). How can you, an ordinary person of the lower realms, presume to act like a sage of the higher stages?

This is contrary to principle and logic; you must change this immediately. I replied, "It cannot be changed. Once the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) has been awakened, it is pursued to its ultimate conclusion; from the initial mind to the final mind, [it remains as it is]."

Equanimity. The four stages of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*) are studied by both ordinary beings and sages alike. Now, if those at the lower level of ordinary beings do not study them, how could there be any prospect of attaining sagehood?

Therefore, one must set out with determination and practice them concurrently. Through cultivation, one naturally clarifies the stages of sagehood. Thus, we know that practitioners on the path of cultivation must constantly contemplate the correct principle;

they must not cling to the literal text, for to do so would deviate from the reality of the meaning. Therefore, one should examine errors according to the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) and accord with them in every thought-moment.
One must rely on wisdom (*jñāna*) and not on consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness is that which is practiced by the mundane; wisdom is the "fishing net" of the Path.

The Sages established the correct regulations so that there might be no arbitrary confusion regarding the clarity of the higher stages. These [regulations] merely rely on the conditions of the stages; yet when one examines their dual movement, they ultimately converge in wondrous enlightenment.
Thus, a sutra says: "Constantly abiding in samādhi, one sees all Buddha-lands without employing dualistic marks. This text may be relied upon as such. As it is said:
The section on "Grasping" has not yet been opened. To further clarify the stages (*bhūmi*), practices (*caryā*), and positions (*avasthā*) through extensive citations from the sūtras and śāstras:

in the first stage, there is purity of giving (*dāna-viśuddhi*); in the second stage, there is purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*). How could it be that one must pass through an entire *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* before practicing giving and discipline?

This also demonstrates the relative depth of the stages and the gradual progression of their characteristics, so that those who strive in cultivation may expect to follow the tracks of the realized ones. If one were to explain it thus...
When the myriad practices are cultivated together and one advances along the common thoroughfare, the path of the mind becomes vast and obscure, and its traces are unknown.
Thus, the records of the teachings appear diverse; yet, if one can unify them with a single principle, one will behold the great view of the sun and moon.
Regarding the eighth point on majestic deportment (*vīrya-rūpa*), it says: "In the Buddha-dharma, the mind is the root and the body is its branch.

Therefore, when Subhūti was in quiet contemplation within his chamber, the Tathāgata praised him as one who 'sees the Dharma-body through prostration. When Huase first arrived at the jeweled steps, the Tathāgata disparaged [him]."

Because one pays homage to the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha), one knows that by contemplating the subtle in a quiet place, every thought-moment tends toward the Way. Observing forms and reflecting on appearances, one sees that from moment to moment one remains in the mundane world;

yet, as the subject-object duality cannot be avoided, perceptions and views arise simultaneously. When the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*) manifests before one, it immediately becomes an obstacle to the Way.

Therefore, the Buddha distinguished between physical and mental reverence based on this. If one can contemplate form as being empty and observe that objects are created by the mind, [the confusion...]
They arise in chaotic profusion; there is nothing that is not either defiled or pure. When consciousness and deluded thoughts have not yet been clarified, perceptions remain inverted.
Only when the time comes for these to empty away will conditioned thoughts be severed. Now, dwelling on the level of ordinary beings, one can only exercise control to this extent.

As every thought naturally proceeds, one gradually becomes able to attain purity. One must constantly give rise to two contemplations and may not practice them in isolation. This means knowing that there is no objective realm; this is the gradual movement toward the Truth. This means...

Knowing that there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) is to gradually turn one's back on the mundane. Cultivating in this manner without ceasing for a long duration, it becomes increasingly clear stage by stage until it is finally accomplished after three great eons (*tri-kalpa*).
To illustrate this, I shall cite the ancient practice of the "Sevenfold Prostration" to clarify the presence or absence of contemplative observation.

(First, prostrating with pride while lacking contemplation incurs an offense. Second and third, prostrating without contemplation of the object merely produces merit. From the fourth onwards, it depends on the depth of one's contemplative wisdom and the clarity with which one perceives the principle.)

Furthermore, it is said (as above): "First, regarding what is called 'the prostration of self-conceit' (*māna-abhimāna*): this refers to performing the ritual according to one's rank and status while lacking a mind of reverence;

exalting one's own virtues while lacking the intent to look up to a teacher; feeling ashamed to ask questions of those below; having no one from whom to seek instruction or receive teachings; and having no Dharma as a basis for the mind.

Like a pestle moving up and down, it is merely a physical action performed by the body alone; the mind does not dwell upon the object [of worship]. Thus, one treats life lightly and disparages the Path, laboring in vain without benefit. This is observed externally..."

Regarding prostration: if one’s internal sense of pride increases so that one is like a wooden man, lacking earnest sincerity, such that the head does not touch the ground and the five wheels (the five points of contact) are not complete—this is the karma of pride, called "prostration with pride" (*māna-pūjā*).
Second, as for "responsive prostration": although it is not characterized by arrogance, the mind lacks pure contemplation;

while the external deportment is roughly correct and body and mind abide in respect, the rising and falling follow one another in a manner that is merely superficial and provides a slight mutual support. Its merit...
[This is] meager and insufficient; it is not true worship. Third, regarding those who pay homage with physical and mental reverence:

upon hearing the invocation of the Buddha’s name, they immediately bring to mind the Buddha’s body as if it were before their eyes—complete with all the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), radiant and magnificent, the perfection of mental characteristics.

Facing the Three Bodies (*trikāya*) as if they were precious jewels, [the Buddha] extends his hand to stroke their crowns, removing their karmic offenses. Therefore, with physical and mental reverence and without any other thoughts, they make offerings.
Cultivating reverence with a heart that never tires is called worshipping the Buddha through the realm of objects.

When the eye of the mind manifests before one, focusing single-mindedly without dullness, such a person guides and benefits humans and devas; they are supreme and foremost. Although their merit is great, it is not yet the wisdom-mind, and later they will frequently fall back and decline.
Fourth is the pure worship of the Buddha through the arousal of wisdom: the practitioner’s wisdom-mind is luminous as they penetrate the realm of the Buddha while worshipping him.

Benefit. One deeply understands that the Dharma-realm is fundamentally without obstruction. Since beginningless time, I have followed the ways of ordinary people, perceiving what is not-existent as existent and what is not-obstructed as obstructed.
Now, having realized that my own mind is empty, pervasive, and without obstruction, I perform prostrations to the Buddha according to the direct manifestation of the mind.
Prostrating to one Buddha is prostrating to all Buddhas; all Buddhas are one Buddha. This is because the Buddha’s Dharma-body is universally pervasive.
Because they are equally unimpeded, paying homage to a single Buddha pervades all [Buddhas]. The same applies by analogy to various offerings of incense and flowers.
The same principle holds for showing increased reverence toward the Dharma and the Saṅgha, because the Three Jewels share the same nature and there is no difference in their underlying reality.
The names of the Three Vehicles differ, but the essence of liberation is the same. Therefore, one should know that a single prostration is a prostration to all.

Being able to thus penetrate the nature of these Three Jewels, one regards all beings within the three realms, the six destinies, and the four modes of birth as Buddhas, making offerings and paying homage to them.
Having purified one's own body and mind, one becomes vast and free from obstructions. As one contemplates the realm of the Buddha, the characteristics of the mind become increasingly clear.

With every prostration and every rising, one regards [the Buddha] as most honored and supreme; this is called the truly real and extraordinarily great fruit of retribution. Because the mind is limitless, pure karma is likewise inexhaustible.
Regarding those who enter the Dharma-realm through the five sciences, performing prostrations and making offerings: the practitioner visualizes themselves...
The mental dharmas have, from the very beginning, never existed outside the dharma-realm or apart from the Buddha’s dharma-body.
One also knows that the bodies, minds, and dharmas of all Buddhas do not exist outside one’s own body.

When one gives rise to understanding and attains penetration such that one’s own body and all other bodies pervade the entire dharma-realm, this is called the dharma-realm—neither increasing nor decreasing, the gate of pure dharma. Understanding it thus, one knows that I now pay homage.

Regarding a single Buddha: the body of one Buddha pervades the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Within this Dharma-realm, in all the stages and positions of the triple world, the untainted *dharmakāya* is entirely the Buddha-body.
Since the Buddha-body thus pervades everything, my own body, following that of the Buddha, also pervades everything.
Therefore, when performing prostrations and making offerings, [one does so] within all bodies, which are fully endowed with adornments. However, this...

The Dharma-realm is by nature eternally quiescent, yet it pervades all things according to conditions. Even in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, as well as in causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions, nothing is apart from the Dharma-realm.
Because the body follows the mind, one attains unimpeded understanding. Through the dependent origination of the Dharma-realm, all phenomena are accomplished.
It is as if within a single room, hundreds of thousands of mirrors are suspended. A person sees them alone, yet within every mirror, images appear.
The Buddha-body is pure, its brilliance surpassing those mirrors; thus, throughout the entire dharma-realm, all are manifested within it.
Therefore, when I make offerings to all ordinary beings and sages, the bodies of both the ordinary and the sage are equally offered. Those with eyes see this; the blind do not behold it.
Practicing and studying in this manner, the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm brings great benefit; it culminates in this realization. Without study, one does not know it.
Therefore, the practitioner must constantly maintain contemplative observation. The merit thereby obtained is beyond measure. Having thus understood my own body, [one understands all bodies].
How could one create karma through delusion within the Buddha-body? Sixth, clarifying right contemplation:
one should pay homage to the Buddha within one’s own body rather than taking external objects as conditions—other Buddhas or other bodies. Why is this?

All sentient beings inherently possess Buddha-nature, which is equal and complete, conforming to the *dharmadhātu* and blazing forth through dependent origination. It is only because of delusion that one perceives an external object to be contemplated.
Due to delusive inversion, one constantly sinks into birth and death; if one can reflect back upon oneself, there will be a time for liberation.
If one turns toward external objects, claiming there is something to be observed, this is the practice of heterodox persons, which the scriptures do not permit. Therefore it is said:

"Do not observe the Buddha, do not observe the Dharma, do not observe the Sangha," because one perceives the true nature of reality within oneself. It is further said: "To perceive me through form and sound is called practicing a heterodox path."
Therefore, the practitioner constantly performs prostrations. Seeing only body and mind, they possess both ritual and reverence, yet have not yet attained thorough understanding.

Through constant practice born of weariness with delusion, they later achieve penetration. Realizing that the mind has no external object, they finally recognize their own mind—the pure intrinsic nature;

this is the Buddha-nature abiding in its own essence (*svabhāva-viśuddha-buddhatā*). Cultivating and clarifying it according to one's capacity is the Buddha-nature brought forth (*niryūḍha-buddhatā*). This is the fruit of the three great incalculable eons (*tri-kalpāsaṃkhyeya*).
The perfection of the ten stages culminates in attaining the Buddha-nature as the fruit. This interpretation is subtle and profound; it is understood only by the sages.

Although one’s current stage is that of an ordinary person, it is not appropriate to fail to understand this, nor to fail to practice it. Seventh, regarding the clarification of the Three Treasures of True Reality (*dharmatā*):

the general meaning of prostrating with the equality of self and other is the same as before. Previously, there was still a distinction between the act of prostration and the object of contemplation, such that self and other were two different things. Now, in this case, there is none.

One's own mind has been intrinsically pure from the very beginning; it is neither empty nor existent, neither defiled nor pure, and is free from all conceptual discrimination.

Commentary on the Four Reliances (This reveals the Patriarch’s intention; it is the ultimate destination, realized solely through the definitive meaning.
Furthermore, (Section Six: Citing the Teachings) Regarding "rely on the Dharma, not on the person": a person exists only as a mental construct, whereas the Dharma is the standard and model.

Its nature is emptiness—the correct principle (the nature of emptiness applies to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna)—and its essence is free from falsehood. One should take this very Dharma as the reliance for the True Dharma, the ultimate teaching of Nirvāṇa.

To flourish and clarify this path (the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Relying on the Dharma" means relying on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); "not relying on persons" means not relying on śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). If one can turn back that worldly mind, [one will attain liberation].

Relying upon the authoritative measure of the Sage, one conceals the mind and applies oneself to practice. Knowing that what is not [ultimately real] is empty by nature, one takes this mind as the vehicle and sustains it as the path.

One portion consists of knowing what is not [real], clarifying compliance with the principle of emptiness; another portion consists of contemplating weariness, clarifying the departure from phenomenal existence. Thus one settles the mind.
The various designations are called "cultivation" and "practice. The true path is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the principle of "relying on the meaning and not on the words": words are mere verbal expressions; cessation is like casting away a fishing trap.

Meaning is that which penetrates the principle—the way to transform sentient beings (where "transforming" means changing). Once realization and understanding have been attained, one cuts off discursive thought and silences speech. If even the Dharma should be relinquished, how much more so that which is not the Dharma?
Therefore, the Sūtras contain the metaphor of abandoning the raft. People cherish the discourse on "witnessing with the eyes" (as the *Zhuangzi* says: "the Way exists in a glance").

Is this not because words serve to explain the meaning, yet once the meaning is grasped, one ceases from words? The moon is like a subtle finger; it is impossible not to understand this. (The former clarifies that meaning is provisionally expressed through language, while the latter shows that once the meaning is seen, one abandons the language.

Now, I say that when the meaning is attained, the meaning itself is the word. A true practitioner of the Way constantly contemplates and constantly breaks [through attachments]; they constantly contemplate...

Rely on the meaning and constantly break away from following the words; that is to say, although one may follow the words, they are merely reciting them (the former refers to having attained the meaning while forgetting the words, yet one must still dispel the notion that the meaning does not exist).
Regarding "rely on wisdom and do not rely on consciousness": "consciousness" refers to active functioning, which discriminates perceptions according to sensory objects.

When the eyes [grasp] forms and the ears [grasp] sounds, one becomes addicted and deluded without awareness, passing through existence like cattle and sheep, and walking together with the ignorant and the heterodox. (The above clarifies that the deluded thoughts of the six consciousnesses are what humans and animals alike depend upon.)

Therefore, there is falling into ruin. Having commanded that one rely on Buddha-wisdom—which is precisely the contemplation of consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātratā)—one is enabled to diminish faults and gradually attain clarity). The Great Sage demonstrated and taught that objects are one's own mind;

yet those of inferior ignorance cling to them as ice, holding that sensory dust exists outside of consciousness. Thus, there is no way to guide and transform them unless they abandon this [view]. It is known, therefore, that stagnation leads back to ordinary consciousness.

The noble mind is overturned and deluded by ignorance; one constantly sinks into the three inversions. With courageous diligence and exceptional penetration, one recognizes the movement of thought as it arises.
Knowing that these inversions are difficult to purify is called "relying on consciousness. Knowing that the flow must be reversed is called "wisdom according to its capacity. Thus one applies effort.

As clarity gradually increases and becomes vast, one later perceives the realm of sensory objects and knows they do not come from without; that the objects are not external to the mind, but are manifestations of one's own mind.
How could there be such delusion as to give rise to aversion or attachment? Through ceaseless contemplation and discernment, one comes to understand this differently than a cow or a sheep.

Regarding the reliance on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) rather than those of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*): both of these types of sūtras are the authoritative word of the Sage (*āptavacana*).
Any who enter the Path should first understand them; then there will be no obstructions or impediments, and all doubts will be resolved. This is done solely for the sake of sentient beings.

The capacities and depths of their natures vary, being either sharp or dull; this causes the Great Sage to provide distinct teachings according to their dispositions. However, according to the ultimate Way, it is nothing other than one’s own mind. Thus, a sutra says:

Furthermore, it says: "Suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)... [and so forth regarding the seeds].

Reaching the ultimate limit of reality and arriving at this very source, one follows the flow to respond to conditions, yet returns to the fundamental school and the definitive meaning.

The *Jieguan pian* (Chapter on the Precepts for Contemplation), the first part of the *Qianzhang jingxin* (Purifying the Mind by Dispelling Obstacles), states: "As one practices the remedies for the afflictions currently active and the various faults of the various schools, defilements gradually perish and the mind becomes increasingly bright and pure.

It is directed toward Bodhi; it is the dwelling place of the spiritual lineage (gotra). Therefore, I instruct you to examine the remedies for afflictions, to promote meritorious deeds, and to cultivate entry into the realm of faith, thereby perfecting the power of the roots of certainty.

As for the three stages of worthiness, the ten stages of sainthood, the stainless, wondrous enlightenment, and the forty-two positions—the true principle of the school of Emptiness (śūnyatā)—it can only be known through hearing.
The coarse appearances of its images are beyond the power of ordinary beings of the lower stages.

Furthermore, you have not yet been able to practice it. Now I shall only cause you to purify the mirror of karma and remove the adventitious dust of the eyes and other defilements, so that you may perceive even a small portion of the Buddha-nature within your own body.
Why do you not drink the nectar of Prajñā to wash away the veils and entanglements, gradually revealing the pure mind?
If the mind is pure, it will purify the realm of sentient beings; once sentient beings are purified, the Buddha-land will be purified. Only then will [the obstructions] be removed.

Afflictions cause the precepts to be purified. Once the precepts are fully perfected, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is likewise purified. Through the purity of precepts and concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) is made pure.

The great and small sages first cultivated the five *sthāpanā* (cessations).

One attains minor liberation. Through the means by which this is achieved—namely, the discipline and meditative concentration that bring about pliancy—one gradually realizes the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

This is called "great liberation. When the ten obstacles are completely extinguished, it is called "true liberation. None of these are not caused by the present five methods of cessation and contemplation (*pañca-nīvaraṇa-pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).

One contemplates the mutual correspondence between body and mind to realize the falsity of seeking the true.

Furthermore, it says: "As for the characteristics of the body, the various classes of beings in the six realms are provisionally formed by the aggregates and the great elements; they manifest as present fruits in response to past karma."

Because it departs from its causes, it is called the "body-form. The body has eighty-four thousand types of forms; the two retributions of the primary and secondary bodies each have their own distinctions.
A single person has universally experienced such various kinds of bodies throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Now, when one is cautioned to contemplate the body, it pertains only to the human realm. A single person has ninety-nine thousand pores, from which eight hundred kinds of winds emerge.
Upon entering therein, eighty thousand families of worms fill the entire body. The four hundred and four diseases arise in alternation.
The three hundred and sixty joints and bones support one another in turn. One hundred and ten types of suffering are experienced at no time.
The thirty-six kinds of impure pus and blood combine to form this aggregate body; from its nine apertures, festering sores leak out as filthy fluids. Such are the sufferings mentioned above.
Karma first forms a single person; the noble ones abandon it as one would cast off a malignant disease—therefore, it is called "contemplating the body.

As for the characteristics of the mind, within a single thought-moment there are ninety *kṣaṇas*, arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing like a flash of lightning; as soon as an object arises, consciousness is produced.
Regarding the retribution invited by the objects of greed, the Sūtra states:

Combined, these constitute the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), the one hundred and eight kinds of defilements, and the five hundred and forty kinds of sensations (*vedanā*). There are nine...
Because there are eighteen kinds of latent proclivities, it is called "contemplating the mind.
