If one enters the contemplative method of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), the activities of the mind gradually subside, proceeding through the nine successive concentrations until returning to the single, truly pure mind. This pure mind is named Buddha-nature.
It is called the True and Eternal Dharmakāya, the mind that is without mind, and the appearance that is without appearance. To observe in this manner is called the purification of the mind.
To speak in detail, one eliminates the hindrances by cultivating contemplation to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore (18), it says: All births and deaths, obstacles to the Path, and the karma of suffering are caused by the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

As explained in the Abhidharma, I shall now briefly state that they cause the cessation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). There are ten fetters that pervade the three realms, totaling ninety-eight types.

Fearing that the text would become too prolix, I shall provide a brief illustrative explanation. These "fetters" are the seeds of the defiled portion within the *ālayavijñāna*; they are so named because—

The fetters (*saṃyojana*) that bind one to receive the retributive fruits of the six realms are called "proclivities" (*anuśaya*). When these proclivities give rise to karma, they increase the seeds of outflows (*āsrava*);

like bandits dwelling in a treacherous place, lying in ambush and gathering together, they are called "fetters. Wielding weapons to plunder and harm, seizing the wealth and treasures of others, they are called "proclivities.

The habitual tendencies of greed and hatred lie latent within the reality (*tattva*), yet they arise again through conditions; they are able to plunder the wealth of precepts and cause one to grasp and cling.
The various sensory objects (dharmas) harm the jewel of wisdom. "Latent tendencies" (anuśaya) refer to their continuous succession;

"fetters" (saṃyojana) refers to their pursuit like a messenger. External observation is called a latent tendency; cessation and deliberation are called fetters. Grasping at conditions is called a latent tendency; binding the mind is called a fetter.

Because these fetters and latent tendencies exist, craving and aversion arise alternately. Due to craving and aversion, the karma of grasping and rejecting is formed. Because of this false grasping and rejecting, there is delusion—the physician [must treat it].
Because it becomes increasingly thick, it obstructs the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*). When the eye of wisdom has not yet opened, it is called the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā-andhakāra*).

With a mind shrouded in darkness, one engages with objects in accordance with perversion (*viparyāsa*). Clinging to the true and eternal nature, one undergoes the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Wandering through the cycles of birth and death, one loses sight of the right path.

Not seeing the True Path is called delusion. To perceive the impermanent as permanent, the suffering as blissful, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure—such madness and error all arise from the fetters (*saṃyojana*). These fetters create inverted karma.

Desiring to sever the fetters and latent tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), one should immediately cultivate the five methods of meditative stabilization (*pañca-sthāpana*) to counteract them. Through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), one enters the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*).

By contemplating emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and detaching from signs (*animitta*), the fetters and latent tendencies are severed. Because body and mind are thus tranquil, afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise.
The place where afflictions are extinguished is called true liberation (*vimukti*). Liberation is none other than Great Nirvāṇa (*mahāparinirvāṇa*).
The eighteen *dhātus* are shown as the objects of observation.

Furthermore, it is asked: "What are called the eighteen *dhātus*? Within the body there are six faculties (*indriya*), namely: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Without, there are six objects (*viṣaya*), namely:

form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*). Between these, the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) arise. The provisional conjunction of these three sets of six is called [the eighteen *dhātus*]."
The eighteen *dhātus*. What is meant by "roots" (*indriya*)? They are called roots because they are able to produce various karmas and because they nourish and sustain [the person].
What is meant by "objects" (*viṣaya*)? They are called objects because they defile the pure mind and, upon contacting the body, form impurities.

What is meant by "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)? It is that which can discern preceding objects; the false arising of discrimination is called consciousness. Now, these roots and objects mutually interpenetrate, and this is termed the twelve *āyatanas*.

Arising through dependent conditions, it lacks any true reality. Sentient beings do not realize this; they claim that the internal and external sense bases possess permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity.
Their minds are tormented by craving, and they cling tenaciously to them with grasping. Deluded and confused, they do not believe in the Noble Path.

When things accord with their desires, greed arises; when they oppose their will, anger is provoked. Through this greed and anger, the fetters and afflictions increase. This is called the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) of ordinary worldlings.
Realizing that existence is itself emptiness, one constantly cultivates practices within existence.

Furthermore, it is said: "Though sensory objects are like illusions, upon seeing forms one gives rise to compassion; with a resolute mind free from flattery and pride, one does not lose the four dignified deportments.

Though the dust of the six sense-objects defiles one's conduct, they are likewise the teacher of the practitioner. One eliminates the illness but does not eliminate the phenomena—the seven factors of enlightenment."

Cultivate these practices in division. Although you contemplate the emptiness of written words, you must read the scriptures extensively and seek out the meanings of the Noble Ones; thus, Prajñā will gradually be perfected.

Although you contemplate the emptiness of the sense faculties and their objects, you must maintain harmony and respect, guard the sentiments of others, fulfill the requirements of monastic discipline, cultivate virtue, and be cautious of ill repute.

Although you contemplate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena, you must practice the five *sthāpanās* in relation to sensory objects; thereby, greed, hatred, and the fetters will be severed, leading to quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

The mind is at peace. Although one contemplates the emptiness of the three realms, one must choose between evil and good; the life-force and formations consist of the factors of awakening (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

Discerning right from wrong with a stainless consciousness, although one knows the emptiness of the three truths, one understands the meaning of the truths to their subtlest depths. Always relying on the two truths to teach, one does not contradict the principle.
The eighteen elements are free from delusion and give rise to precious jewels. One contemplates and understands the meaning of the harmony of conditions; thus, [the afflictions] do not arise.
Nor does one age. The great bodhisattvas of the seventh stage are not said to be "without afflictions. Only after the extinction of the diamond-like mind do they realize the unconditioned path;
thus, the bodhisattva’s contemplation achieves wisdom whose function is unimpeded.
Furthermore (26), it says: A bodhisattva is not defiled by the triple world, yet does not loathe the triple world; they seek the unconditioned path, yet do not abide in the unconditioned;
they constantly dwell within birth and death, yet are free from birth and death. Why are they not defiled by the triple world?

Because their afflictions are exhausted and they are no longer bound by karma. Why do they not loathe the triple world? Because they have compassion for sentient beings and possess great loving-kindness and compassion. They seek the unconditioned...

Because it is the Way; because they desire to benefit both themselves and others; and because they accord with the Mahāyāna. Why do they not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Because they gather in sentient beings.

Why do they constantly dwell within birth and death (*saṃsāra*)? Because their beneficial conduct and activities are identical [to those of ordinary beings], and because their original vows are inexhaustible.
Yet, because the seeds of karma are exhausted and they have attained great mastery, entering the ocean of liberation, they do not remain here.
He does not cling to the middle stream; he is free from both the middle and the extremes. His mind does not abide in the path of extremes. Why is this? Because he does not maintain a self-nature;
for such is the nature of phenomena.
In the *Śālistamba-sūtra*, the exposition on the Truths and the Factors of Enlightenment reveals the root of saṃsāra (27).
It says: "The Four Truths are suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; these are called the four. To understand them as they truly are is called 'truth' (*satya*).
Suffering is the fruit; the origin is the cause. Why is the fruit mentioned first and the cause later? There are three kinds of suffering. Suffering...
Suffering and the suffering of change—these two are coarse and manifest; sentient beings can perceive them through direct experience and thereby give rise to a mind of weary detachment.

The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) is understood by the wise alone. These three types of suffering pervade the worlds of the ten directions; therefore, suffering is taught first. Suffering arises from its accumulation (*samudaya*);

as for the teaching to sever the causes of accumulation, these are the ten fundamental unwholesome actions and the tainted (*sāsrava*) ten wholesome actions. As for cessation (*nirodha*), it is the eternal exhaustion of birth and death, which is realized.
The bliss of liberation. To know how this nirvana may be attained, one must cultivate the Path.

The Path consists of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), beginning with the five contemplations for cessation (*pañca-vipaśyanā*) and extending through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

Therefore, it is called "knowing the Truth of Suffering, abandoning the Truth of Origination, realizing the Truth of Cessation, and cultivating the Truth of the Path. As for the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the obscured mind is devoid of knowledge, like a blind man walking at night.
To be lost in the wilderness and stray from the correct path is called ignorance (*avidyā*). To be greedily stained by worldly phenomena is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

To possess false and delusive cognition and vision is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). When the conscious spirit enters the womb and moves toward the place of birth, merging with the impure [elements], it is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The manifest aggregates form the faculties; because they universally cognize coming and going, they are called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Because the faculties and their objects encounter one another, it is called contact (*sparśa*).

From contact arise the favorable and the adverse, whereby the affairs of craving and aversion are accomplished; thus it is called feeling (*vedanā*). Regarding favorable matters, the mind becomes feverish with greedy attachment;

thus it is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Not relinquishing what one craves is called grasping (*upādāna*). Having grasped, one becomes attached to the self, thereby forming out-flowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*); thus...

This is called "existence" (*bhava*). Once existence and karma are established, they induce subsequent retribution; therefore, this is called "birth" (*jāti*). Because life does not abide, it is called "old age and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Old age and death give rise to birth again, beginning anew after each end. Thus, for thousands of millions of billions of eons, one discards a body and receives another.

Therefore, it is called the twelve links of dependent origination within saṃsāra. The aforementioned Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination are termed the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
The six *pāramitās* that shatter appearances and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) cultivated through conditions are termed the Mahāyāna.

This is extensively and analytically explained in such works as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Furthermore, by merging the Truth of the Path and the eighteen kinds of emptiness, one enters the principle of equality, the inconceivable ocean.

To be free from form and name is the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). As stated in the *Siddhārthabhadra-paripṛcchā*, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā*, the *Śūraṅgamasamādhi*, and other sūtras:

when one abides in the principle of true emptiness, speech is cut off and conditioned activity ceases. Just as the waters of rivers flow only so long as they have not yet entered the great ocean, whereupon they lose their original color and characteristics, so too it is with the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), its cultivation, and the purifying dharmas of skillful means (*upāya*): once they enter the ocean of ultimate reality, they lose their distinct forms.
To briefly explain the ten kinds of Buddha-nature for those who wish to see it:
[Section 28] states, "One must know that all sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature; this is briefly explained in ten kinds, while the detailed exposition is found in various sutras."
First, the afflictions of birth and death arise from true nature, which is likened to a great body of water.

Originally pure and tranquil, it subsequently produces waves due to the wind; later, because of intense cold, it freezes into ice. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is originally pure like this water;
through the winds of vitarka and vicāra, the waves of birth and death arise, and as craving becomes solidified, the ice of affliction is formed. This is intended to reveal...

As for the Buddha-nature: the fire of wisdom melts the ice, and meditative concentration stills the waves. When the ice has melted and the waves have ceased, the water becomes pure and the reflection of the Buddha-nature appears.
Second, it is like gold within ore; while coarse and unfit for use, once it is smelted and refined, the gold finally manifests as the most supreme of treasures, beyond reproach.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings resides within the ore of afflictions; through precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom—
Fire refines out the true nature; within the Dharma-realm, it is supreme and peerless. Thirdly, it is like a cow that has not yet calved: milk and blood are mixed together.

Only when conditions arise does it begin to settle. By churning and heating it, the *sarpis* (clarified butter) is produced. Bright and pure, it changes color according to its vessel and does not maintain its own inherent nature.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is conjoined with afflictions, like milk mixed with blood; it must rely on conditions and cultivation.

Through cultivation, one gradually attains the fruit of Buddhahood and gives rise to supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Adapting to the transformations of sentient beings, one rescues them from suffering by appearing in forms identical to their own;
thus, one does not abide in a fixed self-nature. Fourth, it is like a single person traveling thousands of miles who stays overnight in many houses.

Although there are many houses, the person remains but one. The houses are a metaphor for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the person is a metaphor for Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Sentient beings’ Buddha-nature passes through the aggregates of the five realms of existence (*gati*). The aggregates...
Although there are distinctions, the Buddha-nature is one. Because people are different and houses are different, it is called "not one.
Because the person remains the same person, it is called "not two. When ice has not yet melted, water does not exist; once the ice dissolves, it is water, and thus it is called "not non-existent.
Such is the principle of Buddha-nature: neither one nor two, neither existent nor non-existent. Fifth, the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. The four...
The six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and those subsumed under the Truth of the Path are called the Buddha-nature.
Sixth, the four dharmas of close attendance are called the Buddha-nature: first, attending upon virtuous friends; second, attending upon the True Dharma; third, attending upon quiet reflection;
and fourth, attending upon practice according to the teaching. It is impossible for one to attain Buddhahood apart from these four dharmas. Seventh...

This Buddha-way is neither extreme; it is the Middle Way. The five aggregates (*skandha*) of sentient beings arise by relying upon the Buddha-nature; therefore, it is called "not annihilated" (*anuccheda*).

Their arising and ceasing are like illusions; therefore, they are called "not eternal" (*aśāśvata*). Because people rely upon the five aggregates, they are able to cultivate the Path. The aggregates depend upon the spirit (*ātman*) to be sustained and can only remain established through it.
Eighth, that which is free from the true and the false is called the Buddha-nature. To establish the true and discern the false is to face [the truth].
Delusion falsely manifests the True. If delusive phenomena are extinguished, the name "True" does not arise. Buddha-nature is pure; wisdom cannot know it, and consciousness cannot perceive it.
Ninth, the teaching that can be expounded reveals non-expounding; this emptiness of non-expounding is likewise ungraspable, and for this reason it is called Buddha-nature.
Tenth, emptiness is quiescent, yet it coexists with the turbulence of existence; its essence is detached from form.
It is named "Constantly Manifesting Name-and-Form. These constitute the ten natures. Unobstructed wisdom is identical to the ignorance of ordinary beings;
it is like true liberation, which originally arises from the state of an ordinary being. Although there is this analogy, the meaning of Buddha-nature can only be known by a Buddha.
It is further said: At first, one resolves to seek the Way and runs about in search of it, yet the mind is crooked and views are not yet upright.
One seeks Bodhi south of the Yangtze and north of it, but though we practice together toward Bodhi, we do not recognize one another.

Exhausted by searching for it outside the body, one suddenly attains awakening through quiet contemplation in a single place and realizes even a small portion of the truth; thus one knows that Bodhi is hidden within one's own body. This is the liberation from affliction.
The nature of affliction is empty and like an illusion; before long, it will naturally reach its exhaustion. Nirvana and birth-and-death are of one suchness;
in principle, they are neither two nor identical. If one can clearly understand the dharmas of the faculties and their objects, one will nurture the wings of unimpeded supernormal powers.
Observe that the five aggregates arise through the conjunction of conditions; their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) primordially encompasses the ten powers.
This demonstrates the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit and reveals the essence of the observing subject.
Furthermore, it says: "Simultaneously observe the Buddha-nature; this is the characteristic of the cause. Next, one must observe the fruit. The fruit is the Buddha-wisdom."
The Sūtra says: "The wisdom of all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm does not equal the wisdom of a single srotāpanna.
The wisdom of all srotāpannas in a world-system does not equal the wisdom of a single sakṛdāgāmin. The wisdom of all sakṛdāgāmins in a world-system does not equal the wisdom of a single anāgāmin.
The wisdom of all anāgāmins in a world-system does not equal the wisdom of a single arhat. The wisdom of all arhats in a world-system..."

The wisdom [of a single person] does not equal the wisdom of one *pratyekabuddha*. The wisdom of all *pratyekabuddhas* filling the worlds of the ten directions does not equal the wisdom of a single bodhisattva of the lineage (*gotra*).
Following such successive gradations, it does not equal the wisdom of a single bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).

The wisdom of all bodhisattvas of the tenth stage filling [the worlds] does not equal the wisdom of a single thought-moment of a Tathāgata. Therefore, the ocean of the World-Honored One’s wisdom is like the sands of the Ganges.
O Great Beings, you all contemplate together yet do not know the matter of the Tathāgata’s lifting of his foot;
therefore, you should with single-minded diligence seek the wisdom of the Buddha.
In the *Lingzhi Guan Jing Shu* (Commentary on the Sutra of the Vision of the Divine Mushroom), it is clarified that the contemplative methods of the Pure Land are profound.
To understand the subtlety of these contemplations, one must first recognize the perfection of the teaching.

The commentary states: "It should be known that the teachings and contemplations concerning Amitābha throughout the One Vehicle [of the Buddha’s life] are all the perfect and sudden Dharma of the One Buddha Vehicle; there is nothing else."
Furthermore, citing Ciyun, he says: "The Buddha-dharma has two aspects: first, the Hīnayāna teachings of incomplete meaning; second, the Mahāyāna teachings of complete meaning.

Within the Mahāyāna, there are again those of complete meaning and those of incomplete meaning. What is now discussed regarding the Pure Land is exclusively the teaching of complete meaning within the complete meaning of the Mahāyāna.
As the Sūtra says: "If one seeks with thorough scrutiny throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle; there is only one."

This is what is meant by the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*). To speak of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*): to realize that the Pure Land is none other than one’s own mind, and not some external phenomenon;

to penetrate that Amitābha is none other than one’s own nature, and not some other Buddha. If this is so, then even if one directs one’s spirit toward billions of lands, one is truly born within one’s own heart;
and even if one conceives a physical form within the nine lotuses, how could one escape the span of a single *kṣaṇa*? Therefore...
The Sūtra says: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. This is precisely the revelation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings.

As the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna, how could it surpass this? It continues by saying: "One thereby knows that the pure and impure bodies and lands are entirely the self-mind of sentient beings.
It is solely because the essence of the mind is empty and harmonious that coming and going are unimpeded; it is solely because the nature of the mind is form..."
[This] is universal; it thus allows for neither grasping nor rejecting to be obstructed, thereby revealing the fundamental tenet of the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.

(Question: The world claims that Lingzhi took the contemplation of the Buddha as his primary tenet, yet this is frequently met with refutation. What is the meaning of this? Answer: How can mere hearsay and idle talk be worthy of serious discussion? However, [the critics] do not realize that Lingzhi used the wondrous contemplation of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) to contemplate that [pure land’s] environment.)

Correct. Is this not marvelous? Although Tiantai takes mental contemplation as his primary tenet, when it comes to discussing the object of contemplation, he still contemplates both the dependent and the primary [realms]. As his commentary states: "The Buddha is the supreme object of contemplation," and so forth; the text is extremely clear. Having personally examined the present commentary, I find this to be so.

The propositions established earlier and later—regarding the subject and object, or the pure and the defiled—are nothing other than this single, inconceivable, and subtle mind-nature. In the Tiantai contemplation of the mind, one contemplates both the environment and its inhabitants; how could this ever depart from a single thought-moment? Now, in this commentary on the contemplation of the Buddha, since it is already understood that all is but mind, how could the Buddha be an external object?
Although the formulations differ, there is no difference in their underlying meaning.
The Commentary states: "The 'principle' (*zong*) refers to the central meaning. As for this single master of the sutra, his meaning must be clearly distinguished and demonstrated.

Tiantai says: "This sutra takes the contemplation of the mind as its principle. This speaks solely in terms of the contemplating subject (*nengguan*). (That commentary subsequently demonstrates the supreme objects of contemplation (*suoguan*), thereby revealing that the contemplation of the mind is indeed established solely from the perspective of the contemplating subject.

Is the contemplation of the Buddha’s primary and secondary marks not itself the contemplation of the mind? (Since the primary and secondary marks are ultimately but the one mind, to contemplate them is precisely the contemplation of the mind. Master Yuan [Huiyuan] was excellent at...
The Commentary further states: "The tenets and purposes elucidated in the various sūtras differ from one another. This sūtra takes the samādhi of contemplating the Buddha as its primary tenet;
this is established by encompassing both the subject and the object. It continues: "From this it may be inferred that the merit of contemplating the Buddha is inconceivable."
This is truly because by restraining the deluded mind, one merges with the true reality; by relying on the merit and wisdom of others, one is rescued from one's own poverty;
and by depending on their compassion, one is saved from drowning. This is the vanguard for repelling evil and the initial gateway for entering the Path. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind. It is like a person who has been smeared with incense; their body carries the fragrance. This is...

This is named "Adornment of Fragrant Light" (it should be understood that what follows below clarifies the extraordinary efficacy of the visualization of the Buddha; had it been intended to clarify the actual method of visualization, it would have appeared as cited below).
Regarding the principle and phenomena of *hetuvidyā*, the Commentary states:
"Principle (*li*) is a provisional designation for the void and quiescent; phenomena (*shi*) are the general term for conditioned activities. Although these two names are established separately,"

The essence is truly one and suchness. It is like water moving to form waves, or ink being drawn to form characters. Although the waves take on ten thousand forms, how does their moisture differ from the water?

Though the characters have a thousand variations, the color of the ink remains no different. If one claims that by darkening the mind and dwelling in stillness, subject and object are extinguished, [one has not yet grasped this].

This constitutes the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*). When the mind is raised and thoughts are stirred, such that acceptance and rejection are clearly distinct, this constitutes the contemplation of phenomena (*shi-guan*).
This is a confrontation between principle and phenomena; it is not yet perfect fusion (*yuanrong*).

Now, according to the *Ten Doubts Treatise* by Tiantai, Master Zhiyi ardently sought birth in the Pure Land while realizing that the essence of birth is unattainable—this is true non-arising (*anutpāda*). The ignorant, however, are bound by birth. Upon hearing [this], they...

To perceive arising as arising, and upon hearing of non-arising to perceive it as non-arising, while failing to know that arising is itself non-arising and non-arising is itself arising—failing to penetrate this principle and recklessly asserting right and wrong—is how much error there is! Thus we know that when one penetrates phenomena, they are themselves the principle.
Principle is not external to phenomena; this is true non-arising, and is therefore called "wondrous contemplation.

To clarify the actual application of contemplation, the *Shu* (Commentary) states: Question: According to the principle of contemplating phenomena (*li-guan*), how should one practice? Answer: There are two methods for practicing the Dharma. The first is the contemplator (*neng-kan*).

The mind takes the mental activity of the present consciousness as its substance; this is what is meant by the subsequent statement: "One should give rise to mental conceptions and contemplate the sun with clarity.
Second is the object of contemplation, which takes the adornments of Amitābha’s environment and his own body as its substance;

these are the sixteen kinds of objects enumerated below. Only when the subject and object merge in mutual darkness does the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) become perfected. Question: When one gives rise to the mind to grasp [the object]...

Question: What is meant by "contemplation of principle" (*li-guan*) regarding objects? Answer: To realize that this mind and its objects are all produced through causes and conditions; that being produced from conditions means they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);

and that their essence is neither arising nor ceasing—this is the principle of non-arising. The *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shi yi lun*) states: "Now, as for non-arising and non-ceasing, it is within the midst of conditioned production..."
All dharmas are a combination of conditions and do not maintain their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). When one seeks their essential substance of arising, it is utterly unobtainable;
thus, when this arising occurs, it comes from nowhere, and is therefore called "non-arising. When they perish and disperse, they go nowhere; therefore, they are said to be "non-ceasing."

This does not mean that there exists something separate from what arises through causes and conditions that is neither born nor extinguished. Now, in clarifying the contemplation of principle, we strictly follow the treatise:

using the mind that arises through conditions to contemplate the objects that arise through conditions. Although the mind and its objects differ, their arising through conditions is no different. This is the mind that performs the contemplation.
That which is observed is precisely the Buddha. The mind-dharma and the Buddha-dharma are both inconceivable. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. This is its meaning. Therefore, practitioners should first open their wisdom and understanding so as to attain unimpeded penetration;

thereafter, morning and evening, they should at every thought bind their mindfulness to the sublime realms of the environment and inhabitants of that direction, fervently seeking rebirth there, without hindering the mind.
The objective realm (*viṣaya*) is by its very nature unarisen; it is not something brought about through artificial construction. (Siming said:

"The practitioner should know that, based upon the nature of the mind (*cittatā*), one contemplates those environments and beings (*niśraya-sattva*). When the environments and beings are thus made manifest, one relies upon those environments and beings to contemplate the nature of the mind, whereby the nature of the mind easily manifests.

It continues: "The causal conditions that create and the phenomena that are created are, in their respective places, entirely the nature of the mind. This is precisely what is being contemplated now. Whether environment or being, these are the mind of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-citta*); one contemplates the realm of the Dharma-realm, giving rise to the Dharma-realm," and so forth. Based on this instruction, one indeed uses wondrous contemplation to contemplate.)
That [ancient] basis and its correct application are identical to what is established here.
The *Shi zhongwen zongguan zhufa shu* (Commentary on the General Contemplation of All Dharmas in Various Texts) states:
"Thus we know that among all dharmas, whether mundane or supramundane, their origins and manifestations, their speech and silence, are none other than the wondrous principle."
It is not only this contemplation; among all the contemplative methods established throughout the Mahāyāna teachings of one lifetime, there is none that is not like this.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Contemplate all phenomena as empty, as the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), non-perverted, and so forth.
It also says: "All dharmas are entirely non-existent; they have no permanence, nor do they arise or cease. The *Samantabhadra Contemplation Sūtra* says: "One should know that all dharmas are..."
This is the Buddha-dharma. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "All dharmas are themselves the mark of bodhi. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "All dharmas are unborn;
all dharmas are unceasing. It further states: "To thoroughly know that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is non-existent—thus understanding the nature of dharmas is to see Vairocana.
The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "All conditioned dharmas are like..."
"Like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, or a shadow"—passages such as these appear throughout the entire Tripitaka and cannot be cited in their entirety here.
To discuss the sublime principle apart from all phenomena is to fall into partiality and heterodoxy; it is utterly remote from the Way. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"For example, in constructing a palace or residence, if one relies on solid ground, one may proceed as one pleases without obstruction; but if one relies on empty space, it can never be completed. Thus do the Buddhas [teach].
In expounding the Dharma, one always relies upon the two truths; without destroying conventional designations, one speaks of the true mark of all phenomena.
Since the measure of the sages is such and correct principle is so straightforward, those who truly desire to advance in their practice must investigate and examine it deeply.
The *Tongbian yidai guanfashi shu* states:

"Regarding the contemplative methods elucidated within the temporal teachings of a single lifetime, they may be briefly categorized into five types: first, the general contemplation of all phenomena, as in the sūtras that speak of contemplating the emptiness of all dharmas;
second, the specific contemplation of one's own mind, as in the *Zhiguan*, the *Huanyuanguan*, and the *Fajie* [contemplations]."
1. Contemplation of the pure mind and so forth. 2. Or contemplating matter alone; as the Sūtra says: "Contemplate the true mark of the body;
contemplate the Buddha likewise," as well as the impure skeleton and so forth. 3. Contemplating both matter and mind together; as the Sūtra says:

"Clearly perceive that the five aggregates are empty," as well as the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, counting the breath, and so forth. 4. Contemplating the sublime objects of focus; namely, as in various sūtras, contemplating the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the contemplation of the supreme objects, there are five further distinctions: first, contemplating the ocean of the Buddhas' marks, which is the contemplation of the thirty-two marks of all Buddhas;
second, contemplating the practices of Samantabhadra, which is the contemplation of the body of the Bodhisattva, the six-tusked white elephant;
third, contemplating Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, which is the contemplation of the conduct, vows, and physical forms of these two Bodhisattvas; fourth, contemplating Maitreya above...

First is the visualization of the Tuṣita Heaven palace, seeking rebirth in the Inner Court. Fifth is the present sutra, which involves visualizing the primary and secondary environments of Amitābha, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.
Detailed Discourse on the Questions Concerning Contemplation of the Mind and Contemplation of the Buddha:
May the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra* now be called "Contemplation of the Mind"? Answer: If one realizes that objects are nothing but mind, then what among the body and land of Amitābha is not mind?
However, I fear that if one instead seeks the fundamental aggregates (*skandhas*) and restricts recognition to a mere point of spiritual essence, then [the practice] will be exhausted.

This belongs to other sutras; it is not the primary contemplation of the present [text]. Question: Some say that the Buddha-dharma is too lofty and the phenomena of sentient beings are too vast, and that contemplating the mind alone is essential.

Now, this sutra teaches the contemplation of the Buddha; does this not contradict [the former view]? Answer: The contemplation of dharmas is applied according to the capacities of practitioners, each giving rise to its own result.
If one enters the Path in this world, severing delusions and realizing the Truth, then contemplating the mind is of the utmost importance. However, if one seeks rebirth in the Pure Land...

As for the phrase "cultivating causes to elicit retribution," it means that while the contemplation of the Buddha reaches its ultimate excellence, the clear realization and verification of that insight correctly takes the contemplation of the mind as its primary object;

thus these words were spoken. It does not mean that the sentient Buddha and the Buddha-dharma can never be contemplated together; rather, the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha is intended for all future practitioners.

This principle is not established in vain. Question: Since there is no difference between the mind and the Buddha, and this is the definitive meaning of the Supreme Vehicle, why is it necessary to insist on making such distinctions when clarifying the method of contemplation?

Answer: Although the fundamental principle is inherently unified, the aspects of practice should be distinguished. To provide a basis for cultivation, it is essential that the object and wisdom correspond.
As an ancient master said: "There are two ways of contemplating the Buddha: first, the Buddha seen through the samādhi of one's own mind; second..."

The Buddha who manifests as a result of causes in the Western Quarter is the very Buddha perceived when one contemplates the mind according to the various sutras—that is, when one contemplates one’s own mind.

Now, the sixteen contemplations specifically contemplate that Buddha who manifests as a result of causes in the Western Quarter. Based on these two divisions, there shall forever be no doubt or confusion.

Therefore, the *Ten Doubts on the Pure Land* (Tiantai Shiyi Lun) states: "Generally, those who seek rebirth should give rise to aspirations and mental images, taking as their object the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and the radiance of Amitābha Buddha, and further contemplating the adornments of the seven treasures of that land, exactly as described in the sixteen contemplations of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
The present sūtra’s contemplation of the Buddha provides clear scriptural evidence for this. Question: The sūtra says: "If one sees me by means of form, or by means of sound..."

"Those who seek me through sound follow a deviant path; they cannot see the Tathāgata. Now, when we contemplate the realm of the Buddha, is this not seeing him through form or seeking him through sound?
The answer is: The thirty-two marks are like the bright moon reflected in a hundred rivers;

the four kinds of eloquence and the eightfold voice are like pure echoes arising from a deep valley. Yet there are those who, reaching into a pond to grasp the moon or entering a valley to seek out the sound, fail to realize this.

Because their nature is empty, they do not perceive the Buddha. The realized one is not like this: having understood that form is not form, what prevents them from clearly contemplating the holy countenance?
Having understood that sound is not sound, how could it hinder them from hearing the wondrous Dharma by its side?

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "The marks of form are not the Buddha; sound is likewise so. Yet, without departing from form and sound, one sees the Buddha’s supernormal powers. Behold this wondrous discourse!
How could one still harbor doubts?
Section Two: Various Texts on the Contemplation of Dharmas;

Section Three: Various Texts on the Mind and Objects (First, the two schools are recorded according to their doctrinal limits; subsequently, the meaning of the Patriarchs is set forth—this is what is intended here).
First, the two schools are presented. According to the *Jingzhuan Shuyi* (Commentary on the Sūtra of the Manifestation of the Mind), regarding the school that maintains [the existence of] karma:
"The initial mind that takes precepts as its object pertains only to the present; although each moment passes away, there is no subsequent continuation below."

One takes this very mind as the fundamental cause of the precepts. The Record states: "The object of cognition is restricted to the present; its moment-to-moment continuity constitutes the basis of karma. The Commentary states:

"Regarding the three types of conditions for the arising of the precepts, the scope of their objects varies in breadth and narrowness. In the first fascicle, concerning the conditions for receiving [the precepts], the method for the arising of the precepts was already explained in brief.
However, because the mind arises in accordance with its objects, we shall now discuss them extensively so that one may understand the loftiness and vastness of the virtue of the precepts."
The one who acts as the messenger possesses courageous diligence. First, regarding the mind that takes an object: it takes as its object the present continuous stream of consciousness.

Furthermore, it is shown that the object of the precepts (as stated in the *Chao*, which is not recorded here) is, secondly, with respect to the object of the precepts, universally taking the three periods of time as its object; whenever there is an evil condition, one forms the intention to sever it.
It is not so that non-restraint is not a transgression. How is this made clear? It is like the case of an enemy’s household:

although the family has long since passed away, one may still kill their corpse; this is not without fault. That enemy’s son represents the present; the wrongs committed toward those yet to be born represent the future.

Now, in order to fulfill the precepts, one must universally take [all time periods] as the object of focus. The Record states: "When the father has passed away, it is the past; when the son is present, it is the present;

and when there will be a grandson in the future, it is the future" (there are those who consider the child in the womb to be the future, but this is not the case, as such a being still belongs to the present). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is like a person cutting up a corpse."
Due to these karmic conditions, one would otherwise fall into hell, similar to cases such as Wu Yuan’s flogging of a corpse. The commentary cites a treatise which states:

"In all instances, one obtains the restraint of the precepts within the sphere of sentient beings across the three periods of time; it is like a person making offerings to those they revere from the past."
There is also merit. The same applies to restraint (vinaya). It is further said: "Compassion, giving, and so forth are also meritorious; the same is true for precepts.

This means that through a mind of compassion, one takes the three periods of time as an object to extract suffering and bestow happiness; the dharma of precepts likewise takes the three [periods] as its object.

For example, [the case of] giving throughout the three periods of time may be treated similarly to compassionate action (since compassionate giving extends through the three periods, precepts may likewise be treated similarly).

It is further said: "Compassion and mercy toward all things arise in relation to the present realm; since the past and future have already passed away, the efficacy of compassion is of no benefit. Precepts are not like this;

they must necessarily be universally pervasive to be designated as the karma of precepts" (the benefits of compassionate giving and precepts differ in being universal or non-universal; thus they cannot be treated as identical). Question: Since they are both virtuous practices, why are they different? Answer:

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables] are mundane virtues that expand or contract according to the breadth of one's mind; as the sutras describe, these consist of seven categories. Ethical discipline (*śīla*), however, is a universal practice possessed only by those who formally undertake it; it must necessarily be practiced universally.

Regardless of whether one is dealing with the virtuous or the non-virtuous, one must bring all such thoughts to rest. Even the slightest involvement in resentment or aversion [violates this principle].

Thus, they are not conditions that constitute the complete set [of requisites]. Therefore, the treatise states: "Because the evil mind varies according to the increase or decrease of the precepts," and so forth.

By virtue of being the root of all virtues and the foundational basis for concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they may—just like distinct wholesome states—be considered factors of the Path (*mārga-aṅga*).

The commentary states: "As the Sūtra says, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is itself *nirvāṇa*. The Sūtra refers to the three grades among relatives: first, superior relatives (teachers, monks, parents); second, middling relatives (brothers, sisters, fellow students, etc.).

There are three grades of benefactors (those who bestow wealth upon me, or friends, etc.). There are likewise three grades of enemies: first, superior enemies (those who take the lives of my parents, etc.);

second, middling enemies (those who take the lives of my brothers or seize my wealth); and third, inferior enemies (those who take the lives of my friends, etc.). Those who are neither enemies nor benefactors constitute one grade.

To practice loving-kindness equally toward these seven categories belongs only to the limited sphere of present objects; it is not universal. Regarding the precepts, they must be all-encompassing—this is the third [point].
Because it encompasses all ten directions of the world without exception, one knows that its fundamental substance admits not even the slightest evil, nor can a speck of dust take root therein.
It is comparable to a bright mirror and may be likened to lapis lazuli; that it is praised by all the sages is precisely due to this.
Whether good or evil, whether pleasant or unpleasant, nothing is excluded. If one does not sever [evil] completely, there are two faults: first, the evil mind will not die out.
Second, regarding the increase or decrease of the precepts, I shall cite it myself later.
The definitive precepts prevent transgressions of the past and future. Regarding the passage in the *Shu* (Commentary) stating, "The objects of the precepts span the three periods of time;
the present object is the focal point (*ālambana*)," one asks: "If this is so, is it then not the case that [the precept] pertains to the present?"

Regarding the statement "not guarding": (this refers to the difficulty of preventing non-virtue by following along with the preceding objects of perception). The answer is: when the object of perception exists at a distance, non-virtue has not yet arisen;

thus, the aspiration to sever it does not obstruct the nature of the object. If one discusses actual guarding, it pertains precisely to the confronting, present object. One cannot categorically declare it "non-virtuous.

When the six sense-objects serve as the basis for sublime conduct, this may apply exclusively to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). However, when there are differing views regarding a single object—such as humans and animals—the [distinction] arises.
To rectify existing faults is not because one is unable to overcome them; it is to prevent future faults. To rectify weakness is not to boast of being able to prevent it.

Relying on the teachings to repent and purify is called "preventing transgressions"; thus, there are no manifest faults. The Record states: "When the present objects are without fault, the six sense-fields become sublime practice. This means contemplating that objects are empty and quiescent.
This may pertain only to those beyond training (aśaikṣa), meaning it does not apply exclusively to the most exalted sages. In a single object, there are differences.
It is seen. For example, as a person sees water, a deva sees lapis lazuli, a hungry ghost sees a river of pus, and a fish sees its own dwelling.

This clarifies that what appears before one's senses is not fixed; it may be seen as empty space, or it may vary according to the mind. Since these perceptions are not definitive, there is nothing to be prevented. The Commentary says:

To restate this more emphatically: that which exists in the present but has not yet arisen is not called an offense; as soon as it arises and passes away, it is designated as a transgression. Therefore, the text says:
"Because each moment in the present does not abide, it can be clearly perceived. The commentary states: "The 'text' refers to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*."
He said: "Form is of three kinds: past, future, and present. The past and the present cannot be harmed. Why?
Because the past has already passed away, and the present perishes moment by moment. It is the prevention of the future that is called 'killing.
Since the preceding moment has passed and the succeeding moment is yet to come, this principle becomes even clearer; therefore, it is said that [the object] can be seen."
The *Shuxinjing shu* (Commentary on the Mind-Object Sūtra), relying on many schools, further states:
"The cognizing mind is restricted to a single moment; the cognized object exists only as a single present moment."

(This establishes a thesis distinct from the preceding [view], as it applies to all three time periods. Because the past and future are categories of phenomena (*dharma-saṃkhyāta*)—since those two objects of the past and future consist merely of names and phrases and are therefore subsumed under the *dharmāyatana*—they are not categories of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*).

(Present sentient beings constitute the category of sentient beings; because the Prātimokṣa vows arise based on sentient beings, the past and future, being insentient, are not the objective domain of the precepts. Thus, the treatise (*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, i.e., the *Zaxin lun*) says:

The Pratimokṣa arises based on its origination; the arising of the precepts also occurs in the present. It is attained within a single moment of mind, yet it prevents wrongdoing in both the past and the future.
Since there is no actual wrongdoing in the present, if one speaks of the objects of the precepts, they exist as conditions for them.

Briefly stated, the six great elements—earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—as well as the Tathāgata and the truth of Nirvāṇa, are all conditions for the precepts. However, [only those things] that cause harm...
The meaning of "ruination" and "denigration. Question: Is there anything further that arises outside of the six destinies (*ṣadgati*)?

Answer: The Tathāgata is not subsumed within the destinies; the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is likewise so. Thus, the *Cittaviparyaya-śāstra* says: "The four modes of birth encompass all destinies, but the intermediate state is not subsumed within the destinies.

This is because "destiny" (*gati*) carries the sense of "arrival. The intermediate state merely transmits consciousness (as for "transmitting consciousness": having abandoned this [life] and heading toward that [next], it has not yet arrived in the interim; therefore, it is called the intermediate state).

Regarding the necessity for precepts to encompass all objects, the *Abhidharmakośa* further states: "If one does not [refrain] from all sentient beings, then there is no precept. This is because the goodness of the precept must be universal;
otherwise, the evil intention will not cease. Furthermore, regarding sentient beings, one must be free from the five types of conceptualization (the fivefold discrimination).

Since these can all obstruct the precepts, one must distance oneself from them before the categories of the precepts can arise. [The vows consist of: (1) regarding a specific being, one resolves to abstain from killing and so forth (e.g., "I shall not kill pigs, sheep, and the like");

(2) regarding a specific category, one is able to uphold it (a "category" here refers to a branch; e.g., "I shall uphold the branch of non-killing," etc.); and (3) regarding place and time, even down to months and days.

(3) Regarding the three locations, as it says: "One is able to uphold [the precepts] within this country. (4) Regarding the four times, as it says: "One is able to uphold [the precepts] during this year, this month, and this day. (5) Being free from certain conditions, meaning that one excludes matters of warfare.

(That is to say, one is able to maintain it at ordinary times, or fails to maintain it when encountering such circumstances. If one makes this vow in this manner, one merely attains virtuous conduct; it cannot be called "my [vow]. Furthermore, it says:

Regarding objects that are beyond one's capacity: how can one obtain the power of the precepts? That which can be maintained by one's strength is called an "object within one's capacity"; that which cannot be borne by one's strength is called an "object beyond one's capacity.

It is understood from the meaning that one obtains the precepts regarding objects within one's capacity; it is not obtained regarding objects beyond one's capacity. How could the precepts arise [in such cases]? For instance, a butcher might maintain the precept against killing wild animals, while a hunter might maintain the precept against killing domestic livestock.
(The preceding section cited the facts to characterize the principle; this section provides the explanation. Because one does not harm the lives of any sentient beings, one obtains the precept.
However, from the perspective of the objects [of the vow] that one is capable of protecting, there is increase or decrease, as the "capable" and "incapable" objects interchange and arise.

For example, if a hunter who observes the precept against killing pigs and sheep dies and is reborn among deer, the precept is diminished. Or, if a deer is reborn among sheep, the precept is increased. The same applies to butchers and others.

One attains renunciation through the precepts, which necessarily depend upon causes and conditions. Now, this [practice of] increasing or decreasing [the number of precepts] deeply contradicts the meaning of the precepts.

Even if one were to set aside these conditions, what fault would there be? (These two sentences refute the previous position: even if one did not rely on conditions and the increase or decrease occurred naturally, there would still be no logical fault. Because the evil mind does not die. (This means that according to the previous position, one merely maintains what can be maintained;

it is not the case that one is capable of not maintaining [the precepts]. Thus, the evil mind does not die. For example, one who maintains domestic animals goes hunting but does not catch any; then, on the road, he encounters pigs and sheep.
The mind may yet give rise to the intent to kill. Now, in discussing the precepts, one must maintain a mind free from harm toward all sentient beings;

only then does one fulfill the practice of great compassion, which is the foremost among all virtuous deeds. How can one hope to achieve great goodness by training only partially? Such a principle is impossible.

The *Juejing mingjiejiliang shu* (Commentary Clarifying the Quantity of Precepts Based on Objects) further cites the *Shisong lü piposha lun* (Daolun), which states: "For each and every sentient being, there are seven branches of body and speech.

If one does not receive the precepts, these all become causes for the arising of evil. By virtue of receiving the precepts, they are collectively transformed into goodness. These three types of roots of goodness, applied across the seven branches, constitute two [categories]."
Eleven. The remainder may be understood by analogy. If they arise reciprocally, one may apply the analogy of the seven gates (i.e., the seven poisons). Regarding the objects of lust:

for a man, there are two or three [openings] depending on the case (the mouth and the two [sexual] passages; for a woman, adding the small passage, there are three). For a woman’s body, there are nine [openings]. This constitutes sixty-three precepts.

In the body of a man, there are eight [senses] and fifty-six precepts. As for all other non-sentient things—earth, water, fire, wind, space, grasses, and trees, as well as the teachings and principles of both the mundane and the sagely—whenever one encounters even a single object among them, transgressions arise as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Now, by turning back toward the good, one accomplishes precepts as numerous as those sands.
It is thus immeasurable. As Śubhavyūha said: "Sentient beings are immeasurable; the great ocean is boundless; space is limitless;
grasses and trees are innumerable. The virtue of the precepts is likewise so, having no boundaries or limits. Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Regarding non-sentient beings..."

One also attains immeasurable merit from the goodness of the precepts. Suppose one were to crush every particle of earth throughout the worlds of the ten directions, down to the Golden Wheel, into atoms;
one would incur a sin for each and every atom. Now, by reversing those sins through the goodness of the precepts, one again attains the immeasurable.
It is like destroying a single blade of grass—its sprout, bud, leaf, and flower—one incurs a sin for each part; yet by reversing that sin, it becomes merit, and again, it is immeasurable.
Furthermore, the *Shu-yao* (Commentary), fascicle 1, quotes the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, stating:

"Within the trichiliocosm, from the Avīci Hell below to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heaven above, regarding all sentient beings—whether they may be killed or not killed, or even whether they may be deceived or not deceived [the same applies]."
Each and every sentient being, up to and including the Tathāgata and all living creatures, attains the precepts through three causes and conditions.

Furthermore, by means of these, one deduces that the monastic community of renunciants—both monks and nuns—as well as the three lower assemblies, uphold the vessel of virtuous precepts and follow the traces of the Sages;

their status surpasses that of gods and humans precisely because of this. Remaining composed and self-guarded, their merit and virtue flow forth perpetually. As stated in the *Liao lun*: [text follows].
"Forty-two thousand. The river of merit flows constantly. The commentary explains:
this refers to the forty-two thousand rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), which flow perpetually like a river to wash away the afflictions of broken precepts.

Regarding the number "forty-two thousand," it refers to the root precepts, of which there are four hundred and twenty. The reason for this is that, according to the *Vasudhārā-vinaya*, there are two hundred precepts; [the others] are numerous...
This explains the light precepts (*upodghāta*). There are one hundred and twenty-one heavy precepts, which clarify the major prohibitions;
the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts are distinct, numbering ninety-nine. Together, they total four hundred and twenty. Each individual precept possesses ten merits, such as the gathering of the Saṃgha.
Each of these merits can give rise to ten kinds of right practice, namely: the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), non-attachment (*alobha*), and so forth.
The three roots of goodness, along with the two restraints of body and speech—each consisting of one hundred precepts—combine to form four hundred and twenty.

Is this not forty-two thousand? Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Wishless Vinaya" (apraṇihita-vinaya) refers to the moment the third *karmavācanā* is concluded, when the forty-two thousand rules of training arise simultaneously; because there is not a single precept that does not arise, it is called "wishless."
Seeking [the truth] based on this, the virtue of the precepts flows perpetually.

This concludes the first volume of the *Sūtra on the Ritual for the Intention to Receive the Precepts and the Guidance Thereof*. It quotes the *Sarvāstivāda* school as follows: "Whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one must first provide them with a Dharma discourse to guide and open their understanding."

Explanation: This causes one to give rise to a mind of compassion toward all objects, whereby one attains the *adhiśīla* (higher training in ethical discipline). The *Yejieshu* (Commentary on the Vinaya), fascicle 3, part B, states:

"Ordinary people are ignorant and their wisdom shallow; how could they be able to produce knowledge? Unless one has studied for a long time, sudden instruction will remain as dark as before. Such is the nature of this Dharma of precepts."
The fundamental duty of one who has left the household life is not originally to harbor great ambitions; it is for this reason that it is difficult to accommodate such [worldly] desires.

As for the instruction that one should give rise to compassion upon the borders of one's domain, it is because one practices compassion to rescue and gather in sentient beings, as stated in the *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.

This refers precisely to that which is received by the seven classes of practitioners. Question: Since [this practice] does not take loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as its object, how can it be considered "great"?

Answer: The intention lies in what follows. The *Shuji* (Commentary) cites a sutra stating: "If a bodhisattva wishes to receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts, they must first purify their mind and receive the sevenfold precepts.
It is like a person who, wishing to invite a great king, must first thoroughly clean and prepare the residence where the king will stay. This is based on this sutra.

[The Master] said: "In principle, one who becomes a bhikṣu must necessarily receive the Bodhisattva Mahā-śīla. Now, having received the minor precepts (hīna-śīla), he first contemplates loving-kindness (maitrī) as a preparation for receiving the great precepts;
therefore, it is said that 'the intention lies in what follows. It should be understood accordingly that [this practice] is fully complete even within the limited scope of the Hīnayāna.

Yet, when viewed from the perspective of the Bodhisattva path, it is still merely a skillful means (upāya). Question: "In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* (Duōlùn) and the Sarvāstivāda school, it is stated that one 'arouses loving-kindness. This is a case of partial application (pradeśa-sāmānya). How does this differ [from the previous explanation]?"

The Fundamental Vinaya (Mūla-vinaya) replies: Giving what is small for the sake of what is great is not without its partial application; thus, within various schools, there have occasionally been such views.
However, the principles established by the *Dharmaguptaka* school are clear and manifest, as evidenced by five points, which are cited in full below.

The *Zizhi* asks: "To show compassion for all beings is entirely not the practice of the Lesser Vehicle. The reply: In the *Śīla-sūtra*, that which is received by the seven classes of followers is for the sake of Bodhi.

Regarding the "Expedient Means of the Bodhisattva" (*Bodhisattva-upāya*), the *Yeshu* (Commentary on the Vinaya) states: "If one does not previously take the object of compassion as a focus, how can one accommodate the Great [Vehicle]? This implies that the intention lies in what follows. (Question:

If one awakens the mind according to the Perfect [Teaching], one immediately receives the Small [Vehicle] and then the Great; yet now you say the intention lies in what follows. This seems to contradict the principle of the Perfect [Teaching]. Please clarify this for me. (Answer: This is merely based, for the time being, on the meaning of ascending through the four stages of the *Śīla-sūtra* (Good Precepts), in order to explain and harmonize the passage concerning the "mind of compassion" in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.

The intent is as follows: for a Śrāvaka, the removal of defilement is the primary requirement, and thus the Small Precepts place the renunciation of sexual misconduct at the beginning. For a Bodhisattva, compassionate salvation is the priority, and thus the Great Precepts place the non-killing at the head. Now, regarding the reception of the Small Precepts...

Yet it says, "practicing compassion. Thus we know that the intent lies in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*. If this is so, does it mean that the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) in the present text is not in accord with the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzhi*)? Answer: Are these four phrases regarding the precepts and so forth not the explicit text for the Perfect arousal and reception of full ordination (*samyak-saṃvara*)?

To explain the meaning according to the text, it is as clarified above. Regarding the Perfect reception of ordination, the intention of the Patriarchs is manifest. Question: Does the mention of the "superior grade of mind" (*shangpin xin*) below refer to the Perfect Teaching, or not? Answer: The name "superior grade" exists in those Vinaya treatises, yet it still belongs to the provisional and Lesser Vehicles.

If one causes a layperson to rely entirely upon the Perfect Teaching to wonderfully arouse the superior mind, it is as stated in the *Zizhi ji* (Record of Supporting the Practice): "Regarding the superior grade of mind, when compared to the *Vijñaptimātratā* contemplation," and as Jiyuan says: "Receiving [the precepts] with such a mind immediately arouses the Perfect essence. (From the *Sūtra*).
(Copy various texts; please investigate them in detail). Regarding the general meaning of taking the objective realm as a condition, the *Zizhi* (Vol.

1, Part 3) states: "To recognize the objective realm and give rise to the bodhicitta is the essential core for receiving the essence [of the precepts]. This must not be treated casually; therefore, one must rely upon the underlying principles."

This extensively clarifies the essence and measure [of reality]. Students who reach this point must investigate it deeply. I have often seen those who merely recite words, leading the blind by the blind;
both fall into the abyss—how can they not be afraid? Question: Why is it necessary to demonstrate the objective realm (*viṣaya*)? Answer: Sentient beings commit evil deeds.
Since evil karma arises from being deluded regarding external objects, wholesome precepts likewise arise from those same objects;

this is the basis upon which the disciplinary laws depend and the primary source for the generation of ethical conduct. If one does not clearly understand these objects, with what will one apply the mind? To maintain this [discipline], one must expand upon it extensively.

This contains profound and far-reaching implications. Question: Since the precepts (*śīla*) fundamentally serve to restrain the mind, why is it necessary to regulate external objects? Answer: Sentient capacities are divided into great and small, and the teachings differ as gradual or sudden.
Those of great capacity realize that objects are nothing but mind; they therefore restrain directly from the mind—this is the Bodhisattva precept.

Those of small capacity believe that objects are distinct from the mind; thus, they restrain by way of the object—this is the Śrāvaka precept. Although the teaching regulates the object, in principle, it actually regulates the mind.
The provisional establishment of skillful means is clearly manifested herein.

To correctly demonstrate the scope of the object and reveal the vastness of the precepts, the *Shangsan* (Upper Three) of the *Jiexiaofa shichao* states: "The characteristics of the precepts that are generated are indeed immeasurable; this is because prior to receiving the precepts, evil pervades all phenomena."

The Realm (*dhātu*). Now, wishing to advance toward receiving [the precepts], one reverses the aforementioned evil objects (for objects themselves possess neither good nor evil; they are transformed by the mind). Because one gives rise to wholesome thoughts, the cause for the emergence of the precepts returns to pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*.
If one were to discuss this according to each specific object, the commentary would exceed thirty pages.
To summarize, it does not go beyond sentient and non-sentient beings, the two truths of emptiness and existence, the principle of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), and the holy teachings spoken by the Buddha.
Written scrolls, statues, stupas, and temples; earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—all that is measured by the *dharmadhātu* is the substance of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*).

The Record states: "Terms such as 'emptiness' and 'existence' refer to the phenomena of manifested characteristics (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa-dharma*). When the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths, he encompassed both the mundane and the supramundane, as well as the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages.
Among these, the three truths known as Suffering, Origin, and the Path are termed "truths with existence" (*sa-bhava-satya*); Cessation is the truth of emptiness (*śūnyatā-satya*).

It is also called the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional. The phrase "cessation, etc. refers to the dharma of the essential nature (*dharmatā*). This differs from the aforementioned ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), as it is subsumed under the category of teaching (*deśanā*).

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s teaching, etc.," this refers to the two jewels of the Dharma and the Sangha that are maintained and sustained. Question: Since these are not [merely] conceptual objects, why must they be mentioned again? Answer:

It is because one might fear thinking that the realm of the sages is not a condition for the precepts. Question: How do the two dharmas—the transformative and the principle—give rise to the precepts? Answer: [As follows:]...
The Commentary states: "Both involve the sense of damaging and slandering [the Dharma], such as the case of Deva’s destruction of the Dharma. Question:

Why is the Buddha not mentioned in terms of the manifested form (*nirmāṇakāya*), and why is the Saṃgha not mentioned in terms of the sustaining power (*dharmatā*)? Answer: Because both are subsumed within the realm of mental objects (*ālambana*).

In principle, the Buddha and the Saṃgha do not possess separate substantial entities; this is how it should be understood. Regarding "earth, water, and so forth," these specifically enumerate the six great elements (*mahābhūta*); the first five are insentient, while the last one...
These objects—wind, space, and consciousness—are difficult to perceive as objective phenomena; therefore, they are further demonstrated, as explained in the section on the precept against stealing.
Furthermore, one must understand that according to the various distinctions among the precepts, some involve only insentient objects, such as sexual misconduct and killing;

some involve only sentient objects, such as digging and destroying [the earth]; and some involve both types, such as stealing and lying. Regarding stealing, it is divided into four categories of ownership, wherein the objects may comprise the six great elements. Regarding lying...

Regarding those who are deceived, they further scheme for gain and support. As for what is called the "Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu): if one restricts it to the scope of the teachings, it is limited to the trichiliocosm;

however, following the perfect meaning, one must discuss the Dharma-realm of the ten directions. The essence of non-action manifests in accordance with its object, equal in measure to the Dharma-realm;
therefore, it is said that all of these are the substance of the precepts.

Citing evidence for the vastness of the extent of the precepts, he further quotes the *Śraddhā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (or *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*), which states: "Because sentient beings are infinite, the precepts are also infinite. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states: "It is not merely upon sentient beings that one obtains the immeasurable;

it is like the great earth throughout the ten directions, extending downward to the limit of space. Even if one were to harm [the earth] as much as a single speck of dust, [it would constitute a transgression]. All [of this applies].
One incurs transgression [by violating it]. Now, this is translated as "precept-virtue" (*śīla-kuśala*). Thus, it is said throughout the lands:
"The great earth is boundless; the precepts are likewise boundless. Grasses and trees are immeasurable; the waters of the ocean are boundless. Space is limitless; the precepts are equally so."
The record states: "Good birth consists of five kinds; the preceding and following [categories] clarify this through separation. If one were to discuss it further in detail:

food and drink, clothing, dwellings, bedding, the four types of monastic property (saṃghika-vastu) present before us, and all activities—walking, standing, sitting, lying down, looking up or down, maintaining dignified deportment, defecating or urinating, and every other task—are none of them outside the scope of the prescribed rules (*vinaya*).
Thus, amidst the myriad phenomena that appear as dense forests, what matter is not upheld by these precepts?"
If it were not so, how could one be said to be fully endowed [with the precepts]? If they were not first generated, from what would the practice arise?

Therefore, we know that prior to receiving the full precepts, one must first study them in detail; the establishment of the stage of a śrāmaṇera precisely depends upon this. In these degenerate times, the teachings are obscured—who, indeed, understands this anymore?

The *Zhengshifa xin chao* (Excerpts on the Correct Manifestation of the Resolve) further cites the *Sarvāstivāda*: "If the mind is sincere and profound, then one generates the non-informative [action] (i.e., the unmanifest); if it is light, it is not generated. How could this be done with superficiality or negligence?
In principle, it should be done with earnest gravity. One should say: 'I shall generate the superior grade of mind; I shall attain the superior grade.'"

Regarding the precepts: if one possesses an inferior-grade mind, even up to the level of an Arhat, the precepts are of an inferior grade. The *Vibhaṅga-vinaya* states: "One generates the thought: 'I now seek the Way;
I shall save all sentient beings. Since all sentient beings cherish their own lives, one receives [the precepts] by means of this matter."
This is the lower grade of a weak mind; although one has obtained the Buddha’s precepts, they are still not superior.
The other two grades are explained according to their meaning. What is the middle grade? If one says: "I now direct my sincere mind toward the Way to resolve the doubts of sentient beings;
I act as a bridge and raft for all, and am able to benefit myself as well as others," while upholding the right precepts—this is the middle grade. What is the upper grade? If one says:

I now resolve my mind to receive the precepts in order to fulfill the three groups of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), to enter the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), and to rightly seek the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, by means of this Dharma, I shall guide all sentient beings to reach *nirvāṇa* and cause the Dharma to abide for a long time. The record states:
In the section on "Exhortation," it mentions only the "superior grade" (adhimātra). Therefore, we know that the "intermediate" and "inferior" grades are not the primary intent.

This is for the purpose of clarifying the superior grade so that one may understand its excellence relative to others. As for the "inferior grade" and so forth, these are as explained in the *Abhidharma*: there was an Arhat whose precepts were of the inferior grade, yet a young bhikṣu considered them to be of the superior grade.
This is entirely due to the difference in their initial generation of the resolve (*cittotpāda*). Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*yāvat*): starting from...

From ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) up to those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one passes through various stages of development; yet [the essence of the precept] does not increase further.

Some say that while the substance of the precept (*pratimokṣa-saṃvara*) is fixed, its practice increases accordingly. Others maintain that while the *kṛta-śīla* (precept of action) is fixed, the *avijñapti* (unmanifested precept) may increase.

Both views are fully detailed below. Nevertheless, although all save living beings, their practice varies in depth: first, not harming the life of others; second, guiding them with the Dharma; and third, causing them to reach ultimate realization.

In the end, one transcends; what came before does not encompass what follows, yet what follows must include what precedes it. Inferring from this principle: at the initial stage, one merely protects life and does not seek liberation;

this is the mind of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). What was previously called "seeking the Way" refers precisely to the small fruits [of these vehicles]. The practice of the middle grade involves attaining understanding through the Dharma and benefiting both self and others;
though this transcendence is not ultimate, it refers to the Small Bodhisattvas, who, while aspiring for the fruit of Buddhahood, remain within their current sphere of practice.

The intermediate stage, while superior when compared to the preceding, remains inferior when contrasted with what follows. The superior grade of guidance leads one to *nirvāṇa*, converging upon the Buddha-way;
this is precisely the practice of a Great Bodhisattva. According to the *Śrāmaṇera-varga*, these three stages correspond exactly to the [three grades], fitting perfectly.

At this point, the student must clearly discern the aspirations of the three minds and the respective limits of their practices and fruits. Regarding the "superior grade," it speaks of the "Three Aggregates" (*tri-skandha*).
