To dwell amidst desire while seeking to distance oneself from the dust of the world—I truly fear this is beyond your current reach. Since you dwell as an ordinary person while studying the path of the sages, I shall for now restrain myself.
Act accordingly; do not be negligent, but rather be earnest and diligent. Since these words have been spoken, reflect deeply upon them once more.
Admonish yourself by contemplating the six difficulties and rejoice in your cultivation of the Way (*Jingxin jieguan*; composed by our Patriarch Nanshan for his disciple Cirin).
The *Jingxin jieguan* (Pure Mind Admonition and Contemplation) states: First, among the myriad classes of beings, a human body is difficult to obtain.

As the *Tiewei jing* says, obtaining a human body now is more difficult than for a turtle to encounter a floating log. Second, although one has obtained a human body, it is difficult to be born in a central land (*madhyadeśa*).
This land is the center of the borderlands, where the Mahāyāna and the true Dharma of the sutras and vinaya are complete. Third, although the true Dharma exists...
Faith and delight are further difficult to attain; now, according to my capacity, I believe and do not dare to doubt or slander. Fourth, a human body is difficult to possess;

now I have received a male form, with faculties free from impairment and physical characteristics fully perfected. Fifth, although I possess a male form and my six sense-faculties are complete, [the following is difficult to encounter...]

Enmeshed in the defilements of the five desires, it is extremely difficult to leave the household life. Now that you have been able to sever your attachments, you have left home to practice the Way, donned the robes of the Buddha, and received the pure precepts of the Buddha.
Sixth, although you have received the prohibitive precepts, it is extremely difficult to conform to them; you must therefore abide within the Vinaya.

One should respect and cherish [the Dharma], and maintain a sense of shame and dread of blame with careful self-guarding. If one does not examine these six matters, one will fall into negligence, which deeply obstructs the Noble Path.
Having transcended the six difficulties, one should always rejoice; having attained what is so difficult to attain, do not lose it once attained.
To contemplate in this manner is called "purifying the mind.
Regarding the faults of leaving the household life, which differ from those of the laity, the *Yeshu* (Volume 2, Part B) states:

"According to the treatises, the root of transgressions all arises from being bound by worldly affairs; failing to contemplate with revulsion and turning away, one follows one's own mind and creates them falsely."
As stated in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, there are two fetters for those who have left the household life: namely, various views and gain and honor (*lābha-satkāra*).

As established by the causal conditions in the Vinaya, because of fame and profit, outflows (*āsrava*) arise; thus, the various precepts were instituted to prevent sinful karma and to block the three miserable realms (*durgati*).

Yet nowadays, those who leave the household life instead plant the roots of suffering; they do not fear sinking [into the depths], frequently giving rise to inferior karma. Therefore, that text says: "Furthermore..."
There are two types of abscesses: namely, seeking out the faults of others while concealing one's own transgressions. Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"In future ages, there will be those who leave the household life and enter hell, while laypeople are born in the heavens. This is because laypeople possess no formal precepts upon their persons; they are merely devoted in their faith and thus attain birth in heaven.
Those who have left the household life possess the Dharma and serve as fields of merit for the world, yet they instead violate it and receive [offerings] falsely."
Faith-based offerings open the gates to all evils, causing many sentient beings to practice and learn heedlessness.

Therefore, within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is taught that gains and offerings are difficult to digest. Sixty bhikṣus attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Sixty bhikṣus had hot blood gush from their faces.
And sixty bhikṣus, out of fear of the Buddha’s words, immediately returned to lay life.
One should first examine the root of arising transgressions.
Furthermore, it is said: "Those who wish to cultivate the Way should first sever the two attachments of wealth and sensual form among the three types of action. If one does not crave wealth..."

Thus, there is no flattery or contention. If one does not crave form, there is no feverish affliction. As the Sūtra says: "Turning away from and abandoning desire, one accords with the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma).

One should cultivate the contemplation of the body, applying oneself with diligence and single-mindedness to eliminate worldly craving and attachment, subduing the afflictions (kleśa), and purifying the mind.
By severing wealth and form, one accomplishes untainted roots of goodness (anāsrava-kuśalamūla). This perfumes the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) so as to form the seeds of non-greed."
Gradually exhausting delusions and defilements, one enters the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*). As the Sūtra says: "They are neither practitioners of the Way nor laypeople;

they have no name. Because they seek many worldly gains, they devote themselves exclusively to verbal dexterity, adorning their speech with flowery rhetoric. Engaging in frivolous debate and contention, they slander and envy one another;
thus the three poisons grow ever stronger and afflictions increase.

It is further said: "The causes and effects of all suffering have wealth and sensual desire as their root; the causes and effects of all happiness have precepts and meditative concentration as their root.
Yet these causes and effects all reside within the minute particles of the minds of sentient beings. Why, then, do you not restrain them? A sutra states:

"The eighty-four thousand karmic offenses that obstruct the Path all take wealth and sensual desire as their fundamental cause. Why is this? Because among the sentient beings of the ten directions..."
Since beginningless time, those who have killed one another for the sake of wealth exceed the number of motes of dust; those who have killed one another for the sake of form exceed even that number.

If there is anyone who severs [these attachments], they are called a bodhisattva’s practice, they are called a true upholder of the precepts, they are called a worthy man, and they are called a disciple of the Buddha.

Although the two matters of wealth and form appear superficially light, the retribution for the sins they induce is exceedingly heavy. Deception and delusion as numerous as the sands of the Ganges arise from these.

Wealth and sensual desire arise; they can destroy the eyes of a ruler, as well as the harmony between teacher and disciple, husband and wife, and even ruin internal and external kinsmen, friends, and spiritual mentors.

If one is free from wealth and sensual desire, there is nothing further in the world; humans and devas are liberated from suffering, praised alike by the holy and the ordinary, all outflows are extinguished, and one advances to the fruit of Buddhahood.
For this reason, wealth and sensual desire are the two primary warnings. Through sensual form, arrogance arises; through wealth...

One gives rise to stinginess; being both arrogant and stingy, even if one possesses other virtues, they are insufficient to be observed. First, sever attachment to wealth and sensual pleasures so that your meritorious practice may be established;
afterwards, listen to the sūtras and śāstras—this is the sequence for entering the Path. The verse says: "The base person loves wealth and sensual pleasures;
I warn you to sever greedy attachment. Because of wealth, there is suffering in two worlds; because of form, one enters the fiery cauldrons. Form can obstruct the Noble Ones."
The Path. Wealth can cause one’s practice to become thin; examine your own mind with careful scrutiny. Know that greed is a deluded error; use wisdom to avoid it as one would a pit of fire.

The stubborn and ignorant do not loathe it, but if you commit it, you must repent and eliminate it. Once eliminated, do not commit it again. All things possessing form ultimately end up filling the ditches and ravines.
By maintaining the precepts and restraining the afflictions of the mind, one will later receive great peace and happiness.
The *Wǔrén chílǜ fófǎ zhùshì zīchí* (upper volume), fascicle 1, states:
"The reason why it refers specifically to five people is that they are capable of discerning the various communal dharmas, such as the conferral of the precepts."

The reason for the five-thousand-year period is as discussed in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*: "If one asks, 'Does the Buddha-dharma completely perish after one thousand years? The answer is: it does not completely perish.
During the first thousand years, those who attain the three types of supernormal knowledge (the power to penetrate the three periods of time) appear.

During the next thousand years, Arhats who have exhausted their cravings appear, though they lack the three types of supernormal knowledge. During the following thousand years, Anāgāmins appear. During the subsequent thousand years, Srotāpannas appear..."

For another thousand years, they will attain the stage of *srotāpanna*. For five thousand years, they will study the Dharma and attain the Way; for the subsequent five thousand years, they will study but not attain the Way.
Ten thousand years later, the scriptures and written characters will be completely extinguished, and there will remain only those who have shaved their heads and wear the *kāṣāya* robes.

Because the precepts are identical in essence and virtue to the Buddha, the *Chao* (Commentary) cites the *Pañcaśata-praśna-śāstra*, which states: The Buddha said, "I do not enter parinirvāṇa; I come once every half-month.

It further states: "The Buddha has two bodies. Although his physical body has departed, his dharma-body remains in the world. Those who revere the Dharma are thereby revering and mindfulness of the Buddha."

If one upholds the five precepts, one immediately perceives the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). If one protects the Dharma, one is thereby protecting the Buddha. This is like the analogy of drinking water that kills insects.

Furthermore, it is like the fortnightly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), through which one perceives the "Self" (the Buddha). The Record states: "In all three sections, it is pointed out that the precepts are themselves the Buddha.

The reason for this is that the Buddha possesses two bodies: the birth-body (*janmakāya*) and the Dharma-body. The Dharma-body, in turn, is twofold: first, the Dharma of principle (*li-fǎ*); [second, the Dharma of phenomena].
The Body (*kāya*) is the manifestation of the realized principle. The second is the *dharmakāya*, which is the perfection of the fivefold qualities.

The *janmakāya* (birth-body) is subject to arising and ceasing, whereas these two types of *dharmakāya* are eternally abiding. Therefore, Aśvaghoṣa, in his commentary on the passage "after my parinirvāṇa, cherish and respect the *vinaya*," states:
"The *dharmakāya*, which manifests without end, eternally abides in the world to perform ultimate deliverance. Thus, one knows that the Buddha...

The fundamental self has no body; it is entirely formed through the accumulation of merit. This mass of merit is used to reveal and instruct all sentient beings; therefore, it is called "precept" (*śīla*).
One should know that this precept is none other than the Tathāgata; thus it is said: "If I were in the world, there would be nothing different from this.
If one is deluded regarding this principle, how can the Buddha’s words be understood? Those who study later and reach this point should earnestly contemplate the meaning of the Dharma.
The *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* (Lüzhì záxué yǐfáng zhèngyè chāo) further quotes the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, stating:

"One may study scripts such as those for knowing appointments and assemblies (referring to the appointment of monks by administrators and the gathering for dharma-meals), but one must not neglect one's primary duties out of a fondness for such studies.

Divination, physiognomy, and inquiring of others regarding good or ill fortune are not permitted. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), however, allows for the study and recitation of literary texts.

Furthermore, one should not study worldly treatises (*lokavāda*) for the purpose of refuting non-Buddhists. Among the *Miśrakadharmapada*, it is stated that newly ordained bhikṣus are permitted to study the art of calculation.

However, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, those who take pleasure in composing literary verses and embellishing prose and verse with ornate rhetoric should be regarded as objects of fear; such activities must not be performed. This is also recorded in the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*.
The Buddha said: "I shall teach you a single word and a single verse. As for what should be practiced in future generations, practice it;
as for what should not be practiced, do not practice it. The same applies to what the bhikṣus of future generations may say. The record states:

"Methods of writing, calculation, and divination, as well as secular classics and literary verses, are all worldly dharmas and not the vocation of those who have left the household life. However, due to specific causes and conditions, they may occasionally [be employed]."
Open it up. Nowadays, among the sons of Śākyamuni, both name and reality have been lost. Those capable of calligraphy are titled "Sages of Cursive Script";

those who popularize the classics claim for themselves the title of "Literati"; those who select sites are called "Masters of Mountains and Waters"; and those skilled in divination are addressed as "Masters of the Three Fates."
Who would have thought that one who has abandoned worldly affairs to serve the Buddha would follow the conventional tide of fame;

that one whose original perfection was to weary of the world and transcend it would, instead, accumulate karma for birth and death? Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "To study external texts is like using a blade to cut mud;
the mud is not formed, yet the blade is damaged. To read such texts is like looking at the sun's glare; it causes the eyes to go blind. Nevertheless, even among the eminent monks of antiquity...

There were many heterodox scholars. Some were proficient in cursive and clerical scripts; some were skilled in literary composition; some were renowned for their medical arts; and others were famous for their knowledge of *yin-yang* (cosmology).

All claimed to have reached the ultimate depths of their own fields while peripherally engaging with other traditions, none of whom failed to set their will upon protecting and upholding [the Dharma] and assisting in the propagation of the Buddha’s transformation.
Thus, the *Śīlasūtra* states: "If one engages in debate to refute false views, if two parts are from the Sūtras and one part is from external texts..."
This is the intent behind the recitation of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in four parts. Nowadays, some seek fame and profit, align themselves with power, and boast of their abilities;
though they wear the outer robe of the monastic order, their hearts are tainted by worldly vanity. To spend an entire life in vain is truly lamentable.
The *Jiexing wushi fanqing jielü youchao* (Middle Volume One) states:
"Now there are unworthy people who, unaware of their own spiritual station and level, recklessly presume upon themselves."

To claim that this is the Mahāyāna while deriding the true sūtras and esteeming one's own teachings as superior contradicts the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, which states that the *Vinaya* is precisely the study of the Mahāyāna;
it also contradicts the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which says that the *Aṣṭagrantha* (Eight Recitations) is the *Śīla-pāramitā*. Such are the scriptures and treatises.
If these words do not enter their ears, how could this not be a cause for sorrow? Therefore, the *Māyā-sūtra* states:
"If a young bhikṣu personally reviles the *vinaya* in the midst of the assembly, one should know that this is a sign of the extinction of the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:

"If it is said that the Tathāgata taught that one enters hell for a number of years corresponding to the aforementioned [offenses], all such statements are the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata."
Those who speak thus in a manner that terrifies people should be known as certainly following the sūtras and vinaya of Māra, not what was spoken by the Buddha.

By means of this textual evidence, the Tathāgata knew in advance that such things would exist in the future; therefore, he spoke and revealed them beforehand to definitively distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox, so that there would be no confusion.
Yet, there are those who belong to the same factions as before; they may truly be called the subjects of Māra. Furthermore, the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra* and other such texts all...

This refers to the Vinaya, which he regarded as his Great Master. He thought, "If I were to remain in this world, it would be no different from this [Vinaya]. Therefore, by acting in opposition to it, he brought ruin upon himself.
Thus, the *Śatapañcāśatkāvadāna* (The Sutra of One Hundred Parables) says: "In the past, there was a teacher who had two disciples; each was assigned to one of his feet."
They massaged him at the appropriate times. His senior disciple resented the junior one and broke the leg upon which he was massaged;
the latter, in turn, resented him and broke the leg upon which the senior disciple had been massaged.

This is like those who study the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings and do not [value] the Hīnayāna, while those who study the Hīnayāna likewise do not [value] the Vaipulya; thus, both paths of the Great Sage’s scriptural canon are allowed to perish.

By this one may know and witness with one’s own eyes today that when Bodhisattvas establish their teachings, they open the Way to deliver the common people; they act according to conditions without being stained by worldly customs.

A Great Being at the initial stage of resolve observes the same rules of discipline as the Śrāvakas, guarding against the precepts concerning censure and reproach; in their essential gravity, there is no difference.

This is illustrated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where a Rākṣasa begs for a speck of dust from a life-preserving leather bag, yet the Bodhisattva does not give it to him—this serves as an analogy for such protection.
This refers to the *dukkaṭa* (offense) precepts. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because an ordained bodhisattva guards the precepts, he does not accumulate wealth or goods;
the merit of the precepts surpasses that of giving. For example, by my abstaining from killing, I bestow the life-force of all sentient beings.
Based on this textual evidence, although those who currently study the Mahāyāna in a superficial manner are not to be followed, their words exceed [the truth].
Truly, he felt shame for his own transgressions, yet he falsely exalted himself. I once said to him, "The precepts are a minor dharma;
you should abandon them," but he was unwilling. I then said, "You should uphold them," but again he was unwilling. Is this not because he is conjoined with afflictions (*kleśa*)?
It is ultimately difficult to describe through analogy; is it not also pitiable?

The *Zichi* (Vol. 1, Part 1) states: In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the Vinaya regulations stipulate that a bhikṣu, prior to five years of summer retreats (*varṣa*), must devote himself exclusively to the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Only after he has mastered the observance and transgression of the precepts and is capable of managing the affairs of the bhikṣu community may he then proceed to study the Sūtras and Śāstras.

To bypass this sequence and study prematurely results in a loss of order in practice; since there would be no way to enter the Path, the Great Sage’s censure was certainly not in vain. Furthermore, that Vinaya...
It is said: When the Buddha saw that the bhikṣus were not studying the Vinaya, he then praised the Vinaya;
he praised Upāli in his presence as being foremost in upholding the Vinaya, and subsequently the senior elders and bhikṣus studied the Vinaya under Upāli.

In the present day, those who have merely received the precepts are immediately permitted by the Saṃgha to study the teachings and practice Chan as their monastic conduct, yet they understand none of it. How much less so...
Furthermore, they treat the precepts and restraints with contempt, revile the *vinaya*, and disparage the study of the discipline as being of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

They treat the observance of the precepts with negligence, regarding it as mere attachment to signs. Thus, they become lost and deluded within the secular world, indulging their own ferocity and stubbornness. They crave cups of wine and slices of meat, yet claim to be "comprehensive" in their understanding;

they practice lust and harbor anger, yet in their speech they profess to have attained the Way. Having failed to fathom the intent of the Sage, they have misinterpreted the True Vehicle. Moreover, if the precepts were truly dispensable, why—?

If you were to ascend the altar and receive [the precepts], the Vinaya would surely be subject to violation. Why then have you shaved your hair and donned the dyed robes? This is to treat the precepts lightly, which is entirely self-deprecation;

to destroy the Vinaya is likewise to bring about one's own ruin. Delusive emotions are easy to habituate, while the True Path is difficult to hear. To transcend the mundane and rise above the crowd—[this is the true purpose].
"Out of ten thousand, not one [is truly so]. I pray you examine the sacred instructions closely; can you not follow them?
Furthermore, it is said that those who study today focus exclusively on commentaries and records, vying with one another in debate and discussion, considering this their own mastery.

In body they act as heavy barbarians, while in speech they guard against minor transgressions. Deeming themselves refined and brilliant, they act like thieves, yet instead they encroach upon and damage the four quarters. Those who are skillfully adept..."

In the category of lust, they are even more deluded and confused regarding the three paths. They consume food to satiety in the dim light of evening yet still speak of moderation; they drink until intoxicated at night yet still discourse on the regulations against alcohol.
Before others, they maintain a composed appearance and feign an air of dignity; yet in private, they commit transgressions without the slightest sense of fear or restraint.

This was witnessed by our own eyes; how could it be a false claim? It is truly due to the errors and corruptions of the written records, compounded by the ignorance and vulgarity of the lineage of teachers.
What is not permitted is being taught; one blind man leads a multitude of blind men. The True Doctrine of our Imperial Ancestors is now nearly extinguished.
Reflecting upon this meaning, I cannot help but sigh in lamentation. Having thus committed these words to writing, my grief and pain increase all the more. Were it not for...
O Sage, who can perceive my heart? How tragic!
My mind has not yet entered the Way, yet I have recklessly relied upon the sacred words.
The *Chao* (Excerpts) further states: "Now, my mind has not yet entered the Way, my conduct violates both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, and though my mouth speaks of being without fault..."

Confession. "Lust is the Way. The Record states: "The nature of sin and merit is empty. This appears in the *Samantabhadra-caryā-dharma*. "Lust is the Way" appears in the *Acaranga-sūtra* (Wuxing jing);
it is a general teaching of the Mahāyāna, not confined to a single scripture. It is taught to reveal that the characteristics of karma are all like illusions;
furthermore, to show that the nature of karma is ungraspable; furthermore, to show that defilement and purity share a single source; and furthermore, to show...

Because all phenomena are but the single mind, and because it further causes sentient beings to attain liberation from all evils, this does not mean that you are being directed to engage in impure conduct or to commit evil at this time.
To rely on such words as a pretext to gloss over one’s own faults and to gratify the sentiments of the ignorant is truly to deviate from the intent of the Sage.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "First sever the mind of lust; this is called the practice of the Tathāgatas and the Buddhas of the past."
Venerable One, this is the foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction. Furthermore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states:

"A bodhisattva should give rise to a heart of filial piety and obedience, rescuing and delivering all sentient beings, and purifying the Dharma for others. Yet, if one instead gives rise to sexual desire toward others, or even lacks a heart of compassion, this constitutes a pārājika offense for a bodhisattva.
If one adheres strictly to these words, how then should this [present case] be understood?
How tragic, how tragic!
The *Commentary on the Five and Four Depravities Not Being Right Livelihood* further states:
"As for the five depravities: the first refers to altering one's usual dignified demeanor and falsely manifesting an extraordinary appearance in order to seek gain and offerings."
The marks: second, proclaiming one's own virtues; third, raising one's voice to display authority; fourth, proclaiming the gains one has received to incite others to give;
fifth, forcibly divining the fortunes of others for the sake of profit. These are called the four wrong means (mithyājīva).
First, those who practice heterodoxy by traveling in all four directions to seek food and clothing; second, those who look upward at the stars and constellations, which are merely empty appearances;
third, those who engage in inferior activities such as plowing fields and planting crops;

and fourth, those who subsist on the food of their mouths by practicing minor incantations and arts to seek profit and sustain their lives. This is the explanation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Regarding the Vinaya:
[The text] states: "To preach what is not Dharma as Dharma, and to preach Dharma as what is not Dharma," and so forth.

Regarding the eight impure forms of wealth that increase greed and destroy the Path, the *Chao* (Excerpts), [Volume] Middle 2, says: "First, fields, houses, gardens, and groves; second, planting and cultivating seeds; third, hoarding grain and silk; fourth, livestock..."
1. Keeping servants; 2. Keeping birds and beasts as pets; 3. Money, jewels, and precious objects; 4. Carpets, rugs, and golden cauldrons; 5.

Elephants and gold-adorned couches, as well as other heavy articles. These eight items are extensively enumerated in the sūtras, śāstras, and vinaya as common categories of transgression, revealing that their possession is improper.
Furthermore, the Vinaya and Sūtras state: "If anyone possesses these, they are not my disciple. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* also says: "Certainly..."
They will certainly not believe my Dharma and Vinaya. For these eight reasons, they all increase greed and destroy the Path;

they defile the holy life (brahmacarya) and obtain defiled fruits; therefore, they are called "impure. It continues: "In the Vinaya, the matters are minor and the capacities of those concerned are narrow."
Therefore, [the Buddha] frequently permitted the possession [of wealth]. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"If there are no disciples to provide for my needs, or if the world suffers from famine and food and drink are difficult to obtain, in order to protect and uphold the establishment of the True Dharma, I permit my disciples to accept and possess gold and silver."

Regarding vehicles, fields, houses, grain, rice, and whatever else is required for trade, although it is permitted to accept and possess such items, they must be received through "pure giving" (*viśuddha-dāna*) from a donor of sincere faith.
The Record states: "The preceding clarifies the Mahāyāna, where both the capacity [of the practitioner] and the teaching are urgent; the following clarifies the Hīnayāna."

When both capacity and teaching are lax, the Vinaya—concerned with matters—is light because it involves a violation of a matter; conversely, the core of the Sūtras is revealed as grave because it involves a violation of principle.
Those of small capacity have narrow intentions and are thus granted dispensation; the Mahāyāna is the opposite, for they are capable of bearing the burden, and is therefore grave.
Yet worldly people conversely claim that the Hīnayāna requires precepts while the Great Teaching is universal and flexible—how great is this error!

The *Zizhi* quotes the Vinaya, saying: "Because the sun and moon have four afflictions, they are neither bright nor pure; they cannot illuminate anything, nor do they possess majestic spiritual power.
These are the asuras, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist. A śramaṇa has four great afflictions: drinking alcohol..."
Sexual desire, the possession of gold and silver, and wrong livelihood can cause a śramaṇa to be neither clear nor pure, such that he cannot illuminate anything and possesses no majestic power.
It is said now that when a śramaṇa practices purity, the light of the Buddha-dharma shines forth;
since his conduct is base and defiled, it acts as an obscuration, just like smoke. Furthermore, the *Śīlasūtra* states: "For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, a bodhisattva..."
It is permitted to possess *kauśeya* silk, gold, silver, and so forth. Fools rely on this [text] and rashly equate these with [the prohibitions for monastics]. This is a failure of reflection.

Furthermore, the term "bodhisattva" applies to both the laity and the ordained. As in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, although the possession of [precious materials] is prohibited for ordained bodhisattvas, even if it were said that they are permitted to possess them, both the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* require such items to be given as pure gifts (*viśuddha-dāna*). Even if one follows the *Śīla-sūtra*...
To benefit sentient beings. Yet now, you act in accordance with your own greedy attachments, seeking through flattery and deceit;

for the sake of accumulation, you demand much and never tire, while seeing the poor and sick, you give not even a single hair’s breadth. How can this not be indistinguishable from a great being (mahāsattva) in terms of high and low? It continues, saying:
Yuan Xian lived within a square enclosure of walls; his thatched door could not even be closed. Yan Yuan dwelt in a humble alley, eating from a single bamboo bowl and drinking from a gourd ladle.
The eminent worthies of the Jin and Song dynasties and the sagely men of the Qi and Liang eras regarded wealth and honor as mere refuse and valued frugality and simplicity as the height of nobility.
This is pervasive throughout the historical records. Have you not heard?

The *Chao* further states: "The Buddha, the World-Honored One, desired to cause his disciples to abandon base occupations, so that they might transcend the three realms from afar and serve as a model for the world at close hand.
Yet now, he has instead fallen into self-degradation, personally keeping and catching [animals], no different from the merchants and peddlers of the marketplace. I believe this.

This mist and cloud of the Buddha-dharma has, on the contrary, become a source of self-aggrandizement. They recklessly cast aside the laws and regulations, claiming that if one merely lacks a greedy heart, how could there be any transgression or fault?

Those who utter such words are deluded in their self-conceit; they fail to reflect that they occupy the rank of an ordinary person of the lower realms, yet they lightly dismiss even a fraction of the benefits of the Great Sage.
To still calculate themselves superior to the refined detachment of worldly scholars—how is this different from the wisdom of a cicada trying to block a chariot wheel?
This is no different from the ability of a moth to fly into a flame; it not only shortens one's life and fosters long-term greed, but also initiates the commission of grave theft.

Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one can remain far removed from the eight poisonous dharmas, this is called the pure field of merit of the noble assembly, which should be honored by humans and devas.
Such pure karmic fruition cannot be distinguished by the physical eye."
Food is a condition for the Path; its regulation is not intended to be restrictive. Furthermore, it is said:
"Although food is a great affliction, who among people does not require it? For this reason, throughout the Buddha’s entire ministry, he frequently addressed this matter first;
thus, when inquiring after others, he would ask, "Was almsfood obtained? The ancients have said: "A monastery is where the Sangha from the ten directions gathers to cultivate the Way."
Regarding the boundaries: as they travel and come and go, there is neither "there" nor "here," neither host nor guest. The principles of the Sangha are equal; together they protect the Buddha-Dharma.

Food, drink, and all requisites exist equally throughout the ten directions. When the bell is struck to perform the ritual, the assembly of monks gathers universally to bestow [merit] upon the donor, acting as a field for generating blessings.
I exhort you to broaden your胸怀 (xīnhuái, "mind" or "heart") so that your benefit may follow the Way and provide protection.

It is further said (both passages above appear in the *Senggang pian*): A sincere renunciant fears the manifold sufferings of the four enemies, loathes the impermanence of the three realms, takes leave of the deepest affection of the six kin, and abandons the profound attachment to the five desires; this is truly because of the delusions of worldly life.
One should cast [these thoughts] aside. One ought to return to the path of truth. It is fitting to broaden one’s distant aspirations and to humble and purify base sentiments.

One should not begrudge one’s body or wealth, but rather protect and uphold the True Dharma. Moreover, since the food of the Sangha belongs equally to all throughout the ten directions, it is only right that when others take their own portion, one should rejoice;
yet human nature often harbors narrow-mindedness, leading to unequal attitudes. There are even those who shut their doors and restrict visiting monks from entering. This is not permissible.

This too is a mockery of the original intent of sounding the bell. How could it be otherwise? Having left the household life and renounced attachment, one especially ought not to act in such a manner.
Merely because of this fragile body, you are unable to steadfastly protect the True Dharma;

because of this precarious and false life, you are unwilling to share the monastic provisions widely, thereby violating the teachings of all Buddhas, diminishing the merit of the donors, wounding the sentiments of the assembly for a time, and obstructing the Sangha of the ten directions.
This path has been transmitted erroneously to later generations; the damage it causes is far-reaching. To rectify former delusions and return to the Way—is this not excellent?

(To be stingy with food and eat alone is the karma of a hungry ghost; this is called great delusion. Someone asked: "The affairs of the Sangha are limited, while outside guests are infinite. With limited food,"

"If one must not establish the service of providing for an infinite number of monks," [the opponent] replied, "this is merely the shallow perspective of the vulgar and the narrow-mindedness of petty people;
how could it be called the profound insight of the pure-witted or the lofty vision of the enlightened?

For the offerings of the fourfold assembly and the field of merit of the Three Jewels are like the growth of heaven and earth, or the utilization of mountains and seas—how could they ever come to an end?"
Therefore, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "One should practice the Way with a single mind, following the conduct of the Dharma, and not dwell on the thought of food or clothing.
Even if one were to take a single portion from the white tuft between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows to provide for all his ordained disciples, it would never be exhausted.
From this it may be said: Diligently cultivate the precepts and walk with sincerity to protect the Dharma; profit is gained through the Way, and by means of the Way...
This applies universally. It is even said: "In secular teachings, one still prioritizes concern for the Way over concern for poverty;

how much more so for those who have left the household life, who transcend the mundane world—if they do not worry about protecting the Dharma but instead worry about food and drink, their failure is truly grave."
Evil conduct that defiles the family, violates the precepts, and ruins the Way (this is common in the world; it is cited here to lead others toward reform).

*Chao* (Excerpts), Part Two: Citing the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it says: "If a layperson previously possessed faith and made offerings to the Saṃgha by constructing monasteries and dwellings, yet causes them to decline or diminish, this is called 'defiling the family' (*kula-dūṣaka*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If one commits various kinds of evil deeds and destroys the [virtue] of others..."
To have faith, reverence, and a virtuous mind yet be called one who "defiles the household" means that one acts with impurity, filth, and turbidity, and consequently incurs evil retribution;

this is termed "evil conduct. Furthermore, whenever a bhikṣu seeks anything—whether it be various items offered in faith for the sake of the Triple Gem, himself, or anyone else—and gives them to high ministers, monastics, or laypeople alike, all such actions are termed "defiling the household. Why is this so?
For this reason, all those who have left the household life should be without conditioned activity or desire, maintaining themselves in purity with the cultivation of the Path as their sole aim.
If they act as messengers for laypeople, coming and going on their behalf, they will neglect and disrupt their primary practice, which is not conducive to liberation.

Furthermore, by giving items obtained through offerings of faith to laypeople, they destroy the impartial good intentions of the donors and cause them to feel only joy and attachment toward those who receive the goods.
If one does not receive material goods, even if they are virtuous and good, they will lose the heart of love and respect from others—those who are profound fields of merit.
Generally, laypeople in the household life constantly seek pure blessings from the Triple Gem, sacrificing their own flesh and blood to plant roots of goodness.
Now, those who have left the household life instead take articles of faith and present them as gifts to laypeople, acting in a manner contrary to that of renunciants.
Furthermore, if one gives even a small gift to a layperson and, on that basis, erects a stupa of the seven treasures or builds a vihara,
even if such offerings— extending to the four requisites— fill the entirety of Jambudvīpa, they are not equal to sitting in meditation and purely maintaining the precepts;
this is the true worship of the Dharmakāya.
Chapter Six: The Gate of the Precepts for Various Texts;
Chapter Seven: The Characteristics of the Precepts in Various Texts, Clarifying the Characteristics by Way of Practice.

The *Chao* (upper volume, "Establishing the Thesis") states: "The characteristics of the fourfold purity (*catuḥpariśuddhi*) refer to the perfection of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). Whatever actions one performs, if movement accords with the Dharma, its virtuous qualities will shine forth;

therefore, they are called the 'characteristics of precepts' (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*). The *Jiwen* (Record of Questions) asks: "In the 'Explanation of Characteristics' (*Xiexiang-pian*) section, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is taken as the characteristic; how does this differ from the present [explanation]? Answer:

This [present explanation] clarifies [the characteristics] in terms of practice (*caryā*), whereas that [previous section] distinguishes them according to the Dharma (*dharma*). Nevertheless, practice must follow the Dharma, and the Dharma...
One must certainly follow this practice. As the text says: "When in motion, one accords with the Dharma. Is this not clear?

Regarding the classification of characteristics based on the Dharma, the *Xingshichao* (Excerpts on Practice), in its first section explaining the characteristics, states: "If one relies upon this to practice and skillfully recognizes their various characteristics, then concentration and wisdom will arise, and [the goal] will be achieved."

To sever the afflictions: if one is deluded regarding the object of focus (the *ālambana*—as the commentary notes, this refers to the objective realm, or alternatively, to the characteristics of the teaching), and follows along with the flow of defiled delusions, how can one turn back the stream of birth and death?

One will instead sink further into the wheel of suffering realms. Therefore, relying on the teachings to bring forth their characteristics, the observance and violation [of precepts] are fully revealed.

One must certainly act in accordance with this; then there will be no calamities or harm (where "harm" refers to the three miserable realms). Not only will one avoid such harm, but one can also give rise to meditative concentration and wisdom.

The Record states: Question: What constitutes the characteristics [of an offense]? Answer: As explained later, they are categorized into three sections regarding the precepts: first, the object of the transgression; second, the manifestation of the transgression.
The three instances of opening [the door] without offense constitute the general characteristics. Furthermore, seeking them through their underlying principles, there are three specific distinctions:

first, the distinction between offense and non-offense; second, the distinction of varying degrees of lightness and heaviness within offenses; third, the distinction between preparatory acts (*upakrama*) and the fundamental act (*mūla*).
To summarize these characteristics, they do not transcend the interplay of mind and object (*citta-viṣaya*). If one does not understand this further, [it will remain unclear].
To clarify the enumeration of the characteristics:

furthermore, it is said that the four aspects clarify the characteristics of the precepts. In terms of verbal characteristics, where there is an object, this is present; as for conditions, they extend continuously.

While the gathering of the mind applies generally, here we rely on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which everyone recites and upholds. Its textual characteristics are easy to understand, and the distinctions between observance and violation are not confused. As for the rest...
Regarding the myriad objects of experience, how could one allow words to leak out? Following established precedents, I have gained a slight understanding of the general framework.

The *Record* states: "Characteristics possess form and shape; they can be distinguished upon observation. The preceding section clarified the dharma of precepts, merely describing its functional capacity.

The subsequent section clarified the essence of precepts, discussing only the nature of karma. The final section clarifies the practice of precepts, briefly indicating their cultivation and integration. If one does not discern these characteristics, then the dharma...

There are three aspects: essence (*tǐ*), characteristics (*xiàng*), and practice (*xíng*). First, there is nothing that is not understood. Why is this so? There is no separate dharma apart from dharmas; characteristics themselves are the dharma.

There is no separate essence apart from essence; the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) constitutes the essence. There is no separate practice apart from practice; treading upon characteristics constitutes practice.

Therefore, students must deeply investigate and examine this single gate. Now, as for where characteristics reside, they are found solely in the verbal designations of the teachings. To speak in broad outline: it is as follows.

There are two hundred and fifty rules; the articles and clusters differ. Within each article, there are distinctions of names and types (names being *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, *pāyattika*, and *duṣkṛta*;

types being sexual misconduct, theft, killing, lying, physical contact, and so forth). Within each type, there are offenses and non-offenses. Within each offense, there are causes and effects regarding gravity (the three kinds of preliminary efforts are the cause;

the formal offenses of the five categories are the effect; "heavy" refers to *pārājika*, "light" refers to *duṣkṛta*, with the intermediate grades relative to one another). Regarding the common and specific conditions for offenses (there are seven common conditions: first, renunciation...).

1. A gathering of the assembly; 2. Absence of serious illness; 3. Correspondence of intention; 4. Absence of danger to life; 5. Absence of danger to the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya); 6. Addressing the actual object; 7. Tending toward a formal result. These distinct conditions vary according to the different precepts, such as the four requisites for sexual misconduct, the four requisites for theft, and the factors that constitute an offense.

To provide a summary illustration: it does not go beyond the enumeration of conditions (*pratyaya*). Whether these conditions are few or many, they do not transcend the mind and its objects (*viṣaya*)—the "enumeration of conditions" refers to the aforementioned specific conditions, while "objects" refers to the preceding objects and "mind" refers to the transgressive mind.

A transgression has no inherent substance (*svabhāva*); it must necessarily be constructed by means of conditions (both general and specific). It does not arise without an object, nor is it accomplished without a mind.
If one understands this principle, it will apply universally to all cases as clearly as looking at the palm of one's hand.

Next, regarding the *Jue pianzhu wuqi budong chao* (The Commentary on the Five-Seven Differences in Resolving the Categories of Offenses), it further states (concerning one section on the categories of offenses): "Now, we shall first distinguish the seven differences within the five [categories]. These possess three meanings that cause them to be included within the five:

first, equality of name (each of the five categories is fixed, without distinctions of superior, middling, or inferior); second, equality of substance (the retribution for committing a *pārājika* offense is identical); and third, equality of ultimate result."

Because they do not constitute skillful means for the various chapters, these three are not fully included; rather, they are subsumed within the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* category. Nevertheless, there is a specific purpose for distinguishing the sixth and seventh [categories].

Within the sixth, *duṣkṛta* is combined because they share the same essence (as they are both resultant offenses). Within the seventh, "evil speech" (*durbhāṣita*) is separated because its instances are numerous (compared to the offenses in the other chapters;

furthermore, based on the two divisions of body and speech: that which is committed by the body is called *duṣkṛta*, while that which is committed by speech is called *durbhāṣita*). Question: Above, you have fully set forth the names of the six categories (*ṣaḍ-nikāya*).

[The questioner] asks: "Please explain the five categories (*pañca-varga*) and seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*). What are their names and characteristics? [The respondent] answers: "As for the 'five categories':
first, *pārājika*; second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, *pāyattika* (Skt. *pāyattika*, Ch. *pāyattika*); fourth, *pratideśanīya*; and fifth, *duṣkṛta*. As for the 'seven groups':

first, *pārājika*; second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, *sthūlātyaya*; and so on, up to the seventh, *durbhāṣita*. The record states that the names 'category' (*varga*) and 'group' (*nikāya*) are used interchangeably."
They must correspond in a partial manner; they are distinguished as five and seven only by way of dividing the uniform and the mixed. Therefore, the Commentary states:

"Even if the *piṇḍa* (aggregates) follow the five categories, their meaning possesses the threefold uniformity; the title of the section resides in the seven, which is precisely because they are fundamentally subsumed under the 'mixed' category.

Question: If there are eight sections in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* itself, how do the current divisions into five and seven correspond? Answer: The present mention of "sections and aggregates" (*piṇḍa*) is not restricted solely to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

However, this is merely establishing a name that collectively encompasses all offenses. If one were to apply the number five to correspond with the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, then the thirty-ninth and fortieth rules would be merged into one;

likewise, the *Aniyata* and the methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) would all be subsumed under the *Duskṛta* (Pāyantika). Nevertheless, the original purpose of establishing these names does not follow the literal phrasing of the texts.

Provided that the objects regulated by the Vinaya precepts pervade as many realms as the sands of the Ganges, the gravity of their causes and effects is universally subsumed within five or seven categories.
Specifically, the five categories encompass the fundamental offenses, while the seven include miscellaneous factors that serve as the primary causes for those offenses.

Regarding the display of the broad and concise characteristics of the precepts for monks and nuns, it further states: Question: In the Vinaya, two hundred and fifty precepts are enumerated for monks, and these are fully contained in the *Śīla-sūtra* (Precept Text).

For nuns, however, there are five hundred. Is this statement true or false? (The mention of "five hundred" originates from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and differs from the Vinaya; therefore, this question is raised to resolve the discrepancy. Answer: The fixed numbers listed for both groups are merely approximations. To explain: [the text continues with the specific enumeration].

The term "concise" (*yue*) means abbreviated. Therefore, various schools generally state that one need not rely on specific numbers. Regarding the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*), it is a single non-informative action (*avijñapti*);

yet when its characteristics are clarified according to their objects, they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Thus, two hundred and fifty [precepts] are merely pointed out as the path for observing and violating them.
Within the Vinaya, the Bhikṣuṇīs have three hundred and forty-eight precepts; these may be cited as the objects to be guarded against. Now...

The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Regarding the method for nuns to receive the precepts, the abbreviated version consists of five hundred rules, while the extensive version consists of eighty thousand.
For monks, the abbreviated version consists of two hundred and fifty rules, and the extensive version is likewise the same as that of the nuns' discipline."
Furthermore, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are further traced back as the basis for the manifestation of characteristics.

(The "nature" is the essence of the mind; this essence is fundamentally one. Following conditions and pursuing thoughts, there arise ten thousand differences. Although conditions and thoughts are manifold, they are none other than these three types. Because the essence calls forth its functions, they are called the "three natures.")

It is further stated: First, there is the transgression of the precepts with a virtuous mind (though not gross or evil, it arises from ignorance; the resulting karma is light, as there is no separate offense for violating a regulation).

This refers, for example, to a *karmadāna* (administrative) bhikṣu in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* who is ignorant of the characteristics of the precepts and misappropriates the property of the Triple Gem. Depending on what was violated, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
Or, seeing others weary of life, one provides them with the means for death; or observing a layperson killing, one instructs them to "give [the prey] quickly" so that they may not...

This causes suffering and distress. These are all offenses committed through a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). However, when the external object (*viṣaya*) is contrary [to the intent] and grave, one cannot claim non-offense on the grounds of ignorance.
From this, one may learn that these all constitute root offenses. As the Vinaya text states:

"For a fool, from a *pārājika* down to a *duṣkṛta*, it is likewise. Furthermore, as the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* says: "A young bhikṣu did not know the characteristics of the precepts regarding a stūpa..."
When pulling up grass, one incurs both sin and merit. If one discusses the retribution to come, the punishment for the sin will be light because of the original wholesome intention;

yet one still cannot avoid hell because of violating the nature of the physical body. If one violates a natural precept (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), one fully incurs three types of offenses, namely those pertaining to the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Furthermore, regarding violations of prohibitive rules (*prajñapti-sāvadya*), such as destroying grass and trees, one incurs only a single offense. This is because...

Because within the *Huajiao* (Transformative Teaching), there was originally no prohibition against [disturbing] insentient things. Thus, there is nothing insentient that can be vexed. If one later performs repentance and purification, one returns to original purity;

this differs from the violation of a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherent offense). As the *Jizhilun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states: "Although the ten wholesome precepts may be repented, the three evil realms are not thereby eliminated," and so forth.

Regarding the two unwholesome minds—these arise from the three poisons—they refer to either knowing the characteristics of the precepts or studying them in ignorance (i.e., learning without true understanding), and thus treating the teachings with contempt.

[This refers to] the *Jālinī* [Sūtra]. It disparages the Buddha’s words. As stated in the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra* (Prakriyā-kaumudī): "There are four types of offenses committed with a coarse and evil intention:
first, a mind of turbid, heavy greed, hatred, and delusion; second, lack of faith in the retribution of karma; third, not cherishing the precepts one has received;

and fourth, treating the Buddha’s words with contempt. Thus, if one acts intentionally, one incurs a grave result. This text serves as proof that [the offense arises] from a lack of shame (*ahrīkya*).

Shame. To have no remorse or repentance from the outset is an unwholesome state of mind. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Killing an ant with a malicious intent is heavier than killing a human with a compassionate mind.
Because the fundamental karma is grave, the retribution is certain; even if one confesses and falls into a state of transgression (*pātayantika*), the karmic path is not eliminated.
As in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, after Devadatta had committed a *sthūlātyaya* by causing a schism in the Saṃgha, the Buddha ordered him to repent before the assembly;

yet, regarding the path of karma, he still fell into the Avīci hell. Thus, the *Niraya-sūtra* states: "First, the determination of the action performed; second, the determination of the experience of its fruit.

Even the majestic spiritual power (*mahānubhāva*) of all Buddhas cannot alter these. Regarding those who commit offenses with an *avyākṛta* (neutral) mind: this refers to those who originally lack restraint and protection, and who act according to the flow [of circumstances].

As for their nature: the mind is neither good nor evil; it acts in a general, indeterminate manner. For example, consider a bhikṣu who, while sitting, engages in lofty talk and empty discourse, wasting time and undermining his practice;
or one who lets his body and speech run wild, perhaps damaging plants, trees, earth, or soil with his hands and feet;

or one who acts as a matchmaker for the Sangha, misappropriates monastic property, keeps extra robes beyond the limit, enters among the laity at improper times, or touches monastic vessels with his hands—thus violating the decorum of body and speech. As...

These various categories collectively encompass all transgressions, with the sole exception of those committed while constantly maintaining a protective intent, or those created through error or delusion;
these are not driven by the mental afflictions (*kleśa*) and do not induce future karma. The Record states: "The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is largely distinct:

initially, inanimate matter is restricted to the indeterminate, whereas sentient beings encompass all three natures. Second, among sentient beings: resultant form (*vipāka-rūpa*) is indeterminate, while the mind encompasses all three natures. Third, within the mind:"
The three minds are restricted to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); the mind of practice (*caryā-citta*) permeates all three natures.

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), fascicle 2, upper, states: "To rely upon wholesome conditions to give rise to the teaching refers to such acts as sitting in meditation, reciting and chanting, lecturing and guiding, and bringing about awakening."
To dwell with right livelihood in one’s heart and thereby subdue the afflictions is what is called wholesome dharma (*kuśala-dharma*).

To instead hope for fame and profit while dwelling in wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*)—though its outward appearance may seem wholesome—it conversely becomes the poison of greed, which destroys the mind and obstructs the Path; nothing exceeds this [in its danger].

For this reason, the Great Sage established the teachings to prevent it. As for saying that the teachings were established because of unwholesome conditions, such as the ten non-virtues (*daśākuśala*), their essence is indeed [unwholesome].

It is unwholesome. Because it can extensively increase the afflictions and obstacles of the three miserable realms and hinder the Path, the Noble One established prohibitions based on its faults to prevent it.

Regarding the statement that "the teaching is initiated by relying on neutral conditions (*avyākṛta*)," this is like grass, trees, and the like: although their substance is neutral, if one repeatedly acts upon them without ceasing, it manifests outwardly as reproach and ugliness, and inwardly increases a distracted mind;

therefore, prohibitions were established to restrain such behavior, and the perpetrator incurs a *pāyattika* offense. (The *Shu* [Commentary] clarifies the "neutral" nature in terms of the object of the offense, while the *Chao* [Sub-commentary] relies on...)

[Regarding] "the mind capable of transgression": this clarifies the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature. Question: Why do the *Shu* (Commentary) and the *Chao* (Excerpts) differ on these two points? Answer: The *Shu* relies on the *Jingjiao* (Scriptural Teachings). Since the teachings are established based on objective conditions (*viṣaya-pratyaya*), it explains the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) in terms of those objective conditions.

The *Chao* clarifies that a practitioner’s transgression arises from the mind; although the mind has ten thousand variations, it does not go beyond three types. Thus, it explains the three natures in terms of the mind capable of transgression. Question: Why are both cited here? Answer: Although the scriptural teachings and the practice differ, they are both nothing other than demonstrations of characteristics; therefore, both are cited.
Chapter Seven: The Gate of the Characteristics of Precepts in Various Texts;
Chapter Eight: The Gate of Observance and Violation in Various Texts.
Although the monastic discipline is extensive, observance and violation constitute its primary tenet.
The *Shìchāo* (Zhōng sì) states: "In the Vinaya school, there is nothing other than upholding and violating [the precepts]. The characteristics of upholding and violating are profoundly deep;

unless one has accumulated learning to penetrate the subtle, exhausting the profound and exhausting the principles, this meaning is difficult to perceive. Therefore, throughout successive generations, they have followed one another without any alternative methods (*lù*).
Although there are slight differences in the paths taken, the general intent is not at variance. However, later students have become confused by miscellaneous teachings..."

Those who have not yet mastered the net [of the precepts] and have merely passed through the academy of learning do not know the beginning or the end. If one were to examine the rules of observance and transgression, by what means could they be recognized?

Nevertheless, the texts concerning observance and transgression permeate the entire body of the work; their names are established according to specific objects and are already contained within the *Suixiang* (Chapter on Following Characteristics).

Now, I shall attempt a general discussion based on the underlying principles to point out their essential framework, citing concrete examples to clarify them so that those who seek to study them may find it easy. The *Zizhi* says: "As for the term..."

Regarding the term "only" (kevala), there are two interpretations. First, based on the substance [of the offense], there arise courses of action; these courses of action may be compliant or contrary, thereby resulting in the distinction between observance and violation.

Since the conditions of sentient beings are not uniform, the prohibitions are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. These are subsumed under the designation of the *Vinaya Piṭaka* as the expressive means. When examining its original formulation:
This is not something explained separately; this is a general interpretation based on the fundamental teachings.

Furthermore, in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the initial listing of the monastic precepts for monks and nuns constitutes "abstention through observance" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*), whereas their transgression constitutes "offense through action. The subsequent twenty *khandakas* and so forth constitute "observance through action," wherein non-compliance constitutes "abstention through offense.

This is stated according to the broad outlines; however, if one considers how they mutually complement one another, then throughout the entirety of a single section, all four modes of conduct are present.
This is a detailed explanation based on the specific sections of the text.

Regarding the categories of cessation (*śamatha*), action, observance (*dhāraṇa*), and transgression (*atikrama*), I shall first explain their names (the meanings of the subsequent passages are largely consistent across the commentaries [Sūtra] and [Shō]; what is cited here is selected according to the meaning; the same applies to the two records).

The Commentary states: Regarding the term "restraint and observance" (*zhi-chí*): through skillful means and right mindfulness, one protects what has been originally received [as precepts], restraining body and speech so as not to commit any evils;

this is termed "restraint" (*zhǐ*). To restrain oneself and remain without transgressing the precepts, such that one's essence is luminous and pure and one accords with what was originally received, is termed "observance" (*chí*).

Since observance is accomplished by means of restraint, it is called the "precept of restraint and observance" (*zhì-chí-jì*), such as those in the first category [of the *Prātimokṣa*]. (The upper part indicates the nature of restraint and observance; the lower part cites the *Shū* [Commentary] to indicate "active observance" [*zuò-chí*]).

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: This [category] takes the non-performance of unwholesome dharmas as its primary principle. Since evil has already been abandoned, one must necessarily cultivate wholesome dharmas.

One must diligently exert the three karmas (*trikarma*) to practice the conduct of the precepts; when a wholesome state arises and is protected, it is termed "active" (*kāraṇīya*).
